+# Development security implementation patterns | Microsoft Learn
+
+This article provides practical implementation patterns for the [Development Security discipline](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-development). Use these patterns to integrate security into development environments, engineering workflows, and delivery pipelines while maintaining development velocity.
+
+These patterns are not a replacement for the [Microsoft Security Development Lifecycle](https://www.microsoft.com/securityengineering/sdl/), product documentation, or a workload-specific threat model. They provide a durable SAF-level bridge between development security strategy and technical implementation.
+
+## Use these patterns with the DevSecOps Capability Model
+
+The [DevSecOps Capability Model](/en-us/devops/devsecops/capability-model) and SAF are complementary:
+
+- Use the capability model to assess the maturity of software security practices and identify gaps.
+- Use SAF to connect improvements to business risk, cross-discipline dependencies, and operating-model decisions.
+- Use these patterns as repeatable approaches for closing the highest-priority gaps.
+
+Apply the patterns based on the risk and maturity of your organization and workloads. You do not need to implement every pattern at once.
+
+## Pattern 1: Secure developer environments and toolchains
+
+**Goal**: Reduce the risk that attackers compromise developer endpoints, identities, tools, extensions, or source-control workflows.
+
+Apply these practices:
+
+- Require phishing-resistant authentication where appropriate and enforce least privilege for developer and DevOps roles.
+- Use just-in-time access for privileged development and platform administration.
+- Harden and monitor developer endpoints, cloud development environments, and build systems.
+- Restrict tools, extensions, packages, and integrations to trusted publishers and approved scopes.
+- Protect important branches with review, approval, and policy checks.
+- Keep auditable records for privileged actions and code changes.
+- Include developer environments and source repositories in threat detection and incident-response planning.
+
+Reference guidance:
+
+- [Secure the developer environment for Zero Trust](/en-us/security/zero-trust/develop/secure-dev-environment-zero-trust)
+- [Branch policies in Azure DevOps](/en-us/azure/devops/repos/git/branch-policies)
+- [Reviewing the audit log in GitHub Enterprise Cloud](https://docs.github.com/enterprise-cloud@latest/organizations/keeping-your-organization-secure/managing-security-settings-for-your-organization/reviewing-the-audit-log-for-your-organization)
+
+## Pattern 2: Harden the code-to-production path
+
+**Goal**: Prevent attackers from using repositories, pipelines, artifacts, or deployment automation as a privilege-escalation or software supply-chain path.
+
+Apply these practices:
+
+- Map and document how a change moves from a repository to each deployment environment.
+- Record which branches, identities, pipelines, approvals, service connections, and artifacts can affect production.
+- Protect pipeline definitions and infrastructure-as-code files as production-impacting code.
+- Require independent review and approval for high-risk release actions.
+- Make artifacts immutable where practical and preserve provenance from source through deployment.
+- Scan code, dependencies, secrets, infrastructure as code, and deployment configurations.
+- Generate and retain a software bill of materials when required by risk, customer, or regulatory needs.
+- Keep cloud authorization and CI/CD authorization aligned so that a pipeline cannot bypass the intended access model.
+
+A simple code-to-production access table can make hidden deployment paths visible. Include the branch, whether review is required, the target environment, who can approve, and the identity used for deployment. Store this documentation with the code and update it as the workflow changes.
+
+Reference guidance:
+
+- [Secure the DevOps platform environment for Zero Trust](/en-us/security/zero-trust/develop/secure-devops-platform-environment-zero-trust)
+- [Secure your Azure Pipelines](/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/security/overview)
+- [Securing your end-to-end supply chain](https://docs.github.com/code-security/supply-chain-security/end-to-end-supply-chain/end-to-end-supply-chain-overview)
+
+## Pattern 3: Use federated workload identity instead of pipeline secrets
+
+**Goal**: Replace static credentials with short-lived, explicitly scoped trust relationships.
+
+Apply these practices:
+
+- Configure OpenID Connect (OIDC) federation between CI/CD platforms and cloud identity providers.
+- Scope trust conditions to specific organizations, repositories, branches, environments, and workflows.
+- Apply least privilege to service principals and workload identities.
+- Separate identities for build, test, and production deployment when their privileges differ.
+- Store any remaining secrets in managed secret stores, rotate them, and scan repositories and artifacts for exposure.
+- Treat internal repositories as potentially accessible to an attacker who has compromised an identity or endpoint. Do not use repository privacy as a secret-management control.
+
+Reference guidance:
+
+- [Workload identity federation in Microsoft Entra](/en-us/entra/workload-id/workload-identity-federation)
+- [Configuring OpenID Connect in Azure for GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/secure-your-work/security-harden-deployments/oidc-in-azure)
+- [Azure Key Vault basics](/en-us/azure/key-vault/general/basic-concepts)
+
+## Pattern 4: Validate security throughout the lifecycle
+
+**Goal**: Find issues early, verify important controls before release, and use production feedback to improve future releases.
+
+Apply these practices:
+
+- Use threat modeling and secure design review while the architecture can still change.
+- Run code, dependency, secret, configuration, and infrastructure-as-code checks in development and CI/CD.
+- Tune tools to reduce false positives and define a clear path for expert help and triage.
+- Establish risk-based release criteria for unresolved security findings.
+- Revalidate important controls before release instead of assuming earlier checks always succeeded.
+- Monitor applications, pipelines, identities, and supporting infrastructure in production.
+- Feed vulnerabilities, incidents, penetration tests, postmortems, and operational findings back into design standards and backlog priorities.
+- Include security in blameless postmortems so teams can improve systems and processes without discouraging disclosure.
+
+Reference guidance:
+
+- [Embed Zero Trust security into your developer workflow](/en-us/security/zero-trust/develop/embed-zero-trust-dev-workflow)
+- [Shift DevOps to DevSecOps](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-development-security)
+- [Adopt secure development planning imperatives](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-development-imperatives)
+
+## Pattern 5: Align cloud and CI/CD authorization end to end
+
+**Goal**: Prevent privilege bypass by keeping identity and authorization governance consistent across cloud resources and delivery systems.
+
+Apply these practices:
+
+- Use Microsoft Entra groups as a primary control point for cloud and CI/CD access where supported.
+- Prefer group-based assignments over direct user-to-role grants.
+- Align CI/CD roles with cloud role-based access control intent. For example, a person who cannot write to production in the cloud should not be able to trigger an unrestricted production deployment through the pipeline.
+- Review both direct and indirect privilege paths, including repository administration, pipeline triggers, service connections, environment approvals, artifact replacement, and branch-policy changes.
+- Separate routine engineering access from administrative and emergency access.
+- Use emergency access only through controlled break-glass paths with logging, approval, and post-use review.
+- Include pipeline and repository permissions in recurring access reviews.
+
+Reference guidance:
+
+- [Workload identity federation in Microsoft Entra](/en-us/entra/workload-id/workload-identity-federation)
+- [Best practices for Azure RBAC](/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/best-practices)
+- [Default permissions and access for Azure DevOps](/en-us/azure/devops/organizations/security/permissions-access)
+- [Managing people's access to your organization with roles in GitHub](https://docs.github.com/organizations/managing-peoples-access-to-your-organization-with-roles)
+
+## Pattern 6: Right-size assurance to business risk
+
+**Goal**: Apply stronger assurance where compromise can cause greater harm without forcing every workload through the same process.
+
+Apply these practices:
+
+- Establish a standard production baseline that applies to all workloads.
+- Define additional controls for high-impact workloads based on business criticality, data sensitivity, privilege, external exposure, customer impact, safety, and regulatory obligations.
+- Allow streamlined paths for lower-risk work only when the residual risk is understood and owned.
+- Treat prototype or urgent-release exceptions as temporary states, not permanent profiles.
+- Require every exception to have a named risk owner, compensating controls where practical, an expiration date, and a remediation plan.
+- Reassess the workload when its users, data, privileges, exposure, dependencies, or business importance change.
+- Use the workload's threat model and operational evidence to adjust the required assurance over time.
+
+This pattern helps teams preserve delivery speed while keeping the level of review and control proportional to the potential impact.
\ No newline at end of file

+# SecOps implementation patterns | Microsoft Learn
+
+This article is part of the **Microsoft Security Adoption Framework (SAF)**. It captures practical implementation patterns for the [SecOps discipline](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-security-operations).
+
+Use these patterns to connect SecOps mission and operating model guidance to concrete implementation decisions.
+
+## Pattern 1: Centralize visibility across technology areas
+
+**Goal**: Ensure investigation and response teams can correlate signals across identity, endpoints, applications, data, infrastructure, network, and AI.
+
+Apply these practices:
+
+- Ingest telemetry from core platforms into a central investigation and correlation layer.
+- Normalize and retain key security signals for incident reconstruction.
+- Prioritize data sources required for high-value business scenarios.
+
+Reference guidance:
+
+- [Technology guidance for SecOps](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-operations-technology)
+- [Microsoft Sentinel documentation](/en-us/azure/sentinel/)
+- [Integrate Microsoft Defender XDR into security operations](/en-us/defender-xdr/integrate-microsoft-365-defender-secops)
+
+## Pattern 2: Standardize detection, triage, and investigation workflows
+
+**Goal**: Reduce response-time variability and improve analyst effectiveness.
+
+Apply these practices:
+
+- Use repeatable playbooks for common incident classes.
+- Define escalation paths between triage, investigation, and specialized responders.
+- Tune alert quality continuously to reduce analyst fatigue.
+
+Reference guidance:
+
+- [Plan incident response](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-security-operations-incidents)
+- [Incident response playbooks overview](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-operations-incident-response-playbooks)
+
+## Pattern 3: Phase automation from assisted to autonomous response
+
+**Goal**: Improve speed and consistency without creating uncontrolled automation risk.
+
+Apply these practices:
+
+- Start with analyst-assisted automation for high-confidence actions.
+- Expand to auto-remediation only after validation and quality review.
+- Track false-positive and false-remediation rates as guardrail metrics.
+
+Reference guidance:
+
+- [Automated investigation and response in Microsoft Defender XDR](/en-us/defender-xdr/m365d-autoir)
+- [Respond to security alerts in Microsoft Defender for Cloud](/en-us/azure/defender-for-cloud/managing-and-responding-alerts)
+
+## Pattern 4: Operationalize threat intelligence and hunting
+
+**Goal**: Detect attacker behavior that evades static detections.
+
+Apply these practices:
+
+- Turn intelligence into detection logic and hunting hypotheses.
+- Run recurring hypothesis-driven hunts for priority attacker techniques.
+- Feed hunt and incident outcomes back into detection engineering.
+
+Reference guidance:
+
+- [Investigate incidents with Microsoft Sentinel](/en-us/azure/sentinel/investigate-incidents)
+- [Microsoft Entra security operations guide](/en-us/entra/architecture/security-operations-introduction)
+
+## Pattern 5: Close the loop with posture and architecture teams
+
+**Goal**: Convert incident learnings into risk reduction and design improvement.
+
+Apply these practices:
+
+- Formalize feedback from incidents into posture-remediation priorities.
+- Coordinate with architecture and development disciplines on recurring attack paths.
+- Measure impact reduction over time (dwell time, containment time, recurrence).
+
+Reference guidance:
+
+- [Establish a SecOps discipline](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-security-operations)
+- [Avoid SecOps antipatterns](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-security-operations-common-issues)
+
+## Product documentation coverage review
+
+Legacy content that treated SecOps as a technology pillar was reviewed against current product documentation.
+
+| Former step area | Current product-documentation coverage | Status |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| Automated investigation/remediation | [Defender XDR Automated investigation and response](/en-us/defender-xdr/m365d-autoir) | Covered (legacy link path changed) |
+| Attack surface reduction control guidance | [Defender for Endpoint attack surface reduction overview](/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-overview) | Covered (legacy link path changed) |
+| Sentinel SIEM/SOAR platform guidance | [Microsoft Sentinel documentation](/en-us/azure/sentinel/) | Covered (legacy marketing URLs now redirect) |
+| Microsoft Threat Protection branding references | Current product family uses Microsoft Defender XDR naming | Outdated terminology |
+| Cross-domain SecOps operating patterns in SAF discipline context | Product docs cover tooling, but normalized SAF pattern layer was not explicit | Gap addressed in this article |

+# AI security in the Security Adoption Framework | Microsoft Learn
+
+Artificial intelligence (AI) has a transformational effect on security, driving large and small changes across business scenarios, security disciplines, technologies, and security operations.
+
+Organizations need to manage several changes at the same time: attackers are using AI to improve and accelerate attacks, businesses are rapidly adopting AI to drive growth and efficiency, AI technology introduces new security risks and control requirements, and security teams can use AI to improve the speed and effectiveness of security work.
+
+The Microsoft Security Adoption Framework (SAF) helps organizations address these changes as part of the existing security program rather than creating a separate AI security program. Use this page to understand how AI changes security and find the SAF business scenarios, technologies, workshops, disciplines, and other guidance that can help you manage those changes.
+
+## How AI changes security
+
+AI affects security in four connected ways:
+
+- **Attackers use AI** - Threat actors adopt new technologies quickly because they aren't constrained by the legal, regulatory, moral, and organizational considerations that legitimate organizations face. Attackers use AI to enhance and accelerate existing techniques, including social engineering, phishing, deepfakes, analysis of stolen data, and attack automation. SAF helps organizations strengthen the strategy, architecture, controls, and operational capabilities needed to manage this increased speed, scale, and quality of attacks.
+- **Businesses embrace AI to drive growth and efficiency** - Business leaders are rapidly adopting AI technology to improve existing activities and create new capabilities. Security must enable these opportunities while identifying and managing the additional business risk they introduce. Use the [Adopt and secure AI](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-scenario-secure-ai) business scenario to coordinate the security changes needed across the organization.
+- **AI technology must be secured** - Protect AI-enabled applications and agents against abuse by external threat actors and insiders, including inadvertent errors and malicious use. AI applications, models, agents, identities, data, tools, and infrastructure become part of the technology estate that organizations need to protect. Generative AI is different from classic deterministic computing, and autonomous agents create additional considerations because they can perform actions without a human overseeing every step.
+- **AI enhances security technology and processes** - AI can automate or improve security work that previously required significant human effort, including posture analysis, vulnerability prioritization, detection, investigation, and response. Organizations should use this capability to increase security speed and effectiveness while preserving human judgment, expertise, accountability, and oversight for consequential decisions.
+
+Note
+
+Most AI systems also contain conventional applications, infrastructure, identities, data, and deterministic code. AI security considerations are added to existing security considerations rather than replacing them.
+
+## Understand the AI technology you are securing
+
+AI includes several technologies with different functions, security characteristics, and risks.
+
+### Machine learning
+
+Machine learning (ML) uses algorithms and data to make decisions or predictions without being explicitly programmed for every task. ML helps scale human expertise over datasets that would be difficult or impossible to analyze manually or by using static queries.
+
+The two main types of machine learning are:
+
+- **Supervised ML** - Analysis is performed on a representative dataset, and the model is trained to make decisions or predictions based on data labeled by human subject-matter experts. The trained model can then apply that expertise at scale to large datasets and real-time streams such as telemetry, logs, pictures, audio, and video.
+- **Unsupervised ML** - Analysis finds patterns and anomalies in unlabeled data, including clusters, repeating patterns, and deviations from normal behavior. Human experts can then assess whether the results are benign, malicious, interesting, or actionable.
+
+[![Diagram comparing supervised and unsupervised machine learning.](../media/concepts/ai-ml-types.png)](../media/concepts/ai-ml-types.png#lightbox)
+
+For all machine learning, validate the quality and security integrity of the data. Errors, bias, manipulation, or malicious data poisoning can produce incorrect results at scale. Supervised machine learning also depends on the quality of the labels and the expertise of the people performing the labeling.
+
+Both supervised and unsupervised machine learning are commonly used in security products to analyze large volumes of telemetry, identify vulnerabilities, detect attacks, find anomalies, and prioritize action.
+
+### Generative AI
+
+Generative AI builds on machine learning to provide more advanced data analysis and generate new data that resembles its training and grounding data. This technology includes large language models (LLMs), small language models (SLMs), and other model types.
+
+**Generative AI is dynamic.** Most classic computing is deterministic: it produces the same output when provided the same input and state. Generative AI produces outputs dynamically based on models, prompts, context, data, parameters, and other inputs.
+
+This changes how humans interact with computers and enables software to perform tasks that previously required human interpretation or judgment. It also creates security considerations such as prompt injection, unsafe output, sensitive-data disclosure, manipulation of model behavior, and misuse of connected tools and services.
+
+### AI agents
+
+AI agents combine generative AI with deterministic components, identities, data, applications, and tools to perform tasks with varying degrees of autonomy.
+
+The defining security consideration is **autonomy**: an agent can take actions without a human supervising every step. Organizations must carefully manage what agents are authorized to do, what information and systems they can access, and how their actions are monitored.
+
+[![Diagram showing generative AI components, deterministic code, and access to systems and data as parts of an AI agent.](../media/concepts/ai-genai-agents.png)](../media/concepts/ai-genai-agents.png#lightbox)
+
+Organizations should expect to be accountable for the actions and decisions of AI agents operating on their behalf. Apply least privilege, constrain authorized use cases, establish clear ownership, and monitor agent behavior so autonomy doesn't amplify risk beyond acceptable levels.
+
+## Securing AI technology
+
+Generative AI and autonomous agents introduce additional security considerations beyond classic security:
+
+- **Classic code** requires integrating security during the design, implementation, and operation of software.
+- **Generative AI** adds dynamic software execution, dependence on data integrity and classification, and risk from social trickery and manipulation through inputs.
+- **Autonomous agents** add risk from autonomous execution, requiring careful scoping of authority, strict application of least privilege, monitoring, and intervention capabilities.
+
+[![Diagram showing how security responsibilities expand from classic software to generative AI and autonomous agents.](../media/concepts/ai-security-evolution-agents.png)](../media/concepts/ai-security-evolution-agents.png#lightbox)
+
+Use the [AI technology guidance](/en-us/security/saf/technologies/ai/overview) for detailed guidance on AI applications and systems, models, agents and agent identities, prompts and context, grounding and training data, tools and connectors, communications, hosting infrastructure, and other AI dependencies.
+
+## Use SAF to manage AI security
+
+AI security isn't a single technical control or security discipline. It requires coordinated work across business decisions, security disciplines, technology controls, and operations.
+
+SAF provides several ways into this work depending on the problem you're trying to solve.
+
+### Start with your business outcome
+
+Use the [Adopt and secure AI](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-scenario-secure-ai) business scenario when your organization is introducing AI and needs to balance business opportunity, adoption speed, and security risk.
+
+The scenario helps business, security, and technology stakeholders understand the outcome they are trying to achieve and coordinate the changes required across security disciplines and technologies.
+
+Other SAF business scenarios remain relevant because AI depends on and interacts with the existing technology estate. Organizations still need to protect critical business assets, minimize damage from security incidents, and continuously improve security posture as AI adoption expands.
+
+### Secure AI as a technology
+
+Use the [AI technology guidance](/en-us/security/saf/technologies/ai/overview) when you need to determine what must be protected in AI systems and where security controls need to apply.
+
+AI security also depends on other SAF technology areas, including identity, applications, data, endpoints, infrastructure, and network.
+
+### Coordinate security work across disciplines
+
+AI creates work across many [SAF security disciplines](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-overview) rather than becoming a separate discipline.
+
+For example:
+
+- **Strategy, integration, and governance** establishes priorities, accountability, policy, risk decisions, and measures of success.
+- **Security architecture** establishes trust boundaries and end-to-end control patterns for AI and classic systems.
+- **Access and identity** governs human, workload, and agent identities and applies least privilege.
+- **Data security** discovers, classifies, protects, and governs information used by people, applications, models, and agents.
+- **Development security** integrates threat modeling, secure engineering, testing, and release controls into AI-enabled applications.
+- **Security posture management** discovers AI assets and exposure, prioritizes risk, and measures improvement.
+- **Security operations (SecOps)** detects attacks and misuse involving AI while using AI itself to improve detection, investigation, and response.
+
+These disciplines help organizations integrate AI security into the operating model they already use to manage security risk.
+
+### Use the Zero Trust Workshop for detailed AI security planning
+
+Use the [AI security guidance in the Microsoft Zero Trust Workshop](/en-us/security/zero-trust/workshop-zero-trust-ai-security) when you need a structured technical planning exercise for securing AI implementations.
+
+The workshop helps teams examine areas such as AI risk and posture, agent lifecycle governance, authentication and access, data protection, network and service access, secure development, and detection and response.
+
+The workshop complements SAF rather than creating a separate framework: SAF organizes the broader security outcomes and work, while the workshop provides a focused way to plan AI security controls and implementation.
+
+## AI security transformation
+
+AI is changing both what organizations need to secure and how security work gets done. Microsoft describes several current [AI security transformation themes](/en-us/security/saf/scenarios/ai-security/overview) that can help leaders communicate and prioritize these changes:
+
+- **Secure your foundations** - Reduce preventable exposure across posture, identity, secrets, data, development, infrastructure, and governance so AI adoption doesn't amplify existing weaknesses.
+- **Defend with agents** - Use AI and agents to increase defensive speed and quality across posture management, detection, investigation, and response while preserving appropriate human judgment and oversight.
+- **Secure your agentic insider** - Treat autonomous agents as powerful actors inside the environment. Constrain their identities, privileges, data access, tools, actions, and autonomy so their behavior remains within policy and risk boundaries.
+
+These themes are a useful strategic lens, but they don't create a separate security framework or permanent taxonomy. Use SAF to translate them into durable business outcomes, security work, technology controls, and implementation priorities.
+
+## Where to go next
+
+Use the path that best matches the question you're trying to answer:
+
+- **How do we adopt AI rapidly without introducing unacceptable business risk?** Start with the [Adopt and secure AI](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-scenario-secure-ai) business scenario.
+- **What AI systems, agents, data, identities, and dependencies do we need to protect?** Use the [AI technology guidance](/en-us/security/saf/technologies/ai/overview).
+- **How do we plan detailed security controls for AI?** Use the [AI security guidance in the Microsoft Zero Trust Workshop](/en-us/security/zero-trust/workshop-zero-trust-ai-security).
+- **How does AI change our existing security program?** Use the relevant [SAF security disciplines](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-overview) and the [AI security transformation themes](/en-us/security/saf/scenarios/ai-security/overview).
+- **How do we implement the controls?** Follow the [technical solutions](/en-us/security/zero-trust/implement-overview) and Microsoft product guidance linked from the relevant SAF technology and discipline pages.
+- **How do SFI lessons relate to this work?** Use the [SAF mapping of Secure Future Initiative lessons](/en-us/security/saf/foundations/sfi/saf-mapping) to connect Microsoft's internal security transformation experience with customer security adoption.
\ No newline at end of file

+# Security Foundations for SAF | Microsoft Learn
+
+Security Foundations in the Microsoft Security Adoption Framework (SAF) provide the durable context behind modernization decisions.
+
+They explain **why** specific security priorities matter, **how** they relate to Microsoft and industry guidance, and **where** to apply them across business scenarios, security disciplines, and technology implementation.
+
+## What Security Foundations are
+
+Security Foundations are the cross-cutting principles, lessons, and reference models that shape SAF guidance.
+
+Use Security Foundations to:
+
+- Align strategy, architecture, operations, and implementation decisions
+- Prioritize high-impact actions without creating parallel frameworks
+- Keep modernization efforts coherent as threats, technology, and business priorities evolve
+
+## What this section covers
+
+This section focuses on foundational topics that influence security decisions across SAF:
+
+- Foundational security laws that capture durable realities about security controls, attackers, people, process, and technology to help teams test assumptions and make informed risk tradeoffs across SAF
+- Zero Trust principles and their practical application
+- Post-quantum readiness and cryptographic agility
+- AI security considerations in modernization programs
+- Security roles, responsibilities, and accountability models
+- Microsoft Secure Future Initiative (SFI) lessons and priorities
+
+## How to use Security Foundations
+
+1. Start with your priority [business scenario](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-business-scenarios-overview).
+2. Use Security Foundations to guide decisions in each [security discipline](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-overview).
+3. Implement through [technology guidance](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/overview) and [technical solutions](/en-us/security/zero-trust/implement-overview), then continuously refine through posture and SecOps feedback loops.

+# Plan cryptographic agility and post-quantum readiness | Microsoft Learn
+
+This article is part of the Microsoft Security Adoption Framework (SAF) concept and reference guidance.
+
+Post-quantum readiness is primarily a cryptographic agility challenge: your organization must be able to discover, prioritize, and update cryptographic dependencies over time at enterprise scale.
+
+Cryptographic agility is the ability of an organization to rapidly and safely change which cryptographic algorithms it uses. Building this capability is foundational for becoming quantum-safe.
+
+The likelihood is increasing that quantum computing will eventually defeat some current cryptographic algorithms that underpin technical controls across modern environments. This topic is commonly referred to as post-quantum cryptography (PQC).
+
+## How this impacts security and organizational risk
+
+If quantum-capable attackers can break vulnerable public-key cryptography in use, they can undermine trust in core security controls and significantly increase organizational risk.
+
+Cryptography provides foundational trust for much of the technology environment. Authentication, digital signatures, software integrity, and secure communications such as TLS depend directly on cryptography, while many other security controls depend indirectly on those capabilities. This means post-quantum readiness affects far more than encryption: it can affect identities, applications, infrastructure, devices, software updates, communications, and the trust relationships between them.
+
+PQC readiness affects almost all security domains because authentication, signing, and encryption are embedded across:
+
+- Cloud and on-premises applications
+- Identity and access systems
+- Security service edge (SSE) and VPN infrastructure
+- Network, storage, and platform infrastructure
+- IoT and OT systems
+- Partner and supply-chain integrations
+
+## What causes this challenge
+
+Current cryptography depends on hard mathematical problems that are practical in one direction and difficult to reverse with classical computing.
+
+Quantum computing changes this balance for some algorithm families. As capability matures, organizations need to:
+
+1. Identify vulnerable algorithms and dependencies.
+2. Replace them with quantum-resistant alternatives.
+3. Maintain readiness to evolve again as standards and implementation guidance continue to mature.
+
+This is why cryptographic agility is critical, not optional.
+
+The objective isn't only to replace today's vulnerable algorithms. Organizations need the ability to change cryptography repeatedly as standards, threats, implementations, and cryptanalytic understanding evolve. **PQC creates the immediate migration need; cryptographic agility creates the durable ability to adapt as cryptography changes again.**
+
+## How urgent is quantum-safe planning
+
+Two factors make early action important:
+
+- **Transition lead time is long**: large estates need multiyear planning, dependency mapping, and phased rollout.
+- **Harvest now, decrypt later risk exists now**: long-lived sensitive data can be captured today and decrypted later.
+
+At an operational level, becoming quantum-safe is a large-scale software, hardware, and infrastructure modernization program. Cryptography is embedded throughout operating systems, applications, services, protocols, certificates, libraries, firmware, devices, and partner dependencies. Organizations should therefore treat PQC readiness as a multiyear migration rather than a single cryptographic upgrade.
+
+Starting early can also help organizations avoid resource and supply constraints as adoption accelerates. Some changes might require only software or configuration updates, while others might require new libraries, firmware, certificates, hardware, or replacement of systems whose vendors no longer provide suitable updates. Many organizations could need the same specialized products and services at roughly the same time.
+
+This creates a dynamic similar to preparing for a natural disaster: organizations that prepare early can obtain the resources they need deliberately, while organizations that wait until urgency is widespread might face shortages, higher costs, limited alternatives, and increased exposure to low-quality products or scams.
+
+Delaying increases the chance of compressed timelines, supplier constraints, and rushed implementation risk.
+
+## SAF approach for PQC readiness
+
+Use SAF to coordinate cross-functional execution:
+
+1. **Strategy and governance**: establish ownership, sponsorship, priorities, and risk tolerance.
+2. **Architecture**: build enterprise cryptography and trust-chain inventory and dependency maps.
+3. **Disciplined execution**: sequence changes by risk, business criticality, and attack-path impact.
+4. **Operations and validation**: monitor rollout quality, regressions, and control effectiveness.
+
+## Planning a quantum-safe program
+
+A practical transition plan should include:
+
+1. **Discover** where vulnerable algorithms are used and which systems depend on them.
+2. **Evaluate** vendor and platform support timelines for quantum-resistant options.
+3. **Plan** phased migration waves and rollback-safe change windows.
+4. **Implement** with governance, testing, and evidence tracking.
+
+Additional planning considerations:
+
+- **Treat this as a program**: PQC readiness spans multiple teams and disciplines.
+- **Prepare for different update types** - Migration paths can vary significantly. Some dependencies can be addressed through software or configuration updates, while others might require new cryptographic libraries, certificates, firmware, hardware, or replacement of systems whose vendors no longer provide suitable updates. Track vendor support and quantum-resistant implementation timelines as part of migration planning.
+- **Prioritize strategically**: focus first on high-value assets, identity/control planes, core trust services, and long-sensitivity data paths.

+# Map CIS Controls and CIS Benchmarks to SAF | Microsoft Learn
+
+The Center for Internet Security (CIS) publishes two related but different forms of guidance:
+
+- **CIS Controls v8.1** provide a prioritized set of cybersecurity practices and 153 Safeguards. They help organizations decide **what security work to perform**.
+- **CIS Benchmarks** provide prescriptive, consensus-based configuration recommendations for specific technologies and product families. They help technology owners decide **how to configure an in-scope technology securely**.
+
+The Microsoft Security Adoption Framework (SAF) helps organizations assign the work to appropriate roles and disciplines, apply it across technologies, and connect it to architecture and implementation guidance.
+
+Important
+
+CIS remains the authoritative source for CIS Controls, Safeguards, Implementation Groups, and Benchmarks. This mapping doesn't replace CIS guidance, certify a configuration, or demonstrate that a CIS outcome has been achieved.
+
+## Use CIS Controls and Benchmarks for different decisions
+
+| Guidance | Primary question | Unit of work | SAF use |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| **CIS Controls v8.1** | Which cybersecurity practices and Safeguards should the organization implement and prioritize? | Organization-level Controls and Safeguards | Connect outcomes to business context, security disciplines, accountable and responsible roles, technologies, and measurable improvement work. |
+| **CIS Benchmarks** | How should a particular technology or service be securely configured? | Technology-specific configuration recommendations | Establish an approved security baseline, assign implementation to technology owners, validate compatibility, manage exceptions, and monitor configuration drift. |
+
+## Map the 18 CIS Controls to SAF work and role actions
+
+Role names follow [Security roles and responsibilities in SAF](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-roles).
+
+| CIS Control v8.1 | Primary SAF work | Typical role actions |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| **1. Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets** | Security Posture Management; Infrastructure Security; OT/IoT Security | Product Owners identify business ownership and criticality. Infrastructure/Platform, User Endpoint, Network, and OT/ICS roles maintain inventories and lifecycle state. Security Posture Management measures coverage, unmanaged assets, and remediation. |
+| **2. Inventory and Control of Software Assets** | Security Posture Management; Infrastructure Security; Development Security | Technical engineering and operations roles maintain authorized software inventories and enforcement. Software/Application Architects and development roles identify required software and dependencies. Security Posture Management identifies unauthorized or unsupported software and tracks remediation. |
+| **3. Data Protection** | Data Security; Access and Identity; Security Architecture | Data Officer/Data Governance and Product Owners identify data value, use, and obligations. Data Architects and Access Architects define classification, access, protection, retention, and handling patterns. Data and Identity roles implement them; Security Posture Management measures coverage. |
+| **4. Secure Configuration of Enterprise Assets and Software** | Security Architecture; Infrastructure Security; Development Security; Security Posture Management | Architects establish approved baselines. Technology owners test, implement, and operate configurations. Automation Engineers scale enforcement. Security Posture Management measures conformance, drift, exceptions, and risk. |
+| **5. Account Management** | Access and Identity; Security Posture Management | Access Architects define account lifecycle patterns. Identity roles and application/platform owners implement provisioning, review, and deprovisioning. Product Owners validate business need. Posture roles measure stale, shared, and unmanaged accounts. |
+| **6. Access Control Management** | Access and Identity; Security Architecture | Accountable business and technology owners approve access requirements. Access Architects define policy patterns. Identity, Network, Application, Data, and Infrastructure roles enforce least privilege and separation of duties. Posture and audit roles validate effectiveness. |
+| **7. Continuous Vulnerability Management** | Security Posture Management; Infrastructure Security; Development Security | Security Posture Management prioritizes vulnerability and attack-path risk. Infrastructure/Platform, User Endpoint, Software Security Engineering, and development roles remediate. Product Owners make authorized tradeoffs and fund durable fixes. |
+| **8. Audit Log Management** | SecOps/SOC; Security Architecture; technical engineering and operations | Security Architects and Detection Engineers define telemetry requirements. Technology owners enable and protect logs. SecOps Platform and Data Engineers collect, normalize, retain, and monitor data. Triage and Investigation Analysts use it during operations. |
+| **9. Email and Web Browser Protections** | Infrastructure Security; Access and Identity; SecOps/SOC | User Productivity and Support, User Endpoint, Identity, and Security Engineer roles implement protections. Detection Engineers and analysts monitor abuse and tune detections. Security Education and Engagement reduces human-targeted risk. |
+| **10. Malware Defenses** | Infrastructure Security; SecOps/SOC | User Endpoint, Infrastructure/Platform, and Security Engineer roles deploy and maintain prevention controls. Detection Engineers tune detections. Triage, Investigation, Threat Hunting, and Reverse Engineering roles investigate and respond. |
+| **11. Data Recovery** | Business Management and Operations; Infrastructure Security; Data Security; SecOps/SOC | Product Line Managers/Directors and Product Owners set recovery priorities and acceptable service impact. Infrastructure/Platform and Data roles implement protected recovery capabilities and test restoration. SecOps/SOC coordinates recovery after attacks. |
+| **12. Network Infrastructure Management** | Infrastructure Security; Access and Identity; Security Architecture | Network and Infrastructure roles maintain supported assets and secure configurations. Access and Infrastructure Architects define segmentation, management, and administrative-access patterns. Posture roles measure exposure and drift. |
+| **13. Network Monitoring and Defense** | SecOps/SOC; Infrastructure Security | Network roles provide enforceable control points and telemetry. SecOps Platform and Data Engineers integrate signals. Detection Engineers, Threat Hunters, Triage, and Investigation Analysts detect and respond to threats. |
+| **14. Security Awareness and Skills Training** | Strategy, Integration, and Governance | Security Education and Engagement designs role-specific learning. Human Resources and Organizational Readiness/Training integrate it into workforce processes. Leaders reinforce expected behavior and accountability. Managers verify that people have the skills required for assigned responsibilities. |
+| **15. Service Provider Management** | Strategy, Integration, and Governance; Security Architecture | Cyber Supply Chain Risk Management, Procurement and Acquisition, Legal, Product Owners, and architects identify requirements, evaluate providers, establish contract and assurance expectations, and monitor material provider risk. |
+| **16. Application Software Security** | Development Security; Security Architecture | Software/Application Architects and Software Security Engineers define secure design and engineering requirements. Developers, Software Testers, Software Testing/Quality Managers, and DevOps Leads implement and verify them throughout the lifecycle. |
+| **17. Incident Response Management** | SecOps/SOC; Strategy, Integration, and Governance; cross-functional disciplines | Incident Coordination and Management maintains plans and coordinates response. Analysts, hunters, forensics, reverse engineering, and technical owners investigate and contain. Business leaders, Legal, Communications/Public Relations, Human Resources, and other partners execute authorized business actions. |
+| **18. Penetration Testing** | SecOps/SOC; Security Architecture; Security Posture Management | Attack Simulation roles plan and conduct authorized testing. Architects and technology owners interpret findings and remediate systemic issues. Security Posture Management tracks risk reduction and recurrence. Accountable owners approve scope and risk treatment. |
+
+This table identifies the primary SAF work and role actions. Use the applicable CIS Safeguards as the authoritative requirements and assign local accountability through SAF roles.
+
+## Map CIS Benchmark work to SAF roles
+
+Use the applicable CIS Benchmark as the configuration source. SAF helps assign configuration work across the roles responsible for the technology and its security. Security and technology architects establish the baseline, Product Owners and other accountable leaders provide business context and approve risk decisions, and engineering and operations roles implement and maintain the configuration. Security Posture Management measures conformance and drift, SecOps/SOC roles investigate related security events, and compliance and audit roles validate applicable obligations and evidence.
\ No newline at end of file

+# Map NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 to SAF | Microsoft Learn
+
+Organizations use the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 to understand, assess, prioritize, and communicate cybersecurity outcomes. The Microsoft Security Adoption Framework (SAF) helps organize the work and role actions needed to move from current to target outcomes.
+
+Use the models together without treating them as structurally equivalent:
+
+- **NIST CSF 2.0** defines cybersecurity outcomes and provides a common language for managing cybersecurity risk.
+- **Zero Trust principles** inform security decisions across the lifecycle.
+- **SAF business scenarios, security disciplines, technologies, and technical solutions** connect risk and desired outcomes to coordinated planning and execution.
+- **Microsoft technologies and services** can implement parts of that work, but product deployment alone doesn't demonstrate achievement of a CSF outcome.
+
+Important
+
+NIST remains the authoritative source for the CSF. This mapping is interpretive guidance for using CSF 2.0 with SAF; it isn't a NIST endorsement, a control mapping, or evidence of compliance.
+
+## Understand the CSF 2.0 operating model
+
+CSF 2.0 has three complementary components:
+
+- **Core**: A taxonomy of cybersecurity outcomes organized into Functions, Categories, and Subcategories. The six Functions are GOVERN, IDENTIFY, PROTECT, DETECT, RESPOND, and RECOVER.
+- **Organizational Profiles**: A way to describe an organization's current and target cybersecurity outcomes. Use a Current Profile and Target Profile to identify and prioritize gaps in organizational context.
+- **Tiers**: A way to characterize the rigor of cybersecurity risk governance and management practices. Use Tiers as context for improvement and communication, not as a simplistic maturity score or certification level.
+
+The Core describes **what outcomes matter**. Profiles identify **where the organization is and where it intends to go**. Tiers help leaders discuss **how consistently cybersecurity risk is governed and managed**. SAF helps define **who acts, what work they perform, and where implementation applies**.
+
+## Connect CSF Functions to SAF work and roles
+
+Role names in this mapping follow the role model used in [Security roles and responsibilities in SAF](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-roles), which is based on The Open Group Security Roles and Glossary material.
+
+| NIST CSF 2.0 Function | Primary SAF work | Typical role actions | Technology scope |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| **GOVERN (GV)** | Strategy, Integration, and Governance; Security Architecture; Security Posture Management | Members of the Board of Directors and executive, product, and business leaders set priorities, risk tolerance, and accountability. Security Business Architects/Analysts, Security Compliance Management, Cyber Supply Chain Risk Management, and Security Posture Management translate direction into policy, roadmaps, measures, and oversight. Chief, Enterprise, and Security Architects establish architectural direction. | Cross-cutting across all technologies |
+| **IDENTIFY (ID)** | Security Posture Management; Security Architecture; Strategy, Integration, and Governance | Product and Business Line Leaders, Product Owners, and Business Architects/Analysts identify critical business operations and assets. Security Posture Management measures exposure and gaps. Security Architects and technical engineering and operations roles maintain inventories, dependencies, ownership, and risk context. | Identities, Endpoints, Apps, Data, Infrastructure, Network, AI, and OT/IoT where applicable |
+| **PROTECT (PR)** | Access and Identity; Data Security; Development Security; Infrastructure Security; OT/IoT Security; Security Architecture | Security, Access, Infrastructure, Data, Solution, and Software/Application Architects define reusable patterns and requirements. Identity, Network, User Endpoint, Infrastructure/Platform, Data, OT/ICS, and Security Engineers implement and operate safeguards. Software Security Engineers and development roles build protections into applications and delivery processes. Security Posture Management measures control coverage and drift. | All technologies, based on the assets and business processes in scope |
+| **DETECT (DE)** | Security Operations (SecOps/SOC); Security Posture Management; Security Architecture | SecOps Platform and Data Engineers provide reliable telemetry and analytics. Detection Engineers design and test detections. Threat Intelligence informs priorities. Triage and Investigation Analysts validate and investigate activity. Security Architects ensure telemetry and detection requirements are designed into systems. | Cross-cutting across all technologies |
+| **RESPOND (RS)** | Security Operations (SecOps/SOC), with affected business, technology, legal, communications, and governance roles | Incident Coordination and Management orchestrates the response. Triage and Investigation Analysts, Threat Hunters, Digital Forensics Specialists, and Reverse Engineers determine scope and impact. Technical engineering and operations roles contain and remediate. Accountable leaders make authorized business and risk decisions; Legal and Communications/Public Relations manage their respective obligations. | Cross-cutting, driven by affected assets and business operations |
+| **RECOVER (RC)** | Business Management and Operations; Infrastructure Security; Data Security; SecOps/SOC; Security Posture Management; Security Architecture | Product Line Managers/Directors and Product Owners set business restoration priorities. Technical engineering and operations roles restore services and data to a trusted state. Incident Coordination and Management coordinates recovery. Investigation and Digital Forensics roles preserve evidence and lessons. Posture and architecture roles feed corrective actions into baselines, designs, and roadmaps. | Primarily Infrastructure, Data, Identities, and Apps, with dependencies across the estate |
+
+These are typical actions, not a universal RACI model. Assign one accountable decision-maker for each material outcome, delegate responsibilities explicitly, and document escalation and exception paths.
+
+## Use CSF Categories as a navigation layer
+
+Use the Category-level mapping to find the primary SAF work and continue to detailed implementation guidance.
+
+| CSF Function and Categories | Primary SAF security disciplines | Useful SAF starting points |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| **GOVERN** (GV.OC, GV.RM, GV.RR, GV.PO, GV.OV, GV.SC) | Strategy, Integration, and Governance; Security Architecture; Security Posture Management | [Strategy, Integration, and Governance](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-strategy), [Security Architecture](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-architecture), [security roles](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-roles) |
+| **IDENTIFY** (ID.AM, ID.RA, ID.IM) | Security Posture Management; Security Architecture; Strategy, Integration, and Governance | [Security Posture Management](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-posture), [technologies](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/overview), [Zero Trust assessment](/en-us/security/zero-trust/assessment/overview) |
+| **PROTECT** (PR.AA, PR.AT, PR.DS, PR.PS, PR.IR) | Access and Identity; Data Security; Development Security; Infrastructure Security; OT/IoT Security; Security Architecture | [Security disciplines](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-overview), [technologies](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/overview), [technical solutions](/en-us/security/zero-trust/implement-overview) |
+| **DETECT** (DE.CM, DE.AE) | Security Operations (SecOps/SOC); Security Posture Management; Security Architecture | [SecOps/SOC](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-security-operations), [SecOps operating patterns](/en-us/security/saf/disciplines/security-operations/implementation-patterns), [SecOps roles](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-security-operations-roles) |
+| **RESPOND** (RS.MA, RS.AN, RS.CO, RS.MI) | SecOps/SOC; Strategy, Integration, and Governance; affected technical disciplines | [Incident response readiness](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-operations-incident-response-readiness), [incident response playbooks](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-operations-incident-response-playbooks) |
+| **RECOVER** (RC.RP, RC.CO) | Business Management and Operations; Infrastructure Security; Data Security; SecOps/SOC; Security Posture Management | [Minimize business damage from security incidents](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-scenario-minimize-impact), [Infrastructure Security](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-infrastructure), [Using SAF effectively](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-journey) |
+
+## Use Profiles and Tiers with SAF
+
+Use this operating flow to turn a CSF assessment into coordinated work:
+
+1. **Set scope and business context.** Identify the business operations, assets, dependencies, risk owners, and decision authority in scope.
+2. **Create or update the Current Profile.** Record applicable CSF outcomes and the evidence that describes the current state.
+3. **Define a risk-informed Target Profile.** Select and prioritize outcomes based on mission, threats, legal and contractual obligations, dependencies, and risk tolerance.
+4. **Use Tiers as governance context.** Discuss how repeatable, integrated, and adaptive cybersecurity risk-management practices need to be for the scope. Don't use Tiers as a pass/fail score.
+5. **Map gaps to SAF.** Connect each material gap to a business scenario, security discipline, technology, accountable role, and responsible roles.
+6. **Choose architecture and implementation changes.** Use reference architectures, technical solutions, and product guidance to design the required people, process, and technology changes.
+7. **Execute and measure.** Track implementation, control effectiveness, business impact, exceptions, and residual risk.
+8. **Reassess and improve.** Update Profiles, architecture, operations, and roadmaps as business priorities, technologies, threats, and evidence change.
+
+## Avoid common mapping errors
+
+- Don't convert every CSF outcome directly into a product feature. Many outcomes depend on governance, architecture, operating processes, and human decisions.
+- Don't map every Function to every discipline without identifying the primary work and role actions. Broad applicability is different from primary ownership.
+- Don't treat a Target Profile as a fixed end state. Review it when business context or risk changes.
+- Don't treat Tiers as maturity certifications or use them to rank organizations without context.
+- Don't use framework alignment as a substitute for measuring security effectiveness and residual risk.
\ No newline at end of file

+# Map The Open Group Zero Trust model to SAF | Microsoft Learn
+
+The Open Group Security Forum develops security and Zero Trust guidance that describes security capabilities, architecture principles, roles, and Architecture Building Blocks (ABBs). These provide a useful external reference model for connecting business and security outcomes to architecture, security work, and technology.
+
+The Microsoft Security Adoption Framework (SAF) connects this material to SAF business scenarios, security disciplines, technologies, and roles, and then to Microsoft architecture and implementation guidance.
+
+Important
+
+The Open Group remains the authoritative source for its standards and reference models. Some Zero Trust material is published as standards, while other material is available as evolving Snapshots. The guidance on this page is Microsoft-authored and doesn't change or extend The Open Group publications.
+
+## Map Zero Trust capabilities to SAF
+
+The Open Group Zero Trust model describes capabilities that combine people, processes, and technology to achieve security outcomes across governance, asset management, prevention, detection, response, recovery, and continuous improvement.
+
+[![The Open Group Zero Trust capabilities mapped across the NIST Cybersecurity Framework functions Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover.](media/open-group-zero-trust-capabilities-nist.png)](media/open-group-zero-trust-capabilities-nist.png#lightbox)
+
+The capability model provides a useful bridge to SAF because both models organize security around durable outcomes and security work rather than individual products.
+
+[![Detailed view of The Open Group Zero Trust capabilities for asset-centric security.](media/open-group-zero-trust-capabilities.png)](media/open-group-zero-trust-capabilities.png#lightbox)
+
+The following mapping identifies the primary SAF discipline for each capability.
+
+| The Open Group capability | Primary SAF disciplines | Typical role actions |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| **Integrated Defense and Risk Management** | Strategy, Integration, and Governance; Security Architecture; Security Posture Management; SecOps/SOC | Accountable business leaders set risk appetite and priorities with security leadership. Security and technology leaders and practitioners translate that direction into security strategy and execution, coordinate work across disciplines, and measure results. |
+| **Security Strategy, Integration, and Governance (SIG)** | Strategy, Integration, and Governance; Security Architecture | The CISO leads security strategy and governance with Security Directors and Security Business Architects/Analysts. They coordinate with technology executives, business and product leaders, risk and compliance stakeholders, and other accountable decision-makers to align security priorities with business objectives and risk, establish direction, and translate it into policy, roadmaps, architecture, measures, and oversight. |
+| **Secure Asset Management** | Security Architecture; Security Posture Management | Product Owners and Business Architects/Analysts identify business operations, assets, criticality, and owners. Technical roles maintain lifecycle state. Architects define protection patterns. Security Posture Management measures exposure and control coverage. |
+| **Security Posture Management** | Security Posture Management | Security Posture Management identifies exposures and attack paths, prioritizes improvement, and verifies remediation. Product and technology owners implement or authorize treatment. |
+| **Asset-Centric Security Operations** | SecOps/SOC | SecOps Platform and Data Engineers provide data and platforms. Detection Engineers and Threat Intelligence improve coverage. Triage, Investigation, Threat Hunting, Forensics, Reverse Engineering, Incident Coordination, and technical owners detect, respond, and recover. |
+| **Identity and Adaptive Access Management** | Access and Identity | Access Architects define policy and enforcement patterns. Identity, Network, User Endpoint, Application, and Platform roles implement them. Product Owners authorize business access. Security Posture Management and SecOps/SOC monitor effectiveness and abuse. |
+| **Data Security** | Data Security; Access and Identity | Data Officer/Data Governance and Product Owners define value and obligations. Data and Access Architects design controls. Data, Identity, Application, and Platform roles implement them. |
+| **Security Zones** | Security Architecture; Infrastructure Security; Access and Identity | Security, Access, and Infrastructure Architects define boundaries and enforcement. Network, Infrastructure/Platform, Identity, and Security Engineers implement segmentation and monitor policy. |
+| **Privileged Access and High Value Assets** | Access and Identity; Security Architecture | Business and product leaders identify high-value assets and accountable owners. Access and Security Architects define privileged pathways. Identity, Endpoint, Network, and Platform roles implement them. SecOps/SOC monitors attack paths and activity. |
+| **Software and DevSecOps** | Development Security; Security Architecture | Software/Application Architects, Software Security Engineers, Developers, Software Testers, Software Testing/Quality Managers, and DevOps Leads build and operate secure development and delivery practices. |
+
+## Map security roles to SAF
+
+The Open Group Security Roles and Glossary provides a common vocabulary for describing security work and distinguishes accountability for security outcomes from responsibility for performing security work.
+
+SAF uses this role model to connect security outcomes and disciplines to the people who make decisions and perform the work. Organizations can combine responsibilities across people, teams, service providers, automation, and agents while preserving appropriate accountability and decision authority.
+
+[![Current security accountability and responsibility role groups across an organization, including leadership, business, architecture, development, engineering and operations, governance, and SecOps roles.](media/open-group-security-roles.png)](media/open-group-security-roles.png#lightbox)
+
+For the SAF role model and guidance, see [Security roles and responsibilities in SAF](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-roles).
+
+## Map Architecture Building Blocks to Microsoft technologies
+
+The Open Group Zero Trust Reference Model uses Architecture Building Blocks (ABBs) to describe process and technology capabilities used to implement Zero Trust.
+
+The following mappings connect selected ABBs to Microsoft technologies that can provide corresponding capabilities. These are Microsoft-authored implementation examples, not part of The Open Group model.
+
+### Asset-Centric Security Operations Platform (ACSOP)
+
+[![Microsoft technology mapping to Asset-Centric Security Operations Platform Architecture Building Blocks ACSOP-1.3 through ACSOP-1.3.10.](media/open-group-acsop-abb-microsoft.png)](media/open-group-acsop-abb-microsoft.png#lightbox)
+
+| ABB number | Architecture Building Block | Level | Microsoft technology examples |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| **ACSOP-1.3** | SecOps Data Analysis and Automation Platform | 2 | All Level 3 ABBs below |
+| **ACSOP-1.3.1** | Case Management Platform | 3 | Microsoft Defender XDR; Microsoft Sentinel |
+| **ACSOP-1.3.2** | SecOps Business Intelligence (BI) Platform | 3 | Microsoft Power BI |
+| **ACSOP-1.3.3** | Extended Detection and Response (XDR) | 3 | Microsoft Defender XDR; Microsoft Agent 365; Microsoft Defender for Cloud |
+| **ACSOP-1.3.4** | Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) | 3 | Microsoft Sentinel |
+| **ACSOP-1.3.5** | Security Data Lake | 3 | Microsoft Sentinel data lake |
+| **ACSOP-1.3.6** | SecOps Automation Platform (SOAR) | 3 | Microsoft Defender XDR (AutoIR); Microsoft Sentinel |
+| **ACSOP-1.3.7** | Technical Anomaly Platform (machine learning, reverse engineering, and related analytics) | 3 | Microsoft Defender; Microsoft Defender for Cloud |
+| **ACSOP-1.3.8** | Behavior Anomaly Platform (UEBA) | 3 | Microsoft Defender; Microsoft Sentinel |
+| **ACSOP-1.3.9** | Threat Intelligence Platform (TIP) | 3 | Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence; Microsoft Security Copilot |
+| **ACSOP-1.3.10** | SecOps AI and Agent Platform | 3 | Microsoft Security Copilot; Project Perception (preview) |
+
+The Microsoft Security Architecture Design Session for SecOps/SOC also includes guidance related to ACSOP-1.1 SecOps Core Reactive Processes and ACSOP-1.2 SecOps Proactive Processes ABBs.
+
+### Identity and Adaptive Access Management Platform (IAAMP)
+
+[![Microsoft technology mapping to Identity and Adaptive Access Management Platform Architecture Building Blocks IAAMP-1.2 through IAAMP-1.3.7.](media/open-group-iaamp-abb-microsoft.png)](media/open-group-iaamp-abb-microsoft.png#lightbox)
+
+| ABB number | Architecture Building Block | Level | Microsoft technology examples |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| **IAAMP-1.2** | Adaptive Access Control Platform | 2 | Microsoft Entra |
+| **IAAMP-1.2.1** | Adaptive Policy Information Point (PIP) | 3 | Microsoft Entra ID Protection; Microsoft Defender XDR; Microsoft Intune; Microsoft Purview |
+| **IAAMP-1.2.2** | Adaptive Policy Decision Point (PDP) | 3 | Microsoft Entra Conditional Access |
+| **IAAMP-1.2.3** | Adaptive Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) | 3 | Microsoft Entra Conditional Access; Microsoft Entra Private Access and Internet Access; Microsoft Intune; Microsoft Purview Information Protection and Data Loss Prevention |
+| **IAAMP-1.2.4** | Adaptive Policy Manager | 3 | Microsoft Entra Conditional Access |
+| **IAAMP-1.2.5** | Policy Signal Source | 3 | Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft Entra ID Protection; Microsoft Intune; Microsoft Defender XDR |
+| **IAAMP-1.3** | Identity, Key, and Access Management Platform | 2 | Microsoft Entra |
+| **IAAMP-1.3.1** | Identity Provider (IDP) | 3 | Microsoft Entra ID; Active Directory |
+| **IAAMP-1.3.2** | Identity Lifecycle Management Platform | 3 | Microsoft Entra ID Governance; Microsoft Agent 365 |
+| **IAAMP-1.3.3** | Application Consent Management Platform | 3 | Microsoft Entra ID |
+| **IAAMP-1.3.4** | Personal Data Consent Management Platform | 3 | Microsoft Priva Consent Management |
+| **IAAMP-1.3.5** | Certificate and Key Management Platform | 3 | Azure Key Vault; Active Directory Certificate Services; Microsoft Identity Manager Certificate Manager |
+| **IAAMP-1.3.6** | Authenticated Network Access Control Platform | 3 | Microsoft Entra Private Access and Internet Access; Azure VPN |
+| **IAAMP-1.3.7** | Workload and Agent Authorization Mechanisms | 3 | Microsoft Azure; Microsoft 365; Microsoft Dynamics 365; Microsoft Entra Agent ID; custom workload and agent RBAC, ABAC, and permission models |
+
+Use these mappings to connect The Open Group architecture to SAF security work and then to applicable Microsoft architecture, technical solutions, and product guidance. Because the Zero Trust Reference Model is currently published as a Snapshot, review these mappings as The Open Group publishes updated material.
