+# What's new in Microsoft security guidance | Microsoft Learn
+
+Use this page to discover significant customer-visible updates across the Microsoft Security Guidance Center and find guidance that can help you improve strategy, architecture, implementation plans, engineering, and security operations.
+
+Microsoft's [Secure Future Initiative (SFI)](../../zero-trust/sfi/secure-future-initiative-overview) is Microsoft's internal security transformation program. The [Microsoft Security Adoption Framework (SAF)](../../zero-trust/security-adoption-model) is customer-facing guidance informed by applicable SFI lessons, Zero Trust principles, and security best practices.
+
+## November 2026
+
+### Accelerate and measure Zero Trust
+
+- The [Microsoft Zero Trust Workshop](../../zero-trust/workshop-zero-trust-overview) provides a web-based planning experience across eight Workshop pillars, including DevSecOps. It helps business, security, and technology stakeholders turn current-state discussions, technical findings, risks, and dependencies into a prioritized implementation roadmap.
+- The [Zero Trust Assessment](../../zero-trust/assessment/overview) is a complementary source of programmatically generated findings for supported configurations. Use its results when evidence from the environment can improve prioritization. The Workshop covers eight pillars; the current Assessment evaluates seven and doesn't include a DevSecOps assessment.
+
+### Plan security adoption and architecture
+
+- The [Microsoft Security Adoption Framework (SAF)](../../zero-trust/security-adoption-model) more clearly connects business priorities and risk to business scenarios, security disciplines, technologies, and technical solutions. This structure helps organizations move from desired security outcomes to coordinated security work and implementation.
+- The [Microsoft Cybersecurity Reference Architectures (MCRA)](../../zero-trust/microsoft-reference-architecture) and [SAF technology guidance](../../zero-trust/deploy/overview) make architecture and implementation routes easier to discover and connect durable security concepts with the technologies that implement them.
+
+### Secure AI adoption
+
+- The [AI security transformation themes in SAF](../scenarios/ai-security/overview) connect emerging AI security priorities to durable practices: strengthen security foundations, use agents and automation to increase defensive speed and scale, and apply appropriate controls to AI agents and agentic systems.
+- The [AI security Workshop pillar](../../zero-trust/workshop-zero-trust-ai-security) helps teams organize planning across identities, data, applications, infrastructure, agents, and operations and turn the work into a prioritized roadmap.
+
+### Use standards and framework mappings
+
+- The [security standards and frameworks hub](../../zero-trust/security-standards-and-frameworks) provides a discovery path from external frameworks and models into relevant SAF and Microsoft guidance without treating a framework as a product deployment plan.
+- Updated mappings cover the [NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0](../framework-mappings/nist-cybersecurity-framework), [CIS Controls and Benchmarks](../framework-mappings/cis-controls-benchmarks), [The Open Group Zero Trust](../framework-mappings/open-group-zero-trust), [CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model](../../zero-trust/cisa-zero-trust-maturity-model-intro), and [DoD Zero Trust Strategy](../../zero-trust/dod-zero-trust-strategy-intro). The mappings connect desired outcomes to SAF disciplines, technologies, and implementation guidance while preserving each framework's scope.
+
+### Strengthen security operations and development security
+
+- The [SAF SecOps discipline](../../zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-security-operations) and [SecOps Workshop pillar](../../zero-trust/workshop-zero-trust-security-operations) provide clearer routes from operating-model decisions to telemetry, detection, investigation, response, threat hunting, automation, and continuous improvement.
+- The [SAF Development Security discipline](../../zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-development-security) and [DevSecOps Workshop pillar](../../zero-trust/workshop-zero-trust-devsecops) connect secure engineering governance with identities, repositories, dependencies, pipelines, software supply chains, deployments, and operational feedback.
+
+### Apply Microsoft security best practices
+
+- The [Microsoft security best practices overview](../../zero-trust/security-best-practices-overview) brings together practical guidance across strategy, governance, architecture, implementation, and operations. Use these patterns as implementation input and adapt them to your organization's risks, architecture, regulatory obligations, capabilities, and resources.
+
+## Secure Future Initiative progress and lessons for customers
+
+The [Secure Future Initiative (SFI)](../../zero-trust/sfi/secure-future-initiative-overview) is a multiyear Microsoft security transformation program focused on improving how Microsoft designs, builds, tests, and operates products, services, and infrastructure.
+
+SFI combines changes across culture, governance, engineering, and operations. It applies **Secure by Design**, **Secure by Default**, and **Secure Operations**, together with Zero Trust principles, across six engineering pillars. The updates and lessons below preserve the customer-relevant content from the former separate SFI What's New feed.
+
+### Track ongoing progress
+
+The latest SFI progress report was published in July 2026. It describes continued progress across the six SFI engineering pillars and highlights how Microsoft is adapting its security approach as threats, technologies, and AI capabilities evolve.
+
+The July 2026 report describes three broad areas of progress:
+
+- **Secure foundations:** Strengthen identity, tenant, network, engineering, inventory, and telemetry foundations and continuously validate their effectiveness.
+- **Proactive defense:** Detect and mitigate threats earlier by combining threat intelligence, security research, automation, AI, centralized telemetry, and faster response.
+- **Future-ready security:** Prepare security architecture and engineering for changes such as AI agents, post-quantum cryptography, confidential computing, and evolving attacker capabilities.
+
+Across these areas, Microsoft's experience reinforces a consistent lesson: effective security depends on reinforcing controls across identities, applications, data, infrastructure, networks, engineering systems, and operations rather than isolated security controls.
+
+For detailed status, metrics, and objective-level progress, see the [July 2026 SFI progress report](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/trust-center/security/secure-future-initiative/sfi-progress-report-july-2026). Earlier reports are also available:
+
+- [November 2025 SFI progress report](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/trust-center/security/secure-future-initiative/sfi-progress-report-november-2025)
+- [April 2025 SFI progress report](https://cdn-dynmedia-1.microsoft.com/is/content/microsoftcorp/microsoft/final/en-us/microsoft-brand/documents/sfi-april-2025-progress-report.pdf)
+- [September 2024 SFI progress report](https://cdn-dynmedia-1.microsoft.com/is/content/microsoftcorp/microsoft/final/en-us/microsoft-brand/documents/SFI_September_2024_progress_report.pdf)
+
+### Security in the age of AI
+
+AI changes both the threat landscape and the speed of security work, but it doesn't replace fundamental security practices.
+
+Attackers can use AI to accelerate vulnerability discovery, identify attack paths, and scale operations. Defenders can use the same advances to identify weaknesses earlier, improve detection, accelerate investigations, and respond at machine speed where appropriate.
+
+This shift increases the importance of strong security foundations. Identity controls, asset inventory, secure architecture, telemetry, segmentation, secure engineering, and operational discipline provide the context and control points that AI-enabled defense depends on.
+
+Organizations should also reconsider the boundary between manual and automated security work. Agents, automation, tools, and people can each perform the work they're best suited to perform. Automation and agents can perform suitable repeatable analysis, investigation, and response at greater speed and scale, while people continue to provide judgment, expertise, oversight, and accountability where required.
+
+These changes connect to the [AI security transformation themes in SAF](../scenarios/ai-security/overview): strengthening security foundations, using agents and automation to increase defensive speed and scale, and applying appropriate security controls to AI agents and agentic systems.
+
+### Secure foundations
+
+The latest SFI work reinforces that security foundations must operate as a system of reinforcing controls.
+
+#### Identity and secrets
+
+Microsoft continues to strengthen identity as a primary security control plane. SFI work includes phishing-resistant multifactor authentication, hardware protection for cryptographic keys, standardized identity libraries, reduction of long-lived credentials, stronger token validation, and preparation for post-quantum cryptography.
+
+A key lesson is that identity protection includes more than users. Workload identities, applications, credentials, certificates, tokens, and cryptographic keys all require controlled lifecycles and appropriate protection.
+
+#### Tenants and isolation
+
+Microsoft continues to reduce risk from unused tenants, applications, persistent privileges, unmanaged access paths, and other resources that can create lateral-movement opportunities.
+
+SFI emphasizes lifecycle governance from creation through retirement, secure defaults, least privilege, separation between production and nonproduction environments, and continuous removal of unnecessary access and resources.
+
+#### Networks and infrastructure
+
+SFI network improvements combine accurate asset inventory, identity-aware access, segmentation, secure configuration, and removal of unnecessary public exposure.
+
+Segmentation is part of a broader containment strategy. Identity, application, tenant, network, and infrastructure boundaries work together to restrict lateral movement and reduce blast radius when one control is bypassed.
+
+#### Engineering systems
+
+Microsoft continues to move secure engineering from optional guidance and reactive remediation toward governed development environments, standardized pipelines, secure deployment controls, software supply-chain protection, and security checks that operate throughout the development lifecycle.
+
+These practices help make secure engineering repeatable and easier to adopt consistently across large engineering organizations.
+
+### Continuously validate security
+
+Security foundations remain effective only when organizations can determine whether controls are still operating as intended.
+
+SFI investments in comprehensive inventory, standardized telemetry, centralized security data, enforced baselines, and detection of configuration drift illustrate the importance of continuous validation rather than relying only on periodic assessment.
+
+Continuous visibility helps security teams identify changes, detect gaps, investigate incidents, validate security controls, and prioritize remediation based on current conditions.
+
+This creates a feedback loop between security operations, security posture, architecture, engineering, and governance. Operational evidence can identify systemic weaknesses, and those findings can drive improvements to architectures, engineering practices, policies, and controls.
+
+### Proactive defense
+
+SFI continues to expand Microsoft's ability to find and address security weaknesses before attackers can exploit them. This work includes:
+
+- AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and validation.
+- Threat intelligence and proactive threat hunting.
+- Behavioral and baseline-driven detection.
+- Centralized security telemetry for investigation and hunting.
+- Faster vulnerability mitigation and remediation.
+- Greater automation of suitable detection, investigation, and response activities.
+- Increased transparency about vulnerabilities and security incidents.
+
+The goal isn't simply to add AI to existing manual processes. Organizations should redesign suitable security workflows so that agents, automation, tools, and people can work together to increase speed, consistency, and scale while preserving appropriate oversight and accountability.
+
+### Future-ready security
+
+Security architecture must also prepare for changes in technologies and threats.
+
+Recent SFI work includes preparation for post-quantum cryptography, increased use of hardware-backed protections and confidential computing, security controls for AI agents, improvements to platform integrity, and continued modernization of legacy authentication and cryptographic systems.
+
+These investments illustrate a broader principle: organizations should identify security dependencies that are difficult or slow to change and begin modernization before emerging threats or technology transitions make those changes urgent.
+
+### Progress across the SFI engineering pillars
+
+SFI continues to organize engineering execution around six pillars:
+
+| SFI engineering pillar | Current focus |
+| --- | --- |
+| **Protect identities and secrets** | Strengthen identity systems, credentials, cryptographic keys, authentication, workload identities, and preparation for post-quantum cryptography. |
+| **Protect tenants and isolate systems** | Govern tenant and application lifecycles, enforce least privilege, reduce persistent access, and prevent lateral movement across security boundaries. |
+| **Protect networks** | Maintain accurate inventory, reduce public exposure, strengthen segmentation, and apply secure network controls consistently. |
+| **Protect engineering systems** | Protect source code, development environments, build and release pipelines, software supply chains, and deployment processes. |
+| **Monitor and detect cyberthreats** | Improve inventory, telemetry, log retention, centralized investigation data, behavioral detection, and threat hunting. |
+| **Accelerate response and remediation** | Reduce time to mitigation, improve vulnerability transparency, automate suitable response activities, and strengthen customer communication during security incidents. |
+
+SFI pillars represent how Microsoft organizes and prioritizes its own security transformation. They aren't intended to replace Zero Trust, SAF, NIST CSF, or an organization's existing security governance model. For current objective-level status and metrics, use the latest SFI progress report as the authoritative source.
+
+### Apply lessons from SFI
+
+Organizations should use SFI as a source of Microsoft implementation experience rather than as a blueprint that must be reproduced exactly.
+
+Several lessons apply broadly:
+
+- **Strengthen foundations first.** Identity, inventory, architecture, telemetry, secure engineering, segmentation, and operational controls reinforce one another.
+- **Design security into systems and processes.** Move important controls earlier into architecture, engineering, deployment, and lifecycle management instead of relying primarily on later detection and remediation.
+- **Use secure defaults and paved paths.** Make secure practices easier to adopt consistently while allowing exceptions to be explicitly understood and governed.
+- **Continuously validate controls.** Detect configuration drift, missing telemetry, unmanaged assets, excessive privilege, and other gaps as operating conditions change.
+- **Connect operations back to improvement.** Use incidents, threat intelligence, hunting, posture findings, and attack simulation to improve architecture, engineering, governance, and controls.
+- **Use AI and automation where they improve security outcomes.** Automate suitable repeatable work while preserving human judgment, expertise, oversight, and accountability where required.
+- **Prepare for transitions before they become emergencies.** Long-running changes such as cryptographic modernization, identity modernization, and removal of legacy systems require sustained planning and investment.
+
+Explore implementation patterns for [phishing-resistant multifactor authentication](../../zero-trust/sfi/phishing-resistant-mfa), the [Safe Secrets Standard](../../zero-trust/sfi/safe-secrets-standard), [software supply-chain protection](../../zero-trust/sfi/protect-software-supply-chain), and [security log retention standards](../../zero-trust/sfi/security-log-retention-standards).
+
+Use [How Microsoft Secure Future Initiative (SFI) informs SAF](../foundations/sfi/saf-mapping) and [Apply lessons from SFI](../../zero-trust/sfi/secure-future-initiative-adoption) to translate applicable lessons into sustained outcomes based on your organization's business priorities, risks, roles, technologies, and implementation needs.
\ No newline at end of file

+# Defend with agents using SAF | Microsoft Learn
+
+**Defend with agents** is a current AI security transformation theme. The name can evolve, but the underlying objective is durable: increase the speed, reach, consistency, and quality of security operations without surrendering accountability or high-impact decisions to ungoverned automation.
+
+This page translates the theme into durable outcomes and execution paths. It does not create a separate operating model for AI-assisted security. Use the Microsoft Security Adoption Framework (SAF) to organize the work and canonical Microsoft guidance to implement it.
+
+## What this theme means
+
+Defend with agents means using AI-assisted and agentic capabilities to help security teams collect and correlate signals, detect suspicious behavior, prioritize risk, investigate incidents, recommend actions, and automate bounded response steps.
+
+AI changes the speed and scale at which security operations can work. Agents and automation can perform repeatable analysis, investigation, and response at machine speed, while people provide judgment, expertise, oversight, and accountability where these are required.
+
+Defending at machine scale is not simply adding AI to existing manual processes. Organizations should redesign suitable security workflows so that agents, automation, tools, and people each perform the work they are best suited to perform.
+
+Prioritize redesigned workflows and automations that reduce meaningful risk. Start with well-understood, repeatable activities, establish evidence and approval boundaries, and expand autonomy only when quality, resilience, and control are demonstrated.
+
+## Durable outcome
+
+The durable outcome is a measurable, resilient security operations capability in which people and AI work together under clear governance.
+
+Success looks like:
+
+- Relevant signals from identity, endpoints, applications, data, infrastructure, network, and AI systems are available for detection and investigation.
+- AI-assisted triage and investigation improve speed and consistency without obscuring evidence or decision rationale.
+- Automated actions have defined scope, prerequisites, approval requirements, rollback paths, and accountable owners.
+- High-impact containment and recovery decisions remain subject to appropriate human judgment and authorization.
+- Security teams measure detection quality, investigation time, containment time, false positives, automation reliability, and business impact.
+- Incident response includes AI systems and attacks that use AI, while continuing to address classic threats.
+- Lessons from incidents improve posture, architecture, development, policy, and future detection logic.
+
+## SAF work
+
+### Business scenarios
+
+Use these SAF business scenarios to define outcomes and priorities:
+
+- [Minimize damage from security incidents](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-scenario-minimize-impact) - Improve readiness, detection, containment, recovery, and learning.
+- [Protect critical business assets](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-scenario-secure-assets) - Prioritize monitoring and response around the assets that matter most to the business.
+- [Adopt and secure AI](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-scenario-secure-ai) - Include AI systems and agents in operational security and use AI safely as part of the defense.
+- [Strengthen posture and compliance](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-scenario-improve-posture) - Use operational evidence to reduce exposure before the next incident.
+
+### Security disciplines
+
+Coordinate the work across these SAF disciplines:
+
+- [SecOps](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-security-operations) owns the detection, investigation, response, recovery, and improvement mission.
+- [SecOps implementation patterns](/en-us/security/saf/disciplines/security-operations/implementation-patterns) provide repeatable approaches for putting the operating model into practice.
+- [Incident operations](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-security-operations-incidents) establish preparation, authority, coordination, and response processes.
+- [Security posture](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-posture) turns exposure and incident findings into prioritized prevention work.
+- [Security architecture](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-architecture) designs telemetry, control points, isolation paths, and resilient response patterns.
+- [Strategy, integration, and governance](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-strategy) defines risk tolerance, automation policy, accountability, and measures.
+- [Access and identities](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-identity-access), [Data](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-data), [Development](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-development), and [Infrastructure](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-infrastructure) provide the domain expertise needed for safe investigation and response.
+
+### Roles and collaboration
+
+Use [Security roles and responsibilities in SAF](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-roles) and [SecOps roles](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-security-operations-roles) to define accountability and escalation.
+
+The operating model depends on collaboration among:
+
+- Organizational leadership and incident leadership to set decision authority and business priorities.
+- SecOps/SOC analysts, threat hunters, incident responders, and detection engineers to supervise and improve agent-assisted workflows.
+- Security architecture and posture teams to convert operational learning into durable controls.
+- Identity, data, application, infrastructure, endpoint, and network teams to validate impact and execute domain-specific actions.
+- Application and product development teams to provide telemetry and safe response mechanisms for AI-enabled systems.
+- Legal, privacy, compliance, communications, and business continuity teams when incidents cross business or regulatory boundaries.
+
+### Technologies
+
+Agent-assisted defense is cross-cutting. Apply it across:
+
+- [AI](/en-us/security/saf/technologies/ai/overview)
+- [Identity](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/identity)
+- [Endpoints](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/endpoints)
+- [Applications](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/applications)
+- [Data](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/data)
+- [Infrastructure](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/infrastructure)
+- [Network](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/networks)
+
+The quality of AI-assisted defense depends on the quality, coverage, and context of the signals from these technologies.
+
+## Implementation and product guidance
+
+Use [Microsoft secure Zero Trust implementation solutions](/en-us/security/zero-trust/implement-overview) to connect operational outcomes to technical implementation. Start with the following canonical guidance:
+
+1. [Secure SecOps with Zero Trust](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/visibility-automation-orchestration) to integrate visibility, analytics, automation, and orchestration.
+2. [Plan SecOps incident operations](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-security-operations-incidents) to establish authority, process, communications, and decision paths.
+3. [Prepare for incident response](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-operations-incident-response-readiness) before increasing automation.
+4. [Use incident response playbooks](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-operations-incident-response-playbooks) to standardize repeatable actions and escalation.
+5. [AI security in the Microsoft Zero Trust Workshop](/en-us/security/zero-trust/workshop-zero-trust-ai-security) to include AI systems and agents in the response model.
+6. [Take the SecOps workshop](/en-us/security/zero-trust/workshop-zero-trust-security-operations) to align teams on end-to-end operational improvements.
+
+Use focused implementation guidance where the risk requires it:
+
+- [Implement AI observability](/en-us/security/zero-trust/sfi/observability-ai-systems)
+- [Rapid anomaly detection and response](/en-us/security/zero-trust/sfi/rapid-anomaly-detection-response)
+- [Centralize access to security logs](/en-us/security/zero-trust/sfi/centralize-access-to-security-logs)
+- [Respond to incidents in AI systems](/en-us/security/zero-trust/sfi/incident-response-ai-systems)
+- [Secure autonomous agentic AI systems](/en-us/security/zero-trust/sfi/secure-agentic-systems)
+- [Identify risk for autonomous agentic AI](/en-us/security/zero-trust/sfi/manage-agentic-risk)
+- [Defend against indirect prompt injection attacks](/en-us/security/zero-trust/sfi/defend-indirect-prompt-injection)
+- [Incidents and alerts in the Microsoft Defender portal](/en-us/defender-xdr/incidents-overview)
+- [Monitor Zero Trust with Microsoft Sentinel](/en-us/azure/sentinel/sentinel-solution)
+
+Introduce automation in bounded stages: recommend, require approval, automate low-impact actions, and then expand autonomy where evidence supports it. Keep detailed configuration steps in canonical product documentation, and use SAF to keep people, process, architecture, and technology aligned.

+# Secure your agentic insider with SAF | Microsoft Learn
+
+**Secure your agentic insider** is a current AI security transformation theme. The name can evolve, but the underlying challenge is durable: AI agents can use identities, access data, invoke tools, communicate with services and other agents, and take actions that affect business processes. Organizations must govern those capabilities as carefully as other trusted participants in the enterprise.
+
+The insider analogy helps communicate the combination of legitimate access and potential impact. It does not mean that an agent is a person or that every agent is malicious. It means that intended, mistaken, manipulated, or compromised agent behavior can create insider-style risk when access and actions are not bounded and monitored.
+
+This page translates the theme into durable outcomes and execution paths. It does not create a separate control framework. Use the Microsoft Security Adoption Framework (SAF) to organize the work and canonical Microsoft guidance to implement it.
+
+## What this theme means
+
+Secure your agentic insider means knowing which agents exist, who owns them, what identities they use, which data and tools they can access, what actions they can take, and how their behavior is monitored and constrained throughout the lifecycle.
+
+This work connects several familiar priorities: secure AI and data together, apply least privilege, protect secrets, govern the software and model supply chain, prevent unauthorized actions, and prepare to detect and respond when an agent is manipulated, drifts from intended behavior, or is compromised.
+
+Most of this work builds on established security foundations for identity, data, applications, development, infrastructure, posture, and operations. Agentic systems also introduce AI-specific risks involving delegated autonomy, tool use, memory, agent-to-agent interaction, and manipulation. Integrate protections for these risks into the existing foundations rather than treating agent security as a disconnected control model.
+
+## Durable outcome
+
+The durable outcome is an environment in which agent autonomy is deliberate, bounded, observable, and accountable.
+
+Success looks like:
+
+- Every production agent has a registered identity, accountable business owner, technical owner, purpose, risk classification, and lifecycle state.
+- Agent permissions are limited to the data, tools, connectors, services, and actions required for the intended task.
+- High-impact actions require stronger evidence, additional controls, or human authorization.
+- Sensitive data, prompts, context, memory, model inputs and outputs, and secrets are protected according to business risk.
+- Development teams threat-model agent workflows, validate trust boundaries, test failure modes, and secure dependencies before release.
+- Security teams can observe agent decisions and actions with enough context to investigate misuse, manipulation, drift, and compromise.
+- Response procedures can suspend identities, revoke tokens and secrets, isolate services, preserve evidence, and recover safely.
+- Governance continuously reassesses agents as models, data, tools, permissions, and business use change.
+
+## SAF work
+
+### Business scenarios
+
+Use these SAF business scenarios to define outcomes and priorities:
+
+- [Adopt and secure AI](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-scenario-secure-ai) - Establish guardrails and operating practices for safe AI adoption.
+- [Protect critical business assets](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-scenario-secure-assets) - Limit agent access and actions according to the business impact of assets and data.
+- [Secure and govern privileged access](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-scenario-privileged-access) - Protect control-plane access and other high-impact actions that agents or their operators can perform.
+- [Minimize damage from security incidents](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-scenario-minimize-impact) - Detect, contain, investigate, and recover from harmful agent behavior or compromise.
+- [Strengthen posture and compliance](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-scenario-improve-posture) - Continuously assess agent inventory, permissions, configuration, exposure, and policy coverage.
+
+### Security disciplines
+
+Coordinate the work across these SAF disciplines:
+
+- [Strategy, integration, and governance](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-strategy) defines acceptable use, autonomy boundaries, risk acceptance, policy, and accountability.
+- [Security architecture](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-architecture) defines agent trust boundaries, identity patterns, data flows, control points, and failure containment.
+- [Access and identities](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-identity-access) governs agent, workload, service, and human identities and applies least privilege.
+- [Data](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-data) protects prompts, context, memory, grounding data, outputs, and downstream information use.
+- [Development](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-development) integrates threat modeling, secure design, dependency controls, testing, deployment, and lifecycle management.
+- [Security posture](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-posture) inventories agents and exposure, validates policy coverage, and prioritizes gaps.
+- [Infrastructure](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-infrastructure) secures hosting environments, runtimes, models, tools, connectors, and supporting services.
+- [SecOps](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-security-operations) monitors behavior and coordinates investigation, containment, recovery, and improvement.
+
+### Roles and collaboration
+
+Use [Security roles and responsibilities in SAF](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-roles) to assign accountability and decision rights.
+
+The control model depends on collaboration among:
+
+- Organizational leadership and governance to define risk appetite and accountability for agent use.
+- Business and AI solution owners to define purpose, acceptable behavior, criticality, and business impact.
+- Security strategy, architecture, identity, data, privacy, and compliance teams to establish policy and reusable controls.
+- Application and product development teams to design, test, release, and maintain agent behavior safely.
+- Technical engineering and operations teams to run identity, data, platform, infrastructure, network, endpoint, and observability controls.
+- SecOps teams to detect anomalous behavior, investigate evidence, contain harmful actions, and coordinate recovery.
+- Legal, human resources, procurement, and third-party risk teams where agent actions, vendors, or data use cross organizational boundaries.
+
+### Technologies
+
+Start with [AI technology guidance](/en-us/security/saf/technologies/ai/overview), and apply connected controls across:
+
+- [Identity](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/identity) for agent identities, authentication, authorization, and lifecycle.
+- [Applications](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/applications) for APIs, plugins, connectors, tools, and runtime behavior.
+- [Data](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/data) for prompts, context, memory, grounding, training, inference, and outputs.
+- [Infrastructure](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/infrastructure) for hosting, models, compute, services, and isolation.
+- [Network](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/networks) for service paths, segmentation, filtering, and agent-to-agent communication.
+- [Endpoints](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/endpoints) where agents interact with user devices, local data, or device-bound applications.
+
+Agent risk emerges from the interaction among these technologies. Do not rely on a single AI-specific control to manage it.
+
+## Implementation and product guidance
+
+Use [Microsoft secure Zero Trust implementation solutions](/en-us/security/zero-trust/implement-overview) to connect the business outcome and operating model to technical controls. Start with the following canonical guidance:
+
+1. [Secure AI with Zero Trust](/en-us/security/saf/technologies/ai/overview) to map agent identities, data, tools, connectors, communications, and runtime controls.
+2. [AI security in the Microsoft Zero Trust Workshop](/en-us/security/zero-trust/workshop-zero-trust-ai-security) to align business, security, development, and operations stakeholders.
+3. [Discover AI apps and data](/en-us/security/security-for-ai/discover) to identify usage, applications, agents, owners, and data paths.
+4. [Protect AI apps and data](/en-us/security/security-for-ai/protect) to apply protection to AI applications, access, and information.
+5. [Govern AI for compliance](/en-us/security/security-for-ai/govern) to establish policy, oversight, and evidence.
+6. [Use Zero Trust security to prepare for AI companions, including Microsoft Copilots](/en-us/security/zero-trust/copilots/apply-zero-trust-copilots-overview) for Microsoft Copilot scenarios.
+
+Use focused implementation guidance across the agent lifecycle:
+
+- [Identify risk for autonomous agentic AI](/en-us/security/zero-trust/sfi/manage-agentic-risk)
+- [Secure autonomous agentic AI systems](/en-us/security/zero-trust/sfi/secure-agentic-systems)
+- [Least privilege for AI agents](/en-us/security/zero-trust/sfi/least-privilege-for-ai-agents)
+- [Manage memory safety in agentic systems](/en-us/security/zero-trust/sfi/manage-agentic-memory-safety)
+- [Complete AI threat modeling](/en-us/security/zero-trust/sfi/threat-modeling-ai)
+- [Defend against indirect prompt injection attacks](/en-us/security/zero-trust/sfi/defend-indirect-prompt-injection)
+- [Implement AI observability](/en-us/security/zero-trust/sfi/observability-ai-systems)
+- [Respond to incidents in AI systems](/en-us/security/zero-trust/sfi/incident-response-ai-systems)
+- [Safe Secrets Standard](/en-us/security/zero-trust/sfi/safe-secrets-standard)
+
+Keep detailed product configuration in canonical Microsoft documentation. Use this page to define the durable outcome, assign work through SAF, and route each team to the implementation guidance for the controls it owns.
\ No newline at end of file

+# AI security transformation themes in SAF | Microsoft Learn
+
+Organizations are now operating in a hybrid AI and classic security environment where they must manage both familiar risks and new AI-driven risks at the same time. A practical way to do this is to focus on three connected security themes: secure your foundations, defend with agents, and secure your agentic insider.
+
+This theme structure helps leaders and practitioners prioritize outcomes, explain tradeoffs, and coordinate execution across business, security, and technology teams. The operating imperative is balance: left-of-bang prevention and right-of-bang response, machine-speed automation and human judgment, and innovation and control.
+
+These themes reinforce each other. Strong security foundations make AI adoption safer and provide the identity, data, telemetry, architecture, and operational capabilities needed to use AI effectively in defense. Securing AI introduces new requirements that must be integrated into those foundations, while agents and automation can help security teams operate at greater speed and scale.
+
+SAF provides a durable execution model for turning changing security priorities into sustained outcomes. It connects business priorities and risk to security work, technologies, technical solutions, roles, and implementation guidance. Microsoft product guidance then provides the detailed steps for configuring and operating the required capabilities.
+
+Use [AI security in the Security Adoption Framework](/en-us/security/saf/foundations/ai-security-governance) to understand how these transformation themes connect to SAF business scenarios, security disciplines, technologies, the Microsoft Zero Trust Workshop, and implementation guidance.
+
+## Why these three themes matter
+
+- [Secure your foundations](/en-us/security/saf/scenarios/ai-security/security-foundations) focuses on risk reduction across posture, identity, secrets, data, and governance so AI adoption does not outpace control maturity.
+- [Defend with agents](/en-us/security/saf/scenarios/ai-security/agent-assisted-defense) focuses on defensive speed and quality so organizations can detect, investigate, and respond at machine tempo with human oversight.
+- [Secure your agentic insider](/en-us/security/saf/scenarios/ai-security/ai-agent-security) focuses on constraining autonomous behavior so AI identities, actions, and data access stay within policy and accountability boundaries.
+
+## How the themes relate to each other
+
+These themes are interdependent, not sequential silos. Foundations make trusted automation possible. Agent-assisted defense improves detection and response for both classic and AI-native threats. Agentic-insider controls ensure that increased automation and autonomy do not create unmanaged internal risk. Together they create a durable model that can scale AI safely.
+
+## How SAF enables execution
+
+SAF connects business priorities and risk to execution through four connected components:
+
+1. **Business scenarios** frame desired outcomes in plain language for business, security, and technology stakeholders.
+2. **Security disciplines** organize the security work needed to manage risk and deliver and sustain those outcomes.
+3. **Technologies** identify what must be protected across identity, endpoints, applications, data, infrastructure, network, and AI.
+4. **Technical solutions** translate requirements into product-level implementation and sustainable operations.
+
+Development and SecOps are security disciplines that shape and operate protections across technologies; they aren't technology pillars. Use [technology guidance](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/overview) to determine **where** controls apply and [technical solutions](/en-us/security/zero-trust/implement-overview) for **how** to implement and operate them.
+
+SFI provides important vendor transformation lessons and trust signals, while SAF provides the customer execution map. Use both together to connect strategy, foundations, and cutting-edge capabilities without creating a parallel framework.

+# Secure your foundations with SAF | Microsoft Learn
+
+**Secure your foundations** is a current AI security transformation theme. The name can evolve, but the underlying work remains necessary: understand what you have, reduce preventable exposure, protect identities and data, secure development and infrastructure, and establish clear governance before AI adoption increases scale and complexity.
+
+This page translates the theme into durable outcomes and execution paths. It does not create a separate implementation framework. Use the Microsoft Security Adoption Framework (SAF) to organize the work and canonical Microsoft guidance to implement it.
+
+## What this theme means
+
+Secure your foundations means improving the security of the environment that AI depends on and connects to. AI applications and agents inherit risk from existing identity, data, application, infrastructure, network, endpoint, and operational weaknesses. They can also amplify those weaknesses through speed, reach, and automation.
+
+**AI changes the threat landscape and the speed of security work, but it does not replace fundamental security practices.** Organizations need to address new AI-specific risks while continuing to strengthen the identity, data, application, development, infrastructure, network, endpoint, and operational practices that protect the enterprise.
+
+The practical objective is to secure now where risk is urgent, prioritize defenses that reduce the greatest business risk, and improve posture to get ready for AI. It also means treating secure AI and data as a continuous responsibility across the lifecycle, not as a one-time deployment gate.
+
+## Durable outcome
+
+The durable outcome is an enterprise foundation that can support AI innovation without accepting unmanaged risk.
+
+Success looks like:
+
+- AI applications, agents, identities, data sources, connectors, and owners are inventoried and governed.
+- Critical assets and sensitive data are identified, classified, and protected according to business impact.
+- Human, workload, and agent identities use strong authentication, least privilege, and lifecycle governance.
+- Security teams can measure exposure, configuration, vulnerability, and control coverage across the estate.
+- Development and platform teams use secure patterns for AI applications, agents, APIs, models, tools, and dependencies.
+- Business, security, and technology leaders have clear ownership, decision rights, and exception processes.
+- Posture and operational signals drive a continuous improvement loop rather than a point-in-time compliance exercise.
+
+## SAF work
+
+### Business scenarios
+
+Use these SAF business scenarios to define scope and expected outcomes:
+
+- [Adopt and secure AI](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-scenario-secure-ai) - Establish the business and security outcomes for AI adoption.
+- [Strengthen posture and compliance](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-scenario-improve-posture) - Measure exposure and continuously improve control effectiveness.
+- [Protect critical business assets](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-scenario-secure-assets) - Focus security work on the assets and data with the greatest business impact.
+- [Secure and govern privileged access](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-scenario-privileged-access) - Protect administrative and other high-impact control paths that AI systems can depend on or invoke.
+
+### Security disciplines
+
+Coordinate the work across these SAF disciplines:
+
+- [Strategy, integration, and governance](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-strategy) sets priorities, policy, funding, risk acceptance, and outcome measures.
+- [Security architecture](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-architecture) defines trust boundaries, control patterns, and end-to-end design across classic and AI systems.
+- [Security posture](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-posture) inventories assets and exposure, prioritizes risk, and measures improvement.
+- [Access and identities](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-identity-access) governs human, workload, and agent identities and applies least privilege.
+- [Data](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-data) discovers, classifies, protects, and governs data used by people, applications, models, and agents.
+- [Development](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-development) integrates threat modeling, secure engineering, testing, and release controls into AI delivery.
+- [Infrastructure](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-infrastructure) secures hosting, compute, platforms, services, and dependencies.
+- [SecOps](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-security-operations) detects active threats and feeds incident learning back into posture and architecture.
+
+### Roles and collaboration
+
+Use [Security roles and responsibilities in SAF](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-roles) to assign accountable owners and working relationships.
+
+The foundation depends on collaboration among:
+
+- Organizational leadership and governance to set risk appetite and hold outcome owners accountable.
+- Business and AI solution owners to define intended use, criticality, data access, and acceptable behavior.
+- Security strategy, architecture, posture, identity, and data teams to define policy and reusable patterns.
+- Application and product development teams to build and release AI capabilities securely.
+- Technical engineering and operations teams to implement and operate controls across the estate.
+- SecOps teams to monitor, investigate, respond, and drive lessons back into prevention.
+
+### Technologies
+
+Apply controls across the complete technology estate:
+
+- [AI](/en-us/security/saf/technologies/ai/overview)
+- [Identity](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/identity)
+- [Endpoints](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/endpoints)
+- [Applications](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/applications)
+- [Data](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/data)
+- [Infrastructure](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/infrastructure)
+- [Network](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/networks)
+
+Do not isolate AI from these dependencies. The secure foundation is the combination of controls across them.
+
+## Implementation and product guidance
+
+Use [Microsoft secure Zero Trust implementation solutions](/en-us/security/zero-trust/implement-overview) to connect the scenarios, disciplines, and technologies to technical implementation. Start with the following canonical guidance:
+
+1. [Build a strong AI security posture](/en-us/security/security-for-ai/posture) to establish the overall approach and priorities.
+2. [Prepare for AI security](/en-us/security/security-for-ai/prepare) to strengthen identity, device, data, and threat protection foundations.
+3. [Discover AI apps and data](/en-us/security/security-for-ai/discover) to understand the AI estate and associated data paths.
+4. [Protect AI apps and data](/en-us/security/security-for-ai/protect) to apply controls to AI usage, applications, and information.
+5. [Govern AI for compliance](/en-us/security/security-for-ai/govern) to sustain policy, compliance, and accountable use.
+6. [Secure AI with Zero Trust](/en-us/security/saf/technologies/ai/overview) to apply Zero Trust across AI systems and their dependencies.
+7. [AI security in the Microsoft Zero Trust Workshop](/en-us/security/zero-trust/workshop-zero-trust-ai-security) to align stakeholders and build an implementation plan.
+8. [Zero Trust assessment](/en-us/security/zero-trust/assessment/overview) to measure current capabilities and identify improvement priorities.
+
+Use focused implementation guidance where the risk requires it:
+
+- [Secure identity to get ready for AI](/en-us/security/zero-trust/sfi/secure-identity-to-get-ready-for-ai)
+- [Least privilege for AI agents](/en-us/security/zero-trust/sfi/least-privilege-for-ai-agents)
+- [Safe Secrets Standard](/en-us/security/zero-trust/sfi/safe-secrets-standard)
+- [Complete production infrastructure inventory](/en-us/security/zero-trust/sfi/complete-production-infrastructure-inventory)
+- [Complete AI threat modeling](/en-us/security/zero-trust/sfi/threat-modeling-ai)
+- [Protect the software supply chain](/en-us/security/zero-trust/sfi/protect-software-supply-chain)
+- [Use Zero Trust security to prepare for AI companions, including Microsoft Copilots](/en-us/security/zero-trust/copilots/apply-zero-trust-copilots-overview)
+
+Keep detailed configuration steps in their canonical product documentation. Use this theme page to explain the outcome, organize ownership through SAF, and route teams to the right implementation guidance.

+# Secure AI with Zero Trust | Microsoft Learn
+
+AI systems are now part of the core enterprise technology estate, including AI applications, agents, models, and the data and services they use. As organizations adopt AI, these systems introduce new access paths, dependencies, and risk conditions that must be governed as part of end-to-end security architecture.
+
+In the Microsoft Security Adoption Framework (SAF), the AI pillar applies Zero Trust principles to AI workloads and operations: verify explicitly, use least privilege, and assume compromise. This guidance helps you protect AI capabilities while supporting business outcomes, operational reliability, and continuous improvement.
+
+## What this technology pillar covers
+
+This pillar focuses on securing AI systems as workloads and business-critical resources, including:
+
+- AI applications and systems
+- AI agents and agent runtimes
+- AI and agent identities
+- Models, prompts, and context
+- Data used for grounding, training, and inference
+- Tools, plugins, connectors, and external dependencies
+- Agent-to-agent and agent-to-service communications
+- AI infrastructure and hosting environments
+
+## Core Zero Trust control areas for AI
+
+Use this pillar to plan and implement controls across these areas, aligned to the implementation areas in the [AI security workshop](/en-us/security/zero-trust/workshop-zero-trust-ai-security):
+
+1. **Map and assess AI risk**
+    - Discover and inventory AI applications, agents, and services.
+    - Prioritize risks and establish ownership, governance, and acceptable-use guardrails.
+    - Continuously monitor risk signals and adjust priorities as usage evolves.
+2. **Register agents and enforce lifecycle governance**
+    - Register agents in a centralized inventory.
+    - Classify agents by purpose, business criticality, and risk.
+    - Define ownership, publishing, certification, and lifecycle controls.
+3. **Secure AI authentication and access**
+    - Require strong authentication and authorization for users, services, and agents.
+    - Apply least privilege and delegated permissions for agent actions.
+    - Continuously evaluate identity, device, and risk signals before and during access.
+4. **Secure AI network and service access**
+    - Control how AI services are reached across network paths and service boundaries.
+    - Apply segmentation, filtering, and inspection for AI interactions.
+    - Reduce exposure to prompt injection and unauthorized access paths.
+5. **Secure AI data access and usage**
+    - Classify and protect data used in prompts, context, grounding, and outputs.
+    - Apply data loss prevention and usage controls to reduce oversharing and exfiltration risk.
+    - Enforce governance and compliance policies for AI data handling.
+6. **Build and deploy agents securely**
+    - Secure AI apps, APIs, connectors, and tool-chain dependencies.
+    - Validate trust boundaries and runtime controls before production use.
+    - Apply secure development, testing, and release controls for AI-enabled systems.
+7. **Detect and respond for AI**
+    - Monitor AI activity, prompt flows, access patterns, and tool usage.
+    - Detect misuse, anomalous behavior, and policy violations.
+    - Integrate AI telemetry into incident detection, investigation, and response workflows.
+
+## How this pillar connects to SAF
+
+AI security relies on other SAF technologies and security disciplines:
+
+- **Technologies**: [Identity](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/identity), [Endpoints](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/endpoints), [Applications](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/applications), [Data](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/data), [Infrastructure](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/infrastructure), and [Network](/en-us/security/zero-trust/deploy/networks).
+- **Security disciplines**: [Development](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-development) for secure engineering practices and [SecOps](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-discipline-security-operations) for detection and response operations.
+- **Business scenarios**: [Adopt and secure AI](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-scenario-secure-ai).
+
+## Workshop and implementation guidance
+
+- [AI security in the Microsoft Zero Trust Workshop](/en-us/security/zero-trust/workshop-zero-trust-ai-security)
+- [Build a strong AI posture](/en-us/security/security-for-ai/posture)
+- [Prepare for AI security](/en-us/security/security-for-ai/prepare)
+- [Discover AI apps and data](/en-us/security/security-for-ai/discover)
+- [Protect AI apps and data](/en-us/security/security-for-ai/protect)

+# Configure and Tune the Zero Trust Assessment | Microsoft Learn
+
+Inspect the Zero Trust Assessment configuration and change settings when you identify a bottleneck. Lower concurrency to reduce memory pressure and throttling. Increasing a timeout doesn't fix missing access.
+
+Start with an imported module and diagnostic files for the bottleneck. The following settings and defaults describe the development source. Check the configuration available in your installed package before changing it.
+
+## Prerequisites
+
+- An [installed assessment module](get-started#install-the-powershell-modules), imported into your PowerShell session.
+- The [collector and test diagnostics](troubleshooting#logs-and-diagnostic-files) for the bottleneck you want to investigate.
+
+## Inspect configuration settings
+
+Review current values before deciding what to change.
+
+1. Import the assessment module if it isn't already loaded.
+2. Inspect its configuration:
+
+    ```powershell
+    Get-PSFConfig -Module ZeroTrustAssessment
+    ```
+3. Compare the relevant values with the available settings and the affected collector and test diagnostics.
+
+## Change settings for the current session
+
+Set values before invoking the assessment.
+
+1. Select a setting that addresses the identified bottleneck.
+2. Set the value. For example, reduce test concurrency in the current session:
+
+    ```powershell
+    Set-PSFConfig -Module ZeroTrustAssessment -Name 'ThrottleLimit.Tests' -Value 3
+    ```
+3. [Run the assessment](run-assessment) and review the affected collector or test diagnostics.
+
+The `-ConfigurationFile` parameter accepts JSON for supported settings. Explicit command-line values override configuration-file values. Not every run parameter is a configuration-file setting.
+
+## Persist a setting
+
+Set the value, then register that configuration entry for future sessions.
+
+1. Set and register the entry. For example:
+
+    ```powershell
+    Set-PSFConfig -FullName 'ZeroTrustAssessment.Graph.CacheMaxItems' -Value 10000
+    Register-PSFConfig -FullName 'ZeroTrustAssessment.Graph.CacheMaxItems'
+    ```
+2. Use the configuration inspection command in future sessions to review the registered value.
+
+`Register-PSFConfig` defaults to the current user's settings. `Set-PSFConfig` doesn't have a `-Register` switch.
+
+Duration settings accept standard time spans and PSFramework notation such as `30m`, `2h`, or `2h 30m`. See the [PSFramework documentation](https://psframework.org/) and [assessment configuration definitions](https://github.com/microsoft/zerotrustassessment/blob/6a304637fc53846fd55182d495b6a2980f30b434/src/powershell/scripts/configuration.ps1).
+
+## Available configuration settings
+
+All names in this table use the prefix `ZeroTrustAssessment.`. Defaults describe the development source.
+
+| Setting | Default | Purpose |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| **`Export.DependencyWaitLimit`** | `1d` | Maximum wait for another export that a collector depends on. |
+| **`Export.SignInLog.MaxSizeBytes`** | `1073741824` (1 GB) | Sign-in export size cap; collection stops at the cap. |
+| **`ThrottleLimit.Export`** | `5` | Maximum parallel collectors. |
+| **`ThrottleLimit.Tests`** | `5` | Maximum parallel tests. |
+| **`Tests.Timeout`** | `1h` | Per-test timeout; `0` disables it. |
+| **`Tests.TimeoutType`** | `Idle` | `Idle` measures time since last activity; `Start` measures time since execution began. |
+| **`Tests.RetryCount`** | `0` | Reattempts for failed executions. |
+| **`Tests.RetryTimeout`** | `$false` | Include timed-out executions in retries. |
+| **`Tests.Statistics.MessageCountSoftCap`** | `1024` | Threshold for simplifying stored per-test message objects. |
+| **`Azure.DisableCache` / `Graph.DisableCache`** | `$false` | Disable the respective in-memory request cache. |
+| **`Azure.CacheMaxItems` / `Graph.CacheMaxItems`** | `50000` | Maximum items in each request cache. |
+| **`Azure.CacheLifetime` / `Graph.CacheLifetime`** | `30m` | Expiration of cached entries. |
+| **`Logging.Database.IncludeQueryResults`** | `$false` | Include database row values in logs. Leave disabled normally: it increases volume and exposes tenant data. |
+| **`Logging.InMemoryLog.MinSize`** | `51200` | Minimum PSFramework in-memory message capacity enforced at import. Larger values consume more memory. |
+| **`Debug.KeepWorkflows`** | `$false` | Keep background workflows for debugging instead of normal cleanup. Avoid for routine runs. |
+| **`TabExpansion.TestLimit`** | `10` | Maximum test IDs offered by tab completion at a time. |
+
+## Tune a large-tenant run
+
+Review related limits together rather than increasing every value.
+
+1. Inspect collector and test logs to identify slow collection, throttling, timeouts, or memory pressure.
+2. Consider lowering both throttle limits and bounding caches.
+3. Review sign-in lookback, the collection time budget, the sign-in export size cap, and test and export timeouts together. See [run parameters](run-assessment#invoke-ztassessment-parameters).
+4. Review retry settings only for failed or timed-out executions. They don't turn a failed security recommendation into a pass.
+5. Leave database row-value logging and retained workflows disabled for routine runs.

+# Connect to Zero Trust Assessment Services | Microsoft Learn
+
+Connect the Zero Trust Assessment to the Microsoft 365 and Azure services you want to assess. Use interactive sign-in for a user-run assessment or certificate authentication for app-only access without storing user credentials. Prepare the module and service permissions before connecting.
+
+These instructions describe the development connector. App-only support and connection options can differ between published packages.
+
+## Prerequisites
+
+- Completion of the [assessment installation](get-started#install-the-powershell-modules).
+- The [interactive user access](permissions#interactive-user-access) or [application permissions and roles](permissions#app-only-permissions-and-roles) for the services and resource scopes to assess.
+- For app-only access, an app registration and a certificate with its private key available to the assessment machine, as described in the certificate procedure in the following section.
+
+## Connect interactively
+
+Choose the tenant explicitly to reduce the risk of assessing the wrong organization.
+
+1. Activate eligible roles through Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management before connecting. Arrange consent separately from the assessment user's runtime roles.
+2. Connect to the tenant you want to assess, replacing the example domain:
+
+    ```powershell
+    Connect-ZtAssessment -Tenant contoso.onmicrosoft.com
+    ```
+3. Complete the service prompts and review the connection status messages. Services authenticate separately, but cached sessions and single sign-on can reduce prompts. SharePoint interactive authentication uses the system browser.
+4. Reconnect after changing access or context. Use `-Force` when you need to refresh existing connections.
+
+`-Tenant` is an alias for `-TenantId` and accepts a tenant GUID or verified domain name for interactive sign-in. If you don't include this parameter, Microsoft Graph uses an organizations context and derives the tenant from sign-in.
+
+Consent is requested when the application lacks the required grants. New scopes can require consent again.
+
+## Select services and connection options
+
+By default, `Connect-ZtAssessment` connects to all available services. Select services only after considering the effect on assessment coverage.
+
+1. Identify the services you want to assess:
+
+    | Service selector | Underlying command |
+    | --- | --- |
+    | **`Graph`** | `Connect-MgGraph`. |
+    | **`Azure`** | `Connect-AzAccount`. |
+    | **`AipService`** | `Connect-AipService`. |
+    | **`SharePointOnline`** | `Connect-SPOService`. |
+    | **`ExchangeOnline`** | `Connect-ExchangeOnline`. |
+    | **`SecurityCompliance`** | `Connect-IPPSSession`. |
+2. Use `-Service` to select services. For example, `Connect-ZtAssessment -Tenant contoso.onmicrosoft.com -Service Graph,Azure` selects Graph and Azure. The connector adds Graph first if it isn't already connected.
+3. Review connection outcomes before running the assessment. Skipping Azure limits Infrastructure, Network, and security operations (SecOps) coverage, not just audit and sign-in log export checks.
+
+Use these additional options when needed:
+
+| Option | Purpose or constraint |
+| --- | --- |
+| **`-Force`** | Refresh existing connections after access or context changes. |
+| **`-SharePointAdminUrl`** | Supply the tenant admin URL if the connector can't infer it. |
+| **`-UserPrincipalName`** | Supply the user identity for Security & Compliance. |
+| **`-Environment`**, **`-ExchangeEnvironmentName`** | Select cloud environments. Use the values documented by `Get-Help Connect-ZtAssessment -Full`. |
+| **`-UseDeviceCode`** | Not an all-service unattended mode. Security & Compliance doesn't support that flow in this connector. SharePoint and Azure Information Protection (AIP) have their own authentication behavior. |
+
+## Connect with an application certificate
+
+Authorize the application identity at each service, not just the person who configures it.
+
+1. Register an application in the target tenant. Record its application/client ID and tenant GUID.
+2. Configure and grant consent for the [app-only permissions](permissions#app-only-permissions-and-roles). Assign workload and Azure resource roles to the service principal.
+3. Upload the certificate's public key to the app registration. Install the corresponding certificate and private key in the local user's certificate store on the assessment machine. For Exchange, follow the certificate-provider requirements in the [app-only authentication guide](/en-us/powershell/exchange/app-only-auth-powershell-v2?view=exchange-ps).
+4. If connecting to SharePoint, provide an exportable private key. The current connector passes a temporary certificate file into its Windows PowerShell compatibility session. Protect the key and follow any temporary-file cleanup warning.
+5. Connect with the client ID, tenant GUID, and certificate thumbprint. Replace the placeholders with your values:
+
+    ```powershell
+    Connect-ZtAssessment -ClientId '<application-id>' -TenantId '<tenant-guid>' -Certificate '<certificate-thumbprint>' -Service All
+    ```
+6. Review each service's connection status and any authorization errors before running the assessment.
+
+Both `-ClientId` and `-TenantId` are required with `-Certificate`. Don't combine certificate authentication with `-UseDeviceCode`. For cross-service app-only connections, use the tenant GUID rather than assuming every service accepts a domain name. The connector resolves the initial `.onmicrosoft.com` domain for Exchange and Security & Compliance.
+
+App-only coverage depends on the package, dependency versions, permissions, and commands used by individual checks. Missing connections produce service-related skips; other authorization errors can appear in test diagnostics. Review those outcomes before treating an unattended run as complete.

+# Zero Trust Assessment Permissions and Roles | Microsoft Learn
+
+To run the Zero Trust Assessment, arrange API permissions, administrator consent, directory roles, workload roles, and Azure resource access. Treat these as separate requirements. Grant access only to the services and resources you intend to assess.
+
+These requirements describe the [development source](overview#source-and-package-versions). Published packages can differ. Activate eligible roles through Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management before connecting, and reconnect after changing access.
+
+## Interactive user access
+
+Use a highly privileged administrator for initial setup only, not for every assessment merely because that account granted consent.
+
+For data loss prevention (DLP) checks, verify workload authorization as well as directory roles.
+
+| Service or task | Required access and scope |
+| --- | --- |
+| **Initial Microsoft Graph consent** | For delegated permission grants, Cloud Application Administrator, Application Administrator, or another authorized consent role. Privileged Role Administrator can grant consent for any API, including Graph Application permissions; Global Administrator can also perform this setup. Consent doesn't assign runtime roles to the assessment user. |
+| **Microsoft Graph assessment context** | All Graph permissions below and an active Global Reader or Global Administrator role. The module validates these roles for delegated authentication. Prefer Global Reader for the assessment account. |
+| **Custom security attributes** | Attribute Assignment Reader, or Attribute Assignment Administrator, in addition to `CustomSecAttributeAssignment.Read.All`. Global Reader or Global Administrator alone doesn't grant access to attribute values. |
+| **Azure** | Reader at the subscription/resource scopes to assess, or equivalent read permissions for the relevant resource providers. Azure access is separate from Microsoft Entra ID directory roles. Resource Graph only returns resources the caller can read; check coverage across every intended subscription. |
+| **Exchange Online and Defender protection policies** | Global Reader plus Security Reader for protection-policy checks. With customized workload roles, verify access to `Get-AntiPhishPolicy`, `Get-HostedContentFilterPolicy`, `Get-MalwareFilterPolicy`, `Get-SafeAttachmentPolicy`, `Get-SafeLinksPolicy`, `Get-AtpPolicyForO365`, and `Get-TeamsProtectionPolicy`. |
+| **Security & Compliance (Microsoft Purview)** | Global Reader provides the standard read-only role mapping, including Sensitivity Label Reader and View-Only DLP Compliance Management. Verify effective access to `Get-Label`, `Get-LabelPolicy`, `Get-DlpCompliancePolicy`, `Get-DlpComplianceRule`, `Get-DlpEdmSchema`, and `Get-DlpSensitiveInformationType`. Customized role groups can change access. |
+| **SharePoint Online** | SharePoint Administrator for tenant administration commands, including `Get-SPOTenant`. Global Reader alone isn't sufficient for these PowerShell commands. |
+| **Azure Information Protection (AIP)** | Azure Information Protection Administrator, Compliance Administrator, Compliance Data Administrator, or Global Administrator; alternatively, delegated AIP administrative access configured with `Add-AipServiceRoleBasedAdministrator`. Don't enable the AIP super-user feature or add yourself as a super user just to read its configuration. |
+| **Defender advanced hunting** | `ThreatHunting.Read.All` plus access to the relevant Defender data through the user's effective security roles and data scope. Graph consent alone doesn't remove workload or licensing restrictions. |
+
+These requirements don't guarantee that every check runs. Service configuration, licenses, scoped permissions, and supported authentication modes also affect coverage. Investigate permission errors rather than treating them as tenant security failures or granting broad administrator access without review.
+
+For service-specific authorization details, see:
+
+- [Consent administrator requirements](/en-us/entra/identity/enterprise-apps/grant-admin-consent).
+- [Azure Resource Graph permissions](/en-us/azure/governance/resource-graph/overview#permissions-in-azure-resource-graph).
+- [Exchange cmdlet permissions](/en-us/powershell/exchange/find-exchange-cmdlet-permissions?view=exchange-ps).
+- [Defender and Purview role mappings](/en-us/defender-office-365/scc-permissions).
+- [SharePoint tenant command requirements](/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.online.sharepoint.powershell/get-spotenant?view=sharepoint-ps).
+- [AIP connection requirements](/en-us/powershell/module/aipservice/connect-aipservice?view=azureipps).
+
+## Microsoft Graph permissions
+
+The development source requests these delegated permissions. For app-only authentication, configure the Application permission with the same name and grant administrator consent. A delegated grant doesn't authorize an application token.
+
+- `Application.Read.All`.
+- `AttackSimulation.Read.All`.
+- `AuditLog.Read.All`.
+- `CopilotPackages.Read.All`.
+- `CrossTenantInformation.ReadBasic.All`.
+- `CustomSecAttributeAssignment.Read.All`.
+- `DeviceManagementApps.Read.All`.
+- `DeviceManagementConfiguration.Read.All`.
+- `DeviceManagementManagedDevices.Read.All`.
+- `DeviceManagementRBAC.Read.All`.
+- `DeviceManagementServiceConfig.Read.All`.
+- `Directory.Read.All`.
+- `DirectoryRecommendations.Read.All`.
+- `EntitlementManagement.Read.All`.
+- `IdentityRiskEvent.Read.All`.
+- `IdentityRiskyServicePrincipal.Read.All`.
+- `IdentityRiskyUser.Read.All`.
+- `LifecycleWorkflows-Workflow.Read.All`.
+- `NetworkAccess.Read.All`.
+- `Policy.Read.All`.
+- `Policy.Read.ConditionalAccess`.
+- `Policy.Read.PermissionGrant`.
+- `PrivilegedAccess.Read.AzureAD`.
+- `PrivilegedAssignmentSchedule.Read.AzureADGroup`.
+- `PrivilegedEligibilitySchedule.Read.AzureADGroup`.
+- `Reports.Read.All`.
+- `RoleManagement.Read.All`.
+- `SecurityAlert.Read.All`.
+- `SecurityEvents.Read.All`.
+- `SecurityIdentitiesHealth.Read.All`.
+- `SecurityIdentitiesSensors.Read.All`.
+- `SecurityIncident.Read.All`.
+- `ThreatHunting.Read.All`.
+- `UserAuthenticationMethod.Read.All`.
+
+To list the requirements for your installed version, import the module and query its scope helper:
+
+```powershell
+Import-Module ZeroTrustAssessment
+Get-ZtGraphScope
+```
+
+The list comes from [Get-ZtGraphScope](https://github.com/microsoft/zerotrustassessment/blob/6a304637fc53846fd55182d495b6a2980f30b434/src/powershell/public/Get-ZtGraphScope.ps1). For permission definitions and supported types, see the [Microsoft Graph permissions reference](/en-us/graph/permissions-reference).
+
+## App-only permissions and roles
+
+Certificate authentication uses an application identity, not the signed-in user's roles. Configure the app registration, enterprise application/service principal, and resource assignments separately.
+
+Graph Application permission consent requires Privileged Role Administrator, Global Administrator, or a suitable custom consent role. Application Administrator alone isn't sufficient. Azure resource-role assignment also requires administrative authority at the target scope.
+
+| Service | Application permissions and authorization |
+| --- | --- |
+| **Microsoft Graph** | The Application permissions in the Graph list, with administrator consent. The module checks the complete list even for a single pillar. The delegated user's Global Reader role isn't the app-only Graph context check. |
+| **Azure** | Reader, or equivalent resource-read permissions, assigned to the service principal on each intended subscription/resource scope. Graph permissions don't grant Azure access. |
+| **Exchange Online** | **Office 365 Exchange Online > Exchange.ManageAsApp**, with consent, plus supported directory roles or Exchange role-group assignments to the service principal. Global Reader and Security Reader are supported read-oriented directory roles; verify access to the protection cmdlets listed above. |
+| **Security & Compliance** | **Microsoft Exchange Online Protection > Exchange.ManageAsApp**, with consent, plus supported directory roles or Purview role-group assignments to the service principal. Follow the [Exchange/Purview app-only setup](/en-us/powershell/exchange/app-only-auth-powershell-v2?view=exchange-ps) and configure authorization for both services if using both. |
+| **SharePoint Online** | **SharePoint > Sites.FullControl.All** Application permission, with administrator consent, for tenant administration APIs. This is a broad permission, not a read-only scope or the Graph permission with the same name. See [SharePoint admin API authorization](/en-us/sharepoint/dev/sp-add-ins/sharepoint-admin-apis-authentication-and-authorization). |
+| **Azure Information Protection** | The current connector expects **Azure Rights Management Services > Application.Read.All**, with consent. This is separate from Graph `Application.Read.All`. The pinned AipService 3.1.0.0 exposes certificate service-principal parameter sets even though published cmdlet help doesn't list them. Verify effective access to `Get-AipServiceSuperUser` and `Get-AipServiceSuperUserFeature` in your environment. |
+
+Caution
+
+A read-only assessment doesn't mean every service offers read-only connection permissions. Review the SharePoint full-control grant with your tenant administrator. Don't add content-decryption or write permissions merely to suppress an error.
+
+Exchange and Purview support built-in directory roles and custom workload role groups. Their role groups don't automatically share membership. Use the [app-only role-assignment procedure](/en-us/powershell/exchange/app-only-auth-powershell-v2?view=exchange-ps#step-5-assign-role-permissions-to-the-application) to scope commands.
+
+Some service cmdlets don't support app-only authentication. A successful connection isn't proof of complete coverage; review connection outcomes and test diagnostics.
\ No newline at end of file
