+# Review Zero Trust Assessment Results | Microsoft Learn
+
+Use Zero Trust Assessment reports to review findings across seven pillars, investigate incomplete coverage, and plan security improvements. You can also import mapped findings into Zero Trust Workshop task notes.
+
+Start with generated reports and authorized access to their output directory. The reports and integration described here reflect the development source. Published packages can differ.
+
+## Prerequisites
+
+- Completion of [Run and resume an assessment](run-assessment), with generated reports available.
+- Authorized access to the protected assessment output directory. Reports and exports can contain tenant configuration and personal information.
+
+## Review assessment results
+
+In the following paths, `<Path>` is the output directory you provide to `Invoke-ZtAssessment -Path`, or `.\ZeroTrustReport` by default. The screenshots use [synthetic data from the public demo](https://microsoft.github.io/zerotrustassessment/demo/), not a real tenant.
+
+1. Open a generated report:
+
+    - `<Path>\ZeroTrustAssessmentReport.html` is the redesigned report, opened by default.
+    - `<Path>\ZeroTrustAssessmentReport-classic.html` is the classic report.
+
+    If the run used `-NoBrowser`, open the report yourself.
+2. Review the **Overview** for tenant summaries and assessment results across Identity, Devices, Network, Data, Infrastructure, security operations (SecOps), and AI.
+
+    [![Screenshot of synthetic tenant counts and assessment results across seven Zero Trust pillars.](media/zero-trust-assessment-overview.png)](media/zero-trust-assessment-overview.png#lightbox)
+3. Open a pillar and filter results by risk and status.
+
+    [![Screenshot of Identity assessment results with risk and status filters and synthetic findings.](media/zero-trust-assessment-identity.png)](media/zero-trust-assessment-identity.png#lightbox)
+4. Select a result to read its findings and supporting guidance. See the [assessment terminology](glossary) for the documented ratings.
+
+    [![Screenshot of a synthetic failed assessment check with its risk, findings, and evaluation details.](media/zero-trust-assessment-detail.png)](media/zero-trust-assessment-detail.png#lightbox)
+5. Check skipped tests and errors, not just passed and failed results. An unavailable service, license, or permission can leave part of the tenant unassessed. Investigate these outcomes with the [access reference](permissions) and [troubleshooting guide](troubleshooting).
+
+The assessment doesn't apply remediation. Use the findings and supporting guidance to plan changes.
+
+## Import results into Zero Trust Workshop
+
+Report generation also creates `<Path>\zt-export\ZeroTrustWorkshop.json`. Import this file to bring mapped findings into Workshop task notes.
+
+1. Locate `ZeroTrustWorkshop.json` in your protected assessment output directory.
+2. Open [Zero Trust Workshop](https://aka.ms/ztworkshop) and import that JSON file.
+3. Review the imported notes with the following limitations in mind.
+
+### Current limitations
+
+The integration is experimental and generated on a best-effort basis alongside the reports.
+
+- Skipped tests are omitted. Other outcomes are represented in the notes.
+- Notes are limited to 1,000 characters per task, including the header.
+- A finding longer than 200 characters is compacted to its test title. Excess findings can be omitted, with an indication of how many remain.
+- Exported task status is `not-reviewed`. Assessment findings don't automatically mark Workshop tasks complete.
\ No newline at end of file

+# Run and Resume a Zero Trust Assessment | Microsoft Learn
+
+Run all Zero Trust Assessment pillars or select a pillar and specific test IDs. You can also reuse an existing export to rerun assessment and report processing without collecting a fresh tenant snapshot. Before starting, connect to the services and choose a protected output directory.
+
+The options and defaults in the following section describe the development source. Check your installed version's help when using a published package.
+
+## Prerequisites
+
+- Completion of [Connect to assessment services](connect-services), with the service connections available in the same PowerShell session.
+- A protected output directory with sufficient disk space.
+- Azure read access and subscription tags for Infrastructure scope, if applicable.
+
+## Run a fresh assessment
+
+`Invoke-ZtAssessment` uses the connected tenant; it doesn't take a tenant parameter. Choose the output path and scope before running the command.
+
+Warning
+
+A non-resume run against a nonempty output directory prompts to delete its contents. In a detected continuous integration (CI) environment, the current implementation cleans the directory automatically. Don't point `-Path` at a directory containing unrelated files.
+
+1. Choose a new output directory. The default is `.\ZeroTrustReport`, relative to your current directory.
+2. Run one of these alternatives:
+
+    - To assess all seven current pillars, use:
+
+        ```powershell
+        Invoke-ZtAssessment
+        ```
+    - To assess only Devices and use a custom path, use:
+
+        ```powershell
+        Invoke-ZtAssessment -Path C:\MyAssessment01 -Pillar Devices
+        ```
+3. Follow the progress dashboard and review [diagnostic files](troubleshooting#logs-and-diagnostic-files) when you need to distinguish active work from a failure.
+
+Runtime varies with tenant size, service response times, throttling, and selected tests. `-NoBrowser` disables both the progress dashboard server and automatic opening of the final report.
+
+`All` includes Identity, Devices, Network, Data, Infrastructure, security operations (SecOps), and AI. The `-Preview` switch isn't required for these pillars. It enables preview-only features when present and is separate from [installing a prerelease package](get-started#install-the-powershell-modules).
+
+## Reuse an existing export
+
+Use `-Resume` only when you intend to reuse the existing tenant snapshot and database, not collect current tenant data.
+
+1. Preserve the existing output directory, exports, and database.
+2. Use the original pillar, or an individual pillar if the original export used `All`. A single-pillar export can't be resumed as `All` or as a different pillar.
+3. Keep the necessary service connections available and rerun against the original path:
+
+    ```powershell
+    Invoke-ZtAssessment -Path C:\MyAssessment01 -Pillar Devices -Resume
+    ```
+
+Resume skips export and database rebuild, but reruns assessment and report processing. It isn't a fresh collection or a guarantee of fully offline execution.
+
+## Infrastructure scope
+
+Infrastructure findings use Microsoft Defender for Cloud recommendations. Prepare the intended subscriptions before assessing this pillar.
+
+1. Arrange Reader access, or equivalent read permissions, on each intended subscription/resource scope.
+2. Tag the intended accessible Azure subscriptions with `ZeroTrustAssessment:Infrastructure`.
+3. Run the Infrastructure pillar or `All`, then review any skipped checks.
+
+Only accessible subscriptions with the required tag are included. No matching tagged subscriptions produces a skip, not a passed assessment.
+
+## Invoke-ZtAssessment parameters
+
+Use this table to select run options. Explicit command-line values override supported configuration-file settings. Not every parameter is a configuration-file setting.
+
+| Parameter | Behavior |
+| --- | --- |
+| **`-Path <string>`** | Output folder; defaults to `.\ZeroTrustReport` relative to the current directory. |
+| **`-Pillar <string>`** | `All` by default, or `Identity`, `Devices`, `Network`, `Data`, `Infrastructure`, `SecOps`, or `AI`. |
+| **`-Preview`** | Enable preview-only features when present. Not needed for the seven current pillars. |
+| **`-Resume`** | Reuse exports and database at `-Path`; use the original pillar or a subset of an `All` export. |
+| **`-Tests <id[,id...]>`** | Exact test IDs, without wildcards. Otherwise, run the selected pillar's tests. |
+| **`-Days <1-30>`** | Sign-in log lookback; defaults to 30 days. |
+| **`-MaximumSignInLogQueryTime <minutes>`** | Sign-in collection time budget; defaults to 60. `0` removes the time limit, but the export size limit still applies. |
+| **`-NoBrowser`** | Don't start the progress dashboard server or open the final report. |
+| **`-ShowLog`** | Show a high-level console log summary. |
+| **`-ExportLog`** | Create a PSFramework support package under `<Path>\log` near the end of the run. Per-run diagnostic files don't require this switch. |
+| **`-ConfigurationFile <path>`** | JSON configuration for supported settings. Explicit command-line values take precedence. |
+| **`-DisableTelemetry`** | Disable the assessment telemetry event. See [data handling and telemetry](get-started#protect-assessment-data). |
+| **`-Timeout <timespan>`** | Overall wait for tests; defaults to 24 hours. Accepts values such as `12h` or `3d`. |
+| **`-TestTimeout <minutes/timespan>`** | Per-test timeout; defaults to 60 minutes. `0` disables it. The default measures idle time since activity, not total elapsed time. Interruption of external and remoting operations is best effort. |
+| **`-ExportThrottleLimit <n>`**, **`-TestThrottleLimit <n>`** | Parallel export collectors and tests, respectively; default to 5 each. |
+
+For the complete interface, use `Get-Help Invoke-ZtAssessment -Full` and review the [command source](https://github.com/microsoft/zerotrustassessment/blob/6a304637fc53846fd55182d495b6a2980f30b434/src/powershell/public/Invoke-ZtAssessment.ps1). For configuration persistence and large-tenant settings, see [Configure and tune assessments](configure-assessment).
\ No newline at end of file

+# Troubleshoot the Zero Trust Assessment | Microsoft Learn
+
+Investigate Zero Trust Assessment connection failures, skipped checks, slow runs, dependency conflicts, and report problems. Start with the affected stage, then collect diagnostics if the symptom-specific checks don't resolve the issue. Keep the PowerShell session or available diagnostics for your investigation.
+
+Before you begin, gather your assessment and PowerShell versions, run scope, and error summary. See Prerequisites for the information you need.
+
+## Prerequisites
+
+- The assessment PowerShell session, if still available, or its generated diagnostics.
+- The assessment and PowerShell versions, selected pillar and test IDs, affected stage, and error summary.
+
+## Troubleshooting checklist
+
+Identify the failure stage before changing permissions, dependencies, or timeouts.
+
+### Identify the affected stage
+
+Identify which assessment stage failed so you can select the relevant diagnostics.
+
+1. Review connection messages and the per-run diagnostic files to identify whether the problem occurs during connection, export, database creation, tests, or report processing.
+2. Record the assessment version, PowerShell version, selected pillar and test IDs, and a sanitized error summary.
+3. Preserve completed exports and the database if you might use [resume](run-assessment#reuse-an-existing-export).
+
+### Check access and coverage
+
+Use the symptom table to select the next check. A successful Microsoft Graph connection doesn't establish every other service, and a skipped check isn't evidence of a secure configuration.
+
+| Symptom | What to check |
+| --- | --- |
+| **Graph consent or role validation fails.** | Compare grants with `Get-ZtGraphScope`, activate the required user role or configure app permissions, and reconnect. A new package can require additional consent. |
+| **A service fails to connect or tests are skipped.** | Check the service's role, license, platform, and connection message. See [connection guidance](connect-services). |
+| **A protection, label, data loss prevention (DLP), or hunting check returns an authorization error.** | Check workload role assignments and data scopes for the command or API, not just Microsoft Entra ID role names. Use the [access tables](permissions). |
+| **Infrastructure has no findings.** | Verify Azure read access and [subscription tags](run-assessment#infrastructure-scope). No tagged/accessible subscriptions isn't a passed assessment. |
+| **Runtime is long, requests are throttled, or memory pressure increases.** | Inspect collector and test logs. Review lookback, concurrency, caches, and timeouts in [configuration settings](configure-assessment). |
+| **A certificate connection fails.** | Check certificate validity/private key, app public-key registration, tenant GUID, consent, and service-principal roles. SharePoint also needs an exportable key in the current connector. |
+| **Constrained Language Mode prevents execution.** | Use an approved host/policy that supports the assessment. Don't bypass organizational controls; the advanced override doesn't make restricted operations work. |
+
+## Causes and solutions
+
+Use the following procedures for dependency and report errors. Check the affected version before choosing a workaround.
+
+### Resolve Graph assembly conflicts
+
+For `Could not load file or assembly Microsoft.Graph.Authentication`, start with a clean process instead of removing shared modules.
+
+1. Start a new `pwsh -NoProfile` process.
+2. Let the assessment load its pinned dependencies before other cloud modules.
+3. Check the [dependency cache and clean-host guidance](get-started#bundled-powershell-modules) if the problem persists.
+
+Another installed module isn't automatically a conflict, but already-loaded assemblies can be incompatible. Removing or reimporting a module doesn't reliably unload assemblies. Avoid blanket removal of shared Graph modules and third-party cleanup scripts as the default remedy.
+
+### Resolve DuckDB initialization errors
+
+The error `The type initializer for 'DuckDB.NET.Data.DuckDBConnectionStringBuilder' threw an exception` can have different underlying causes.
+
+1. Inspect the inner exception. On Windows, a `DllNotFoundException` for `duckdb` can indicate a missing native dependency.
+2. If missing, install the [Microsoft Visual C++ Redistributable (x64)](/en-us/cpp/windows/latest-supported-vc-redist?view=msvc-170#latest-microsoft-visual-c-redistributable-version).
+3. Retry in a fresh PowerShell session. Don't assume every database error has the same cause.
+
+### Recover from report-rendering errors
+
+Older reports could show `Unexpected Application Error! Invalid array length`. Related reports include [microsoft/zerotrustassessment#1235](https://github.com/microsoft/zerotrustassessment/issues/1235), [microsoft/zerotrustassessment#1272](https://github.com/microsoft/zerotrustassessment/issues/1272), [microsoft/zerotrustassessment#1310](https://github.com/microsoft/zerotrustassessment/issues/1310), and [microsoft/zerotrustassessment#1388](https://github.com/microsoft/zerotrustassessment/issues/1388).
+
+1. Check the issue and [release history](https://github.com/microsoft/zerotrustassessment/releases) for your version. Don't assume a prerelease is always required.
+2. If exports and database creation completed, preserve them.
+3. After installing an applicable fix, reconnect and use `-Resume` with the original path and pillar to rerun assessment and report processing.
+4. Use the classic HTML report if it was generated successfully.
+
+### Inspect assessment activity
+
+Review the [PowerShell source](https://github.com/microsoft/zerotrustassessment/tree/dev/src/powershell), progress dashboard, and per-run logs to understand the assessment's activity. The upstream [advanced troubleshooting guide](https://github.com/microsoft/zerotrustassessment/blob/dev/docs/troubleshooting.md) covers support-package analysis.
+
+## Advanced troubleshooting and data collection
+
+Different diagnostics capture different stages. Choose the location that matches the failure before collecting or sharing data.
+
+### Logs and diagnostic files
+
+`<Path>` is the directory you pass to `Invoke-ZtAssessment -Path`, or `.\ZeroTrustReport` by default. The optional support package, per-run files, and extended PSFramework logs are three separate diagnostic locations.
+
+| Location | Contents and use |
+| --- | --- |
+| **`<Path>\log\`** | A PSFramework support-package ZIP created by `-ExportLog` near successful completion, containing a `.cliDat` snapshot. It can be absent if the switch wasn't used or the run failed before this stage. |
+| **`<Path>\zt-export\logs\<run>\1-export_progress.log`** | Export collector progress and status. Start here for data-collection problems. |
+| **`<Path>\zt-export\logs\<run>\2-database_progress.log`** | Database build progress and timings. Resume skips this phase. |
+| **`<Path>\zt-export\logs\<run>\3-test_progress.log`** | Assessment execution progress and status. |
+| **`<Path>\zt-export\logs\<run>\1-Export\export_<Name>.md`** | Collector status, duration, timestamps, endpoint/type, module version, and diagnostic messages. |
+| **`<Path>\zt-export\logs\<run>\2-Tests\<TestID>.md`** | Test title, status, duration, timestamps, module version, and detailed messages, potentially including query text. |
+| **`%APPDATA%\PowerShell\PSFramework\Logs\` on Windows** | Extended message logs and XML error records, independent of the output path. Useful for connection/import issues, exceptions, source locations, stack traces, and messages outside individual tests. |
+
+`<run>` uses the timestamp format `yy-MM-dd-HHmmss`. Files appear as their phases execute; a partial or resumed run need not contain every file. Per-run files are generated independently of `-ExportLog`.
+
+Extended PSFramework files include computer/process identifiers and numbered segments, such as `<computer>_<pid>_message_0.log` and `<computer>_<pid>_error_0.xml`. Availability and retention depend on the logging provider configuration.
+
+On Windows, `%APPDATA%` identifies the user's Roaming folder, normally `%USERPROFILE%\AppData\Roaming`. In PowerShell, use `$env:APPDATA`; the equivalent log path is `Join-Path $env:APPDATA 'PowerShell\PSFramework\Logs'`.
+
+The rest of `<Path>\zt-export` is assessment data, not just logs: exported entities, `ztConfig.json`, `db\zt.db`, `ZeroTrustAssessmentReport.json`, and `ZeroTrustWorkshop.json`. These files can help reproduce or resume a run but can contain sensitive tenant data. Deleting `<Path>` doesn't remove separate PSFramework logs.
+
+### Capture a support package
+
+If a run fails before it creates an optional support package, capture diagnostics in the same PowerShell session before closing it.
+
+1. Choose a separate destination for the diagnostic package. It doesn't need to match the assessment output path. Replace the example destination with a folder for your run:
+
+    ```powershell
+    New-PSFSupportPackage -Path C:\AssessmentLogs\Run01 -Force
+    ```
+2. Extract the generated ZIP to access its `.cliDat` file.
+3. Review and redact diagnostics before sharing. For importing and investigating the snapshot, see the [advanced log analysis guide](https://github.com/microsoft/zerotrustassessment/blob/dev/docs/troubleshooting.md).
+
+A support package snapshots available session diagnostics, including message and error history and potentially command history or console output. It isn't an automatic archive of all exported tenant files.
+
+Warning
+
+Reports, exports, support packages, and extended logs can contain personal information, tenant identifiers, query values, and configuration details. Never attach them unreviewed to public GitHub issues or upload them to an unapproved tool. Share additional diagnostics only through an approved private channel agreed with the recipient.
+
+### Report an issue or provide feedback
+
+Search or file [GitHub issues](https://github.com/microsoft/zerotrustassessment/issues) or use the [feedback channel](https://aka.ms/zerotrust/feedback). Include the assessment version, PowerShell version, selected pillar and test IDs, affected stage, and a sanitized error summary.
+
+The assessment is a community project, not an official Microsoft product. Community issue reporting isn't a support contract or a guarantee of a response. Read the [support policy](https://github.com/microsoft/zerotrustassessment/blob/dev/SUPPORT.md) before sharing diagnostics.
\ No newline at end of file

+# Remove the Zero Trust Assessment | Microsoft Learn
+
+Remove Zero Trust Assessment packages and data when you no longer need them. Keep cleanup scoped to the assessment resources you intend to retire, without removing shared modules or access used by other tools. Before cleanup, identify the affected packages and outputs, and review your retention requirements.
+
+## Prerequisites
+
+- Identification of the assessment packages, output directories, and manually created diagnostic packages you intend to remove.
+- Your organization's retention requirements for reports, exports, and logs.
+
+## Remove assessment packages
+
+Close assessment sessions before removing the packages they use.
+
+1. Close the PowerShell sessions running the assessment.
+2. Remove installed assessment versions:
+
+    ```powershell
+    Uninstall-PSResource ZeroTrustAssessment -Version '*'
+    ```
+3. If the legacy `ZeroTrustAssessmentv2` package is installed, remove it separately with `Uninstall-PSResource ZeroTrustAssessmentv2 -Version '*'`.
+4. Review the isolated [dependency cache](get-started#bundled-powershell-modules) separately from the package. Don't remove it while any assessment session is using it.
+
+For a routine stable package update instead of removal, see [Install the PowerShell modules](get-started#install-the-powershell-modules).
+
+## Clean up resources
+
+Package removal and data/access cleanup are separate tasks. Review each location before deleting anything.
+
+1. Delete only the assessment output directories and manually created diagnostic packages you intend to remove. Reports and exports can contain sensitive tenant information.
+2. Review the [extended PSFramework log location](troubleshooting#logs-and-diagnostic-files) under your retention policy. Those logs are outside the assessment output directory and can include other PSFramework-using tools.
+3. If retiring a dedicated app registration, review and remove its grants and resource-role assignments before deleting it. Don't delete a shared Microsoft Graph PowerShell application or revoke shared consent without assessing the impact on other tools.
\ No newline at end of file

+# Microsoft Zero Trust Workshop - DevSecOps | Microsoft Learn
+
+DevSecOps integrates security into the people, processes, platforms, code, pipelines, and infrastructure used to build and deliver software. The DevSecOps workshop pillar helps organizations reduce implicit trust across the software development lifecycle by governing identities and repositories, securing code and dependencies, hardening CI/CD pipelines, and protecting the software supply chain.
+
+The DevSecOps workshop pillar helps organizations identify security gaps and create a prioritized implementation roadmap across developer platforms, source code, pipelines, build infrastructure, deployment environments, and security operations.
+
+The DevSecOps workshop pillar corresponds to the SAF [Development Security](security-adoption-discipline-development-security) discipline rather than to an SAF technology.
+
+## Why focus on DevSecOps?
+
+Compromised developer accounts, exposed secrets, vulnerable dependencies, untrusted pipeline components, insecure build runners, and weak release controls can provide paths from source code to production. The DevSecOps Workshop applies the Zero Trust principles of verify explicitly, use least privilege, and assume breach throughout the software development lifecycle.
+
+The expected output is an actionable backlog of DevSecOps projects prioritized into First, Then, and Next based on organizational risk, dependencies, implementation effort, developer impact, coverage, and readiness.
+
+## DevSecOps implementation areas
+
+| **Area** | **Details** |
+| --- | --- |
+| **Establish DevSecOps strategy, ownership, and governance** | Define accountable owners, operating responsibilities, security requirements, metrics, remediation service-level objectives, exception processes, maturity reviews, and compliance evidence across engineering and security teams. |
+| **Inventory and govern developer platforms and repositories** | Discover source repositories, DevOps organizations, build infrastructure, accounts, privileged groups, and service connections across platforms. Assign ownership, establish secure defaults, and prioritize onboarding into governance and security tooling. |
+| **Secure developer identities and access** | Integrate supported developer platforms with Microsoft Entra ID, apply Conditional Access, govern privileged groups and administrative roles, use access reviews and time-bound access where appropriate, and maintain tested emergency-access procedures. |
+| **Protect credentials and workload identities** | Detect and block exposed secrets, eliminate plaintext credentials, rotate existing secrets, and migrate pipelines and applications toward managed identities or workload identity federation. Scope permissions to the minimum required resources and operations. |
+| **Establish repository and code-review protections** | Apply organization-wide repository baselines, branch protections, CODEOWNERS or equivalent ownership controls, peer-review and approval requirements, protected environments, and controls for untrusted contributions and fork-based workflows. |
+| **Implement application security testing** | Integrate static, dynamic, API, and organization-specific security testing into developer workflows and CI/CD. Tune findings, surface feedback in pull requests or work items, and use third-party tools where they provide necessary coverage. |
+| **Secure dependencies and open-source usage** | Enable dependency inventory, alerts, updates, and pull-request review. Govern approved packages and registries, assess software composition and license risks, and prioritize vulnerable dependencies based on severity, exploitability, reachability, and business impact. |
+| **Protect the software supply chain** | Generate software bills of materials, establish artifact signing and build provenance, verify integrity at deployment boundaries, govern trusted publishing, use approved base images, and secure AI or machine-learning model artifacts where applicable. |
+| **Harden CI/CD pipelines and build infrastructure** | Use version-controlled pipeline definitions, pin third-party actions and tasks to trusted immutable references, protect reusable templates, apply least privilege, use ephemeral or hardened runners where appropriate, and evaluate pipeline risks against recognized practices such as the OWASP CI/CD Top 10. |
+| **Secure infrastructure as code and deployment controls** | Scan infrastructure-as-code changes in pull requests and pipelines, define approved modules and security baselines, deploy policy as code, monitor configuration drift, and require approvals and security gates for protected environments and releases. |
+| **Protect containers and cloud-native delivery** | Scan container images in pipelines and registries, govern approved base images, sign and verify images where appropriate, protect registries and clusters, and integrate runtime container protection with build and deployment controls. |
+| **Manage findings, vulnerabilities, and remediation** | Create a unified triage process for code, secret, dependency, pipeline, infrastructure, and cloud findings. Assign owners, apply risk-based remediation timelines, manage exceptions, clear existing backlogs, and track progress through centralized dashboards. |
+| **Integrate DevSecOps signals into security operations** | Connect developer platforms and cloud security services to centralized monitoring and SIEM workflows. Establish code-to-cloud traceability, attack-path analysis, DevOps-specific incident-response playbooks, and coordinated vulnerability-disclosure processes. |
+| **Build secure engineering practices and culture** | Embed security requirements in backlogs and design reviews, establish threat modeling, provide role-based secure-development training, support security champions, govern AI-assisted development tools and data handling, and continuously improve using measurable outcomes. |
+
+These areas summarize the DevSecOps workshop pillar. Use the detailed DevSecOps project guidance to review individual projects and implementation considerations.
+
+## How to use the DevSecOps Workshop
+
+Use the web-based Workshop with development, platform engineering, application security, cloud security, identity, infrastructure, data protection, compliance, and security operations stakeholders. For each relevant project:
+
+- Review the project objective and applicability to your environment.
+- Record the current status, notes, decisions, owners, and known dependencies.
+- Consider licensing, implementation effort, developer impact, technical prerequisites, coverage, and cross-pillar dependencies.
+- Prioritize the project into First, Then, or Next and incorporate it into the implementation roadmap.
+
+[Open the Zero Trust Workshop](https://aka.ms/ztworkshop) and select the DevSecOps pillar.
+
+[Review the detailed DevSecOps project guidance](https://microsoft.github.io/zerotrustassessment/docs/category/devsecops) for project-level information.
+
+## Assess your DevSecOps posture
+
+The Microsoft Zero Trust Assessment does not currently assess the DevSecOps pillar. Use the DevSecOps Workshop and detailed project guidance to evaluate your development platforms, repositories, pipelines, software supply chain, deployment controls, and operational processes. Findings from other assessed pillars can still provide useful cross-pillar context.
+
+[Learn about the Zero Trust Assessment](/en-us/security/zero-trust/assessment/overview) and its current pillar coverage.
+
+## Who should participate?
+
+- Software engineering, application architecture, and engineering leadership teams.
+- Platform engineering, DevOps, site reliability engineering, cloud platform, and release-management teams.
+- Application security, product security, cloud security, identity, data protection, security operations, and incident response teams.
+- Governance, risk, compliance, legal, procurement, open-source program, and business or application owners.
\ No newline at end of file

-# Evaluate Tenant Security with the Zero Trust Assessment | Microsoft Learn
+# Get Started with the Zero Trust Assessment | Microsoft Learn
 
-The Zero Trust Assessment checks your tenant configuration and recommends ways to improve security as described in our [overview](overview).
+Install the Zero Trust Assessment PowerShell module, connect to your tenant's services, and run an assessment to review your security configuration.
 
-[![Screenshot of a sample test from the Zero Trust Assessment tool.](media/sample-test.png)](media/sample-test.png#lightbox)
+Before you begin, prepare a supported PowerShell host and arrange access to the services you want to assess. See Prerequisites for the full requirements.
+
+These instructions describe the development source. Published packages can have different requirements and capabilities.
 
 ## Prerequisites
 
-- PowerShell 7. To install it, see [Install PowerShell on Windows, Linux, and macOS](/en-us/powershell/scripting/install/installing-powershell).
-- To connect and consent to the required permissions the first time, you need to be a [Global Administrator](/en-us/entra/identity/role-based-access-control/permissions-reference#global-administrator).
-- Subsequent runs require a user with the following roles:
-    - [Global Reader](/en-us/entra/identity/role-based-access-control/permissions-reference#global-reader)
-    - [Security Reader](/en-us/entra/identity/role-based-access-control/permissions-reference#security-reader)
-    - [Exchange Administrator](/en-us/entra/identity/role-based-access-control/permissions-reference#exchange-administrator)
-    - [SharePoint Administrator](/en-us/entra/identity/role-based-access-control/permissions-reference#sharepoint-administrator)
-- If you installed a previous version of the Zero Trust Assessment, uninstall it before continuing.
+- Access to the tenant and services you want to assess, including the [permissions and roles](permissions). Initial consent and runtime access are separate requirements.
+- PowerShell 7.6 or later for the current development dependency set. The pinned ExchangeOnlineManagement 3.10.1 uses .NET 10 and requires PowerShell 7.6+. Older packages can differ. See [Exchange module prerequisites](/en-us/powershell/exchange/exchange-online-powershell-v2?view=exchange-ps) and [Install PowerShell on Windows](/en-us/powershell/scripting/install/installing-powershell-on-windows). Windows PowerShell 5.1 isn't the assessment host.
+- Windows for full service coverage. SharePoint Online and Azure Information Protection (AIP) use Windows PowerShell compatibility sessions. On other platforms, these services are unavailable and their related tests are skipped.
+- The [Microsoft Visual C++ Redistributable (x64)](/en-us/cpp/windows/latest-supported-vc-redist?view=msvc-170#latest-microsoft-visual-c-redistributable-version) for the native DuckDB dependency on Windows.
+- A clean PowerShell process, preferably on a dedicated Windows virtual machine (VM), before importing other modules.
+- Applicable service subscriptions and licenses. Missing services, licenses, or data access can produce skipped checks, not evidence that the tenant meets a recommendation.
+- A protected output directory with sufficient disk space. Use a new directory for each fresh assessment.
+
+## Protect assessment data
+
+Decide how to protect local assessment data and whether to send assessment telemetry before you run the module.
+
+1. Limit access to the output directory. Reports, exports, and diagnostics can contain tenant configuration and personal information. Remove them when no longer needed. Importing Workshop JSON or sharing diagnostics is a separate action you control.
+2. Review the telemetry behavior. Telemetry is enabled by default; use `Invoke-ZtAssessment -DisableTelemetry` to disable the assessment telemetry event.
+
+The telemetry event's only tenant-specific custom property is the tenant ID. It also includes a name, timestamp, instrumentation key, and fixed anonymized IP address and operating system (OS) tags. Assessment results aren't included. Network services can process standard connection metadata, such as the source IP address. See the [telemetry implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/zerotrustassessment/blob/6a304637fc53846fd55182d495b6a2980f30b434/src/powershell/private/Send-ZtAppInsightsTelemetry.ps1).
 
 ## Install the PowerShell modules
 
-Follow these steps to install or update the assessment and connect to Microsoft Graph and your tenant.
+Install a published package in a clean process so that unrelated modules don't load conflicting assemblies first.
 
-1. Open a new PowerShell 7 window.
-2. Run the following command to install the `ZeroTrustAssessment` module:
+1. Open a fresh PowerShell 7 process, preferably with `pwsh -NoProfile`.
+2. Install the stable assessment package for your user:
 
     ```powershell
-    Install-Module ZeroTrustAssessment -Scope CurrentUser
+    Install-PSResource -Name ZeroTrustAssessment -Scope CurrentUser
     ```
+3. Review repository trust prompts before accepting them. Let the assessment initialize its dependencies when imported or first used.
 
-## Connect to Microsoft Graph and Microsoft Azure
-
-To run the Zero Trust Assessment module, you connect to multiple Microsoft cloud services including Microsoft Graph, Microsoft Azure, Microsoft Exchange, Microsoft SharePoint and Azure Information Protection.
-
-Run this command to connect to all the services.
+To opt into a prerelease package instead, use:
 
 ```powershell
-Connect-ZtAssessment
+Install-PSResource -Name ZeroTrustAssessment -Prerelease -Scope CurrentUser
 ```
 
-When you connect by using Microsoft Graph PowerShell, it requests these permissions:
-
-- AuditLog.Read.All
-- CrossTenantInformation.ReadBasic.All
-- DeviceManagementApps.Read.All
-- DeviceManagementConfiguration.Read.All
-- DeviceManagementManagedDevices.Read.All
-- DeviceManagementRBAC.Read.All
-- DeviceManagementServiceConfig.Read.All
-- Directory.Read.All
-- DirectoryRecommendations.Read.All
-- EntitlementManagement.Read.All
-- IdentityRiskEvent.Read.All
-- IdentityRiskyUser.Read.All
-- IdentityRiskyServicePrincipal.Read.All
-- NetworkAccess.Read.All
-- Policy.Read.All
-- Policy.Read.ConditionalAccess
-- Policy.Read.PermissionGrant
-- PrivilegedAccess.Read.AzureAD
-- Reports.Read.All
-- RoleManagement.Read.All
-- UserAuthenticationMethod.Read.All
-
-Note
-
-The consent prompt appears only if the Microsoft Graph PowerShell app doesn't already have these permissions. The next time you connect, you don't need to consent to the permissions again.
+Installing a prerelease selects a package version. The assessment's `-Preview` switch enables preview-only features when present; it isn't required for the seven current pillars. Neither option means every repository change has been published.
 
-### Sign in to Microsoft Graph
+To update an existing stable installation, run `Update-PSResource -Name ZeroTrustAssessment`, then start a fresh PowerShell process. You don't need to remove unrelated modules to update the assessment.
 
-1. Sign in to Microsoft Graph as a Global Administrator.
-2. Select **Accept**.
+### Bundled PowerShell modules
 
-### Sign in to Microsoft Azure
+The [development module manifest](https://github.com/microsoft/zerotrustassessment/blob/6a304637fc53846fd55182d495b6a2980f30b434/src/powershell/ZeroTrustAssessment.psd1) pins these versions. They describe the source snapshot, not necessarily the latest stable Gallery package.
 
-A second window opens for the Microsoft Azure sign-in. When you're prompted, sign in to Microsoft Azure as a Global Administrator.
+| Module | Required version | Service | Platform |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| **`PSFramework`** | `1.14.457` | Logging, configuration, and runspaces. | All. |
+| **`Microsoft.Graph.Authentication`** | `2.40.0` | Microsoft Graph. | All. |
+| **`Microsoft.Graph.Beta.Teams`** | `2.40.0` | Teams beta APIs. | All. |
+| **`Az.Accounts`** | `5.5.3` | Azure. | All. |
+| **`ExchangeOnlineManagement`** | `3.10.1` | Exchange Online and Security & Compliance. | All, where supported by the service. |
+| **`Microsoft.Online.SharePoint.PowerShell`** | `16.0.27612.12000` | SharePoint Online. | Windows. |
+| **`AipService`** | `3.1.0.0` | Azure Information Protection. | Windows. |
 
-The Microsoft Azure sign-in is required to check for the export of audit and sign-in logs. If you don't have Microsoft Azure, close the window without signing in, and ignore the warning. The assessment skips the test that relies on Microsoft Azure.
+The [dependency initializer](https://github.com/microsoft/zerotrustassessment/blob/6a304637fc53846fd55182d495b6a2980f30b434/src/powershell/Initialize-Dependencies.ps1) resolves these versions into `%APPDATA%\ZeroTrustAssessment\Modules` on Windows or `~/.cache/ZeroTrustAssessment/Modules` on macOS/Linux. It prepends that cache to `$env:PSModulePath`. Don't substitute arbitrary dependency versions.
 
-If you have multiple subscriptions, select a tenant and a subscription when prompted.
+### Use a clean assessment host
 
-A sign-in prompt appears for each cloud service, including Microsoft SharePoint and Microsoft Exchange.
+A dedicated Windows VM with PowerShell 7, the Visual C++ Redistributable, and the assessment's dependencies minimizes assembly conflicts.
 
-![Screenshot of the Azure subscription selection options in the PowerShell 7 console.](media/subscription-options.png)
+An installed module isn't automatically a conflict. Profiles, automatic imports, or earlier commands can load incompatible assemblies into the same process. Removing or reimporting a module doesn't reliably unload those assemblies. Retry in a fresh `pwsh -NoProfile` process rather than uninstalling shared modules.
 
-## Run the assessment
+## Connect to Microsoft Graph and Microsoft Azure
 
-The Zero Trust Assessment is read-only. It runs and stores all data locally on the desktop. It's a good practice to store the assessment report securely and delete the generated folder and its contents from the local drive once the assessment is complete.
+The connector establishes separate connections to Microsoft Graph, Azure, Exchange Online, Security & Compliance, SharePoint Online, and AIP.
 
-After you provide Global Administrator consent to the permissions in the first run, subsequent runs can be performed as a Global Reader.
+1. Arrange the [interactive user access](permissions#interactive-user-access) for the services you intend to assess. Activate eligible roles through Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management before connecting.
+2. Connect to the intended tenant. Replace the example domain with your tenant's verified domain:
 
-To run the assessment, use this command:
+    ```powershell
+    Connect-ZtAssessment -Tenant contoso.onmicrosoft.com
+    ```
+3. Complete the service prompts and review each connection status. Cached sessions and single sign-on can reduce prompts; there's no guaranteed prompt count. Reconnect after changing access.
 
-```powershell
-Invoke-ZtAssessment
-```
+For service selection, connection options, and certificate-based unattended access, see [Connect to assessment services](connect-services).
 
-The assessment saves the results in the current working folder `.\ZeroTrustReport\ZeroTrustAssessmentReport.html`. After the assessment completes, the report opens automatically in the default browser.
+### Sign in to Microsoft Graph
 
-Caution
+Use the assessment account's runtime roles, preferably Global Reader, after an authorized administrator arranges consent. Consent doesn't assign runtime roles. New scopes can require consent again; see [Permissions and roles](permissions).
 
-The report and the export folder contain sensitive tenant information that threat actors might use to their advantage. Share the report and folder only with authorized personnel in your organization.
+### Sign in to Microsoft Azure
 
-Use the `-Path` parameter to provide a custom location to store the assessment report. For example, the following command saves the report in the folder `C:/MyAssessment01/ZeroTrustAssessmentReport.html`:
+Use an account with Reader access, or equivalent read permissions, at the intended subscription/resource scopes. Select the intended tenant and subscription if prompted. Azure access is separate from Microsoft Entra ID directory roles. Skipping Azure limits Infrastructure, Network, and security operations (SecOps) coverage as well as log export checks.
 
-```powershell
-Invoke-ZtAssessment -Path C:\MyAssessment01
-```
+## Run the assessment
+
+Run the assessment in the same PowerShell session after checking the service connections. The assessment doesn't apply tenant remediation.
+
+Warning
 
-Tip
+A fresh, non-resume run against a nonempty output directory prompts to delete its contents. In a detected continuous integration (CI) environment, the current implementation cleans it automatically. Use a dedicated new directory, never a folder containing unrelated files.
 
-For large tenants, the Zero Trust Assessment might take more than 24 hours to run. Don't stop the assessment while it's running, even if the assessment logs warnings or errors.
+1. Choose a working directory where the default `.\ZeroTrustReport` output folder is new. For a custom path or a selected pillar, see [Run and resume assessments](run-assessment).
+2. Run the assessment:
+
+    ```powershell
+    Invoke-ZtAssessment
+    ```
+3. Follow the progress dashboard and review warnings or errors. Runtime varies with tenant size, service response times, throttling, and selected tests. Use the [diagnostic files](troubleshooting#logs-and-diagnostic-files) to distinguish active work from a failure.
 
 ## Review assessment results
 
-After the assessment runs, the report opens the **Overview** tab in your default browser. The **Overview** tab shows key Zero Trust information about the tenant.
+The redesigned report opens by default at `.\ZeroTrustReport\ZeroTrustAssessmentReport.html`. Review all seven pillars, including skipped checks and errors, before drawing conclusions. See [Review results and import into Workshop](review-results).
 
-[![Screenshot of assessment results on the Overview tab.](media/results-overview.png)](media/results-overview-full.png#lightbox)
+## Turn assessment results into action
 
-The **Identity**, **Devices**, **Network**, and **Data** tabs show a list of results from the tests run against the tenant. The results show the [**Risk**](glossary#risk-level) and result **Status** of each test.
+Use the **Risk**, **Status**, and recommended remediation for each result to build a prioritized improvement backlog. Assign each item to the team that owns the affected technology, and track the security outcome rather than treating assessment completion as the end of the work.
 
-[![Screenshot of assessment results on the Identity tab.](media/results-identity.png)](media/results-identity.png#lightbox)
+### Identity, endpoint, network, and data owners
 
-To see more details about a test, select a result. The details describe what was tested and list recommended remediation actions to address the tenant configuration. For more detail about some of the terms used in each check see our [glossary](glossary).
+Use the assessment tabs to continue into the corresponding implementation guidance:
 
-[![Screenshot of a sample test from the Zero Trust Assessment tool.](media/sample-test.png)](media/sample-test.png#lightbox)
+- **Identity:**[Implement Zero Trust for identity](../deploy/identity).
+- **Devices:**[Implement Zero Trust for endpoints](../deploy/endpoints).
+- **Network:**[Implement Zero Trust for networks](../deploy/networks).
+- **Data:**[Implement Zero Trust for data](../deploy/data).
 
-## Remove the Zero Trust Assessment module
+### Security leaders and architects
 
-To remove the Zero Trust Assessment module:
+Use these paths to coordinate remediation across teams and connect findings to the broader security program:
 
-1. Remove the PowerShell module.
-2. Delete the folder that the Zero Trust Assessment module created.
+- [Prioritize remediation with security posture management](../security-adoption-discipline-posture).
+- [Organize security improvements with the Microsoft Security Adoption Framework](../security-adoption-model).
+- [Map findings to security standards and frameworks](../security-standards-and-frameworks).
+- [Plan integrated security capabilities with MCRA](../microsoft-reference-architecture).
 
-## FAQs
+## Remove the Zero Trust Assessment module
 
-### Export troubleshooting logs
+When you no longer need the module or its data, follow [Remove the assessment](uninstall). Remove only the outputs and diagnostic packages you intend to delete; extended PSFramework logs are stored separately.
 
-If an issue occurs, export a log using these instructions.
+## FAQs
 
-Run the following command in the same session where you ran the assessment to create the export package (update the date to reflect the date of your run).
+These links preserve access to procedures that now have dedicated articles.
 
-```powershell
-New-PSFSupportPackage -Path C:\AssessmentLog_2025_01_01 -Force
-```
+### Export troubleshooting logs
 
-Zip this folder along with the folder that was created by `Invoke-ZtAssessment` (default is `ZeroTrustAssessment`).
+Capture diagnostics in the same PowerShell session and review them before sharing. See [Capture a support package](troubleshooting#capture-a-support-package).
 
 ### Viewing logs during test execution
 
-To view the progress of long running tests, open the `/zt-export/logs` folder found inside your assessment folder.
+For per-run progress logs, collector and test details, and extended PSFramework logs, see [Logs and diagnostic files](troubleshooting#logs-and-diagnostic-files).
 
 ### Uninstall previous versions
 
-Run the following commands to ensure all versions of the past modules are uninstalled
-
-```powershell
-Uninstall-Module ZeroTrustAssessment -Force -AllVersions
-```
-
-Restart PowerShell and install the latest version.
+For current and legacy package cleanup, see [Remove assessment packages](uninstall#remove-assessment-packages). For a routine stable update, use the installation guidance.
 
 ### Could not load file or assembly Microsoft.Graph.Authentication
 
-This error happens when you have conflicting versions of Microsoft Graph PowerShell installed.
-
-To fix this error we recommend uninstalling all Microsoft Graph PowerShell modules installed on your system. You can use a helper module like [uninstall-graph.merill.net](https://uninstall-graph.merill.net/) to run the cleanup.
-
-When uninstalling Microsoft Graph you should also uninstall all versions of the Zero Trust Assessment, restart PowerShell and then install the latest version.
-
-```powershell
-Install-Module Uninstall-Graph
-Uninstall-Module ZeroTrustAssessment -Force -AllVersions
-Uninstall-Graph
-```
+Start with a clean process and the assessment's pinned dependencies, not blanket removal of shared modules. See [Resolve Graph assembly conflicts](troubleshooting#resolve-graph-assembly-conflicts).
 
 ### How can I know what the script does?
 
-The code for this assessment is open source. Review it at `https://github.com/microsoft/zerotrustassessment/tree/psnext/src/powershell`.
+Review the source, progress dashboard, and [assessment diagnostics](troubleshooting#inspect-assessment-activity).
 
 ### Why did I get the exception error, "The type initializer for 'DuckDB.NET.Data.DuckDBConnectionStringBuilder' threw an exception."?
 
-On a new installation of Windows, you might see the following error:
-
-> 
-> The type initializer for 'DuckDB.NET.Data.DuckDBConnectionStringBuilder' threw an exception. Inner exception: Unable to load DLL 'duckdb' or one of its dependencies: The specified module could not be found. (0x8007007E) Inner exception type: DllNotFoundException
-
-This error occurs because you're running on a system that doesn't include `Microsoft Visual C++ 2015-2022 Redistributable (x64) - Microsoft.VCRedist.2015+.x64`. VCRedist usually installs when you install Microsoft products such as Microsoft Office or Microsoft Entra Connect Sync. If you're using a new device, you might need to install this component manually. See [Latest Microsoft Visual C++ Redistributable version](/en-us/cpp/windows/latest-supported-vc-redist).
-
-Support for Windows on ARM64 devices is not available at this time.
+Inspect the inner exception before choosing a remedy. See [Resolve DuckDB initialization errors](troubleshooting#resolve-duckdb-initialization-errors).
 
 ### How do I get support?
 
-Raise support issues on the [Zero Trust Assessment GitHub repo](https://github.com/microsoft/zerotrustassessment/issues).
\ No newline at end of file
+The assessment has community help, not official Microsoft product support. See [Report an issue or provide feedback](troubleshooting#report-an-issue-or-provide-feedback).
\ No newline at end of file

-# Zero Trust Assessment Overview | Microsoft Learn
+# What Is the Zero Trust Assessment? | Microsoft Learn
 
-We publish extensive guidance on how to configure [Microsoft Entra](/en-us/entra/fundamentals/configure-security), [Microsoft Intune](/en-us/intune/intune-service/protect/zero-trust-configure-security), [Azure networks](/en-us/azure/networking/security/zero-trust-network-security) and [Microsoft Purview](/en-us/purview/configure-security) for increased security, but manually checking these against a tenant's configuration can be time-consuming and error-prone. The Zero Trust Assessment transforms this process with automation to test for hundreds of security configuration items aligned with the Secure Future Initiative (SFI) and Zero Trust pillars, then guides you through remediation steps to help operationalize Zero Trust principles.
+The Zero Trust Assessment is a community PowerShell module that checks your Microsoft 365 tenant and Azure configuration against security recommendations. Use its reports to review findings and plan improvements across seven Zero Trust pillars.
 
-These tests are drawn from trusted sources in cybersecurity, including:
+The assessment doesn't apply remediation. It collects configuration data and produces local reports that help you decide what to address.
 
-- Industry standards like those developed by NIST, CISA, and CIS
-- Microsoft's internal security baselines that protect Microsoft's own infrastructure
-- Real-world customer insights from thousands of security implementations
+## Why run this assessment?
 
-[![Screenshot of a sample report output from the Zero Trust Assessment tool.](media/results-overview.png)](media/results-overview-full.png#lightbox)
+Manually comparing tenant configuration with security guidance can be time-consuming. The assessment automates these checks and shows where your configuration aligns with recommendations and where you need to investigate.
 
-## Why run this assessment?
+The report includes findings, risk and status filters, and supporting guidance. Review skipped checks and errors as well as passed and failed checks: missing access, services, or licenses can leave part of your environment unassessed.
+
+For guidance on interpreting reports, see [Review assessment results](review-results).
+
+[![Screenshot of a synthetic assessment overview with tenant summaries and results across seven pillars.](media/zero-trust-assessment-overview.png)](media/zero-trust-assessment-overview.png#lightbox)
+
+## Supported pillars
+
+The current default run includes all seven pillars. Use the linked guidance and coverage summaries to plan your assessment.
+
+| Pillar | Guidance or coverage |
+| --- | --- |
+| **Identity** | [Configure Microsoft Entra for increased security](/en-us/entra/fundamentals/configure-security). |
+| **Devices** | [Configure Microsoft Intune for increased security](/en-us/intune/intune-service/protect/zero-trust-configure-security). |
+| **Network** | [Apply Zero Trust principles to Azure networks](/en-us/azure/networking/security/zero-trust-network-security). |
+| **Data** | [Configure Microsoft Purview for increased security](/en-us/purview/configure-security). |
+| **Infrastructure** | Infrastructure assessment scope. |
+| **Security operations (SecOps)** | Security operations assessment coverage. |
+| **AI** | [Configure agent identity security](ai-pillar). |
+
+### Infrastructure
+
+Infrastructure findings use Microsoft Defender for Cloud recommendations. The assessment includes only accessible Azure subscriptions tagged with `ZeroTrustAssessment:Infrastructure`. If no matching subscription exists, the assessment skips rather than passes. See [Infrastructure scope](run-assessment#infrastructure-scope).
+
+### Security operations (SecOps)
+
+The default run includes SecOps. Azure connections support SecOps, Infrastructure, and Network assessments, not just audit and sign-in log export checks. Arrange the relevant [service and resource access](permissions) and review skipped checks or authorization errors before treating the run as complete.
+
+## How the assessment works
+
+The assessment separates service connections, assessment execution, and report review:
+
+1. [Connect to the services](connect-services) you intend to assess. Each service has its own authentication and authorization requirements.
+2. [Run the assessment](run-assessment) to collect data and evaluate the selected checks.
+3. [Review the local reports](review-results), investigate incomplete coverage, and use the findings to plan improvements. You can also import the generated JSON into Zero Trust Workshop.
+
+Reports, exports, and diagnostics can contain sensitive tenant configuration and personal information. Review [data handling and telemetry](get-started#protect-assessment-data) before running the assessment.
+
+Before connecting, see [Review permissions and roles](permissions) to identify the access requirements for your assessment.
+
+## Source and package versions
+
+These articles cover the [development source](https://github.com/microsoft/zerotrustassessment/blob/6a304637fc53846fd55182d495b6a2980f30b434/src/powershell/doc/readme.md). Published packages can differ. Check the [release history](https://github.com/microsoft/zerotrustassessment/releases) and the help for your installed version before relying on a version-specific dependency, parameter, or permission.
 
-Running this assessment helps you confirm you've configured a strong baseline of security for your tenant. It lets you know where you might need to make investments and where you already align with best practices. From this baseline, you might implement even stronger or more advanced controls.
+[Release 2.6.0](https://github.com/microsoft/zerotrustassessment/releases/tag/2.6.0) introduced the redesigned report and all seven default pillars. Later source changes include updated dependencies and the `AttackSimulation.Read.All` scope. Installing a prerelease package and using the assessment's `-Preview` switch are separate choices.
 
 ## Open source and transparent
 
-**See exactly what the assessment does.** The entire codebase is open source and available for review:
+Microsoft employees maintain the assessment as a community project. It isn't an official Microsoft product and Microsoft provides it as-is, without support through a Microsoft support program or service.
 
-- View the source code: [GitHub repository](https://github.com/microsoft/zerotrustassessment/tree/main/src/powershell)
-- Report issues: [GitHub issues](https://github.com/microsoft/zerotrustassessment/issues)
-- Contribute improvements: Community contributions welcome
\ No newline at end of file
+Review the [PowerShell source](https://github.com/microsoft/zerotrustassessment/tree/dev/src/powershell) and [support policy](https://github.com/microsoft/zerotrustassessment/blob/dev/SUPPORT.md). For community help, see [Report an issue or provide feedback](troubleshooting#report-an-issue-or-provide-feedback).

+## How the CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model maps to SAF
+
+The CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model (ZTMM) organizes Zero Trust maturity around five pillars and three cross-cutting capabilities. SAF uses a different but complementary model to organize the security work needed to achieve and sustain these outcomes.
+
+The mapping below connects CISA Zero Trust maturity areas to relevant SAF security disciplines and technologies. It does not replace the CISA ZTMM or imply a one-to-one relationship between the two models. Organizations can use the mapping to identify the security work, technology areas, and Microsoft implementation guidance that support their Zero Trust maturity objectives.
+
+In SAF, security disciplines describe the work needed to manage security risk and improve security capabilities, while technologies identify what must be protected. **The CISA cross-cutting capabilities span multiple technology areas and map primarily to SAF security disciplines.**

+| **Visibility and analytics** | [SecOps](security-adoption-discipline-security-operations); [Security Posture Management](security-adoption-discipline-posture) | [Spans technologies](deploy/overview) | Telemetry, detection, investigation, posture measurement, and analytics. |

+| **Governance** | [Security Strategy, Integration, and Governance](security-adoption-discipline-strategy); [Security Architecture](security-adoption-discipline-architecture); [Security Posture Management](security-adoption-discipline-posture) | [Spans technologies](deploy/overview) | Policy, ownership, risk management, measurement, and oversight. |

-# Zero Trust deployment for technology pillars overview | Microsoft Learn
+# Technologies in the Security Adoption Framework | Microsoft Learn
 
-This article summarizes technology pillars in our [Zero Trust adoption model](../security-adoption-model).
+Organizations must protect different types of technology assets with controls appropriate to the nature of each technology, including identity, endpoints, applications, data, infrastructure, network, and AI.
 
-Technology pillars represent the core areas of your security architecture. They group related capabilities and controls into logical domains such as identity, endpoints, data, apps, infrastructure, networks, and security operations.
+Each technology presents different security requirements, risks, and implementation considerations. Security disciplines apply security practices across these technologies, and technical solutions implement controls and capabilities across one or more of them.
 
-Each pillar answers the same fundamental question:
+Zero Trust principles apply across all of these technology areas. Rather than organizing guidance around individual products or features, the [Security Adoption Framework](../security-adoption-model) uses technologies as durable areas for understanding and applying security guidance.
 
-**How do we apply Zero Trust principles to this part of the environment?**
+![Diagram showing elements of visibility, automation, and orchestration in Zero Trust.](../media/diagram-zero-trust-security-elements.png)
 
-Instead of thinking in terms of individual products or features, pillars provide a stable way to organize security design and implementation across your environment.
+## Technologies in SAF
 
-![Diagram of elements of visibility, automation, and orchestration in Zero Trust.](../media/diagram-zero-trust-security-elements.png)
+These areas are represented as technologies in the Microsoft Security Adoption Framework (SAF) and are also used as pillars in the [Zero Trust Workshop](../workshop-zero-trust-overview).
 
-## Technology pillars in the adoption model
+SAF connects four complementary components:
 
-Our structured adoption model focuses on three components:
+- [Business scenarios](../security-adoption-business-scenarios-overview) define desired security outcomes based on business priorities and risk.
+- [Security disciplines](../security-adoption-discipline-overview) describe the security work needed to manage risk, make decisions, and improve security capabilities.
+- **Technologies** identify areas of the environment that must be protected, including identity, endpoints, applications, data, infrastructure, network, and AI.
+- [Technical solutions](../implement-overview) provide implementation guidance for security requirements and capabilities that often span multiple technologies.
 
-- [Business scenarios](../security-adoption-business-scenarios-overview) - Define the most critical security outcomes for the organization. They focus on **why** we're adopting Zero Trust security.
-- [Security disciplines](../security-adoption-discipline-overview) - Guide teams to define strategy, architecture, processes, and controls across common areas of security so that we can deliver the business scenarios. They focus on **what** Zero Trust capabilities are required.
-- **Technology pillars** - Secure specific areas of the organization such as identity, data, and devices. They focus on **where** security capabilities are implemented.
-- [Technical solutions](../implement-overview) - As adoption moves towards deployment, technical solutions provide detailed guidance for implementing security controls across technology pillars. They focus on **how** security is implemented.
+These components work together rather than forming a sequential process. A business scenario can require work across multiple security disciplines and technologies, while a technical solution can implement security requirements across several technology areas.
 
-In the Zero Trust adoption model, technology pillars sit between strategy and implementation.
+Zero Trust principles apply across this model, from business and security decisions through architecture, technology, implementation, and operations.
 
-Technology pillars don't define outcomes (business solutions) or steps (technical solutions), but they do:
+## Technologies
 
-- Define technical boundaries where security controls are applied. These boundaries are used by solutions to organize implementation guidance and logic.
-- Act as the bridge between intent (why) and implementation (how).
+| Technology | Description |
+| --- | --- |
+| [![Fingerprint icon](../media/icon-identity-small.png)](identity)[Identity](identity) | Protect identities and access. Verify identities, manage privileges, and make access decisions based on appropriate context and risk. |
+| [![Endpoints icon](../media/icon-endpoints-small.png)](endpoints)[Endpoints](endpoints) | Protect devices that access organizational resources. Assess device state and risk and apply appropriate configuration, protection, and access controls. |
+| [![Ones and zeroes icon](../media/icon-data-small.png)](data)[Data](data) | Protect data throughout its lifecycle using capabilities such as classification, access control, encryption, and monitoring. |
+| [![Application window icon](../media/icon-applications-small.png)](applications)[Applications](applications) | Protect applications, services, and APIs and the identities, permissions, sessions, and data they use. |
+| [![Data storage disks icon](../media/icon-infrastructure-small.png)](infrastructure)[Infrastructure](infrastructure) | Protect compute, platforms, and supporting infrastructure through secure configuration, access control, protection, and monitoring. |
+| [![Network diagram icon](../media/icon-networks-small.png)](networks)[Network](networks) | Protect connectivity and communications using controls such as segmentation, traffic inspection, secure access, and monitoring. |
+| [![AI diagram icon](../media/icon-ai-small.png)](/en-us/security/saf/technologies/ai/overview)[AI](/en-us/security/saf/technologies/ai/overview) | Protect AI applications, agents, models, data, prompts, context, and tool integrations. Apply appropriate security controls across identity, data, applications, infrastructure, and network technologies. |
 
-## Pillars
+## How Zero Trust workshop pillars map to SAF
 
-| Technology pillar | Description |
-| --- | --- |
-| [![Fingerprint icon](../media/icon-identity-small.png)](identity)[Identities](identity) | Control access decisions. Every request starts with identity verification and enforcement of least privilege. |
-| [![Endpoints icon.](../media/icon-endpoints-small.png)](endpoints)[Endpoints](endpoints) | Evaluate and enforce device trust. Access depends on device health, compliance, and risk. |
-| [![Ones and zeroes icon.](../media/icon-data-small.png)](data)[Data](data) | Protect the asset itself. Security persists with the data through classification, labeling, encryption, and access control. |
-| [![Application window icon.](../media/icon-applications-small.png)](applications)[Apps](applications) | Govern how data is accessed. Apply controls at the application and API layer, including permissions and session controls. |
-| [![Data storage disks icon.](../media/icon-infrastructure-small.png)](infrastructure)[Infrastructure](infrastructure) | Secure compute resources. Harden servers, VMs, containers, and services through configuration, access control, and monitoring. |
-| [![Network diagram icon.](../media/icon-networks-small.png)](networks)[Network](networks) | Control connectivity and movement. Segment and monitor traffic to prevent lateral movement and enforce secure communication. |
-| [![Gear icon.](../media/icon-visibility-automation-orchestration-small.png)](visibility-automation-orchestration)[SecOps](visibility-automation-orchestration) | Integrate and operationalize all pillars. Detect, investigate, and respond using signals from across the environment. |
+The [Zero Trust Workshop](../workshop-zero-trust-overview) uses **pillars** as its organizing concept for planning and implementation. Most workshop pillars correspond to technologies in SAF, including identity, endpoints, applications, data, infrastructure, network, and AI.
+
+Two workshop pillars map differently in SAF:
+
+- **SecOps** maps to the SAF [SecOps](../security-adoption-discipline-security-operations) security discipline.
+- **DevSecOps/Development Security** maps to the SAF [Development Security](../security-adoption-discipline-development) security discipline.
+
+This approach allows the Zero Trust Workshop to retain its familiar pillar-based structure while SAF distinguishes between technologies that must be protected and the security disciplines that perform security work across them.
 
 ## Zero Trust implementation workshops
 
-Microsoft's Zero Trust implementation workshops are available for each pillar. [Learn more](../workshop-zero-trust-overview).
+The [Zero Trust Workshop](../workshop-zero-trust-overview) provides practical guidance for applying Zero Trust principles across these areas.
 
 ## What's next?
 
-- [Review](../implement-overview) technical solutions.
-- [Learn about](../security-adoption-model) our Zero Trust adoption model.
-- [Review](../security-adoption-business-scenarios-overview) critical security business scenarios.
\ No newline at end of file

 # Secure app identity with permissions and access | Microsoft Learn
 
-This article continues from the [Zero Trust identity and access management development best practices](identity-iam-development-best-practices) article to help you use a Zero Trust approach to identity in your software development lifecycle (SDLC).
-
-Here's an overview of the **Permissions and access** articles in this [Developer Guide](overview) so that you can dive into identity components that include authentication, authorization, and identity management.
-
-- [Integrate applications with Microsoft Entra ID and the Microsoft identity platform](integrate-apps-microsoft-identity-platform) helps developers to build and integrate apps that IT pros can secure in the enterprise.
-- [Register applications](app-registration) introduces developers to the application registration process and its requirements. It helps them to ensure that apps satisfy Zero Trust principles of use least privileged access and assume breach.
-- [Supported identity and account types for single- and multitenant apps](identity-supported-account-types) explains how you can choose if your app allows only users from your Microsoft Entra tenant, any Microsoft Entra tenant, or users with personal Microsoft accounts.
-- [Authenticate users for Zero Trust](user-authentication) helps developers to learn best practices for authenticating application users in Zero Trust application development. It describes how to enhance application security with the Zero Trust principles of least privilege and verify explicitly.
-- [Acquire authorization to access resources](acquire-application-authorization-to-access-resources) helps you to understand how to best ensure Zero Trust when acquiring resource access permissions for your application.
-- [Develop delegated permissions strategy](developer-strategy-delegated-permission) helps you to implement the best approach for managing permissions in your application and develop with Zero Trust principles.
-- [Develop application permissions strategy](developer-strategy-application-permissions) helps you to decide upon your application permissions approach to credential management.
-- [Request permissions that require administrative consent](permissions-require-admin-consent) describes the permission and consent experience when application permissions require administrative consent.
-- [Reduce overprivileged permissions and apps](overprivileged-permissions) helps you to understand why applications shouldn't request more permissions than they need (overprivileged). Learn how to limit privilege to manage access and improve security.
-- [Provide application identity credentials when there's no user](identity-non-user-applications) explains Managed Identities for Azure resources best practices for services (nonuser applications).
-- [Manage tokens for Zero Trust](token-management) helps developers to build security into applications with ID tokens, access tokens, and security tokens that they can receive from the Microsoft identity platform.
-- [Customize tokens](zero-trust-token-customization) describes the information that you can receive in Microsoft Entra tokens and how you can customize tokens.
-- [Secure applications with Continuous Access Evaluation](secure-with-cae) helps developers to improve application security with Continuous Access Evaluation. Learn how to [ensure Zero Trust support](overview) in your apps that receive authorization to access resources when they acquire access tokens from Microsoft Entra ID.
-- [Configure group claims and app roles in tokens](configure-tokens-group-claims-app-roles) shows you how to configure your apps with app role definitions and assign security groups.
-- [API Protection](protect-api) describes best practices for protecting your API through registration, defining permissions and consent, and enforcing access to achieve your Zero Trust goals.
-- [Example of API protected by Microsoft identity consent framework](protected-api-example) helps you to design least privilege application permissions strategies for the best user experience.
-- [Call an API from another API](api-calls-api) helps you to ensure Zero Trust when you have one API that needs to call another API. Learn how to securely develop your application when it's working on behalf of a user.
-- [Authorization best practices](developer-strategy-authorization-best-practices) helps you to implement the best authorization, permission, and consent models for your applications.
\ No newline at end of file
+Use this guide to build applications that authenticate identities, authorize access, minimize privilege, and protect APIs and tokens by using Zero Trust principles. It's for developers, application architects, identity professionals, and platform teams that design or govern application access.
+
+Start with the task that matches your current decision. If you're designing a new application identity, use this sequence: **register -> authenticate -> authorize -> minimize permissions -> protect APIs and tokens -> validate continuously**.
+
+## Register and authenticate applications
+
+Establish the application's identity boundary, supported account types, and authentication method.
+
+- [Integrate applications with Microsoft Entra ID and the Microsoft identity platform](integrate-apps-microsoft-identity-platform) to build apps that IT professionals can secure in the enterprise.
+- [Register applications](app-registration) by using least privilege and assume-breach principles.
+- [Choose supported identity and account types](identity-supported-account-types) for single-tenant, multitenant, and personal Microsoft account scenarios.
+- [Authenticate users for Zero Trust](user-authentication) by verifying explicitly and applying least privilege.
+
+## Choose delegated or application permissions
+
+Choose whether the application acts on behalf of a user or uses its own identity, then design authorization and consent accordingly.
+
+- [Acquire authorization to access resources](acquire-application-authorization-to-access-resources).
+- [Develop a delegated permissions strategy](developer-strategy-delegated-permission) for applications that act on behalf of a signed-in user.
+- [Develop an application permissions strategy](developer-strategy-application-permissions) for services and background processes that act without a user.
+- [Request permissions that require administrative consent](permissions-require-admin-consent).
+- [Apply authorization best practices](developer-strategy-authorization-best-practices).
+- [Coordinate developer and administrator responsibilities](identity-developer-administrator-responsibilities) for registration, authorization, and access.
+
+## Reduce excessive privilege and protect workload identities
+
+Limit access to what the application needs, and use managed identities where possible.
+
+- [Reduce overprivileged permissions and apps](overprivileged-permissions).
+- [Provide application identity credentials when there's no user](identity-non-user-applications) by using managed identities for Azure resources.
+
+## Protect APIs and tokens
+
+Treat tokens, API permissions, and downstream calls as part of the application's security boundary.
+
+- [Manage tokens for Zero Trust](token-management).
+- [Customize tokens](zero-trust-token-customization).
+- [Configure group claims and app roles in tokens](configure-tokens-group-claims-app-roles).
+- [Protect APIs](protect-api) through registration, permissions, consent, and access enforcement.
+- [Review an API protected by the Microsoft identity consent framework](protected-api-example).
+- [Call an API from another API](api-calls-api) when the application works on behalf of a user.
+
+## Operate and validate continuously
+
+Reevaluate access as risk, session context, application behavior, and organizational policy change.
+
+- [Secure applications with Continuous Access Evaluation](secure-with-cae).
+- [Understand Zero Trust compliance for applications](identity-zero-trust-compliance).
+- Use [Zero Trust identity and access management development best practices](identity-iam-development-best-practices) throughout the software development lifecycle.
+- Apply [standards-based development methodologies](identity-standards-based-development-methodologies).
\ No newline at end of file
