@@ -57,6 +57,28 @@ The strategy has four goals.
 
 Microsoft has an expanding array of Zero Trust capabilities powered by a unified identity platform and pre-integrated, fit-for-purpose security tools. These security tools provide comprehensive coverage across the seven pillars of the DoD Zero Trust Strategy for target and advanced activities.
 
+## How the DoD Zero Trust Strategy maps to SAF
+
+The DoD Zero Trust Strategy and supporting architecture organize Zero Trust around pillars, capabilities, activities, and implementation outcomes. SAF complements this model by organizing the security work and technology areas needed to put those objectives into sustained operation.
+
+The mapping below connects DoD Zero Trust areas to relevant SAF security disciplines and technologies. It is not a replacement for the authoritative DoD Zero Trust Strategy, Reference Architecture, or execution guidance, and it does not imply a one-to-one relationship between the models.
+
+Organizations can use the mapping to identify the security disciplines that perform the required work, the technologies where Zero Trust controls are applied, and relevant Microsoft implementation guidance. DoD includes automation and orchestration and visibility and analytics among its seven pillars. These areas span multiple technologies and map primarily to operational security disciplines such as Security Operations (SecOps) and Security Posture.
+
+This mapping operates at the DoD Zero Trust pillar and capability-area level. It is intended to help organizations navigate from DoD Zero Trust objectives to relevant SAF and Microsoft guidance, not to provide a capability-by-capability or activity-by-activity crosswalk.
+
+| DoD area | Primary SAF security disciplines | SAF technologies | Mapping rationale |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| **User** | [Access and Identity](security-adoption-discipline-identity-access); [Security Posture Management](security-adoption-discipline-posture); [SecOps](security-adoption-discipline-security-operations) | [Identity](deploy/identity) | User identity, authentication, authorization, privilege, risk, and access. |
+| **Device** | [Infrastructure Security](security-adoption-discipline-infrastructure); [Security Posture Management](security-adoption-discipline-posture); [SecOps](security-adoption-discipline-security-operations) | [Endpoints](deploy/endpoints); [Infrastructure](deploy/infrastructure) | Device identity, configuration, compliance, protection, and monitoring. |
+| **Applications and workloads** | [Development Security](security-adoption-discipline-development); [Security Architecture](security-adoption-discipline-architecture); [Access and Identity](security-adoption-discipline-identity-access); [SecOps](security-adoption-discipline-security-operations) | [Applications](deploy/applications); [Infrastructure](deploy/infrastructure); [AI](/en-us/security/saf/technologies/ai/overview) where applicable | Secure applications and workloads, workload identities, access, and runtime protection. |
+| **Data** | [Data Security](security-adoption-discipline-data); [Access and Identity](security-adoption-discipline-identity-access); [Security Architecture](security-adoption-discipline-architecture) | [Data](deploy/data) | Classification, protection, rights, access, encryption, and governance. |
+| **Network and environment** | [Infrastructure Security](security-adoption-discipline-infrastructure); [Security Architecture](security-adoption-discipline-architecture); [SecOps](security-adoption-discipline-security-operations) | [Network](deploy/networks); [Infrastructure](deploy/infrastructure) | Segmentation, network enforcement, communications protection, and telemetry. |
+| **Automation and orchestration** | [SecOps](security-adoption-discipline-security-operations); [Security Strategy, Integration, and Governance](security-adoption-discipline-strategy); [Development Security](security-adoption-discipline-development) where appropriate | [Spans technologies](deploy/overview) | Automated policy enforcement, response, orchestration, and integration. |
+| **Visibility and analytics** | [SecOps](security-adoption-discipline-security-operations); [Security Posture Management](security-adoption-discipline-posture) | [Spans technologies](deploy/overview) | Collection, correlation, detection, analytics, investigation, and measurement. |
+
+Microsoft implementation guidance is the downstream layer for applying these concepts with Microsoft technologies. It can support applicable DoD capabilities and activities, but it does not replace the authoritative DoD Zero Trust Strategy, Reference Architecture, or execution guidance and does not by itself demonstrate organizational achievement, maturity, or compliance. Start with the canonical [Security standards and frameworks](security-standards-and-frameworks) hub for related mappings and SAF guidance.
+
 ## Pillars, capabilities, and activities
 
 The DoD Zero Trust Strategy covers seven pillars representing protection areas for Zero Trust. Use the following links to go to sections of the guide.
@@ -86,4 +108,4 @@ When activities have more than one part, Microsoft guidance assumes you implemen
 
 This document prioritizes recommendations by product, or feature area, listing the most essential items first. When implementation actions span features in different Microsoft services, these actions are ordered in the required configuration sequence. Activity-level guidance lists all recommendations relevant for each activity. Your organization might complete the activity by doing a portion of the recommended configuration or implementing alternative solutions.
 
-The DoD Zero Trust Strategy assigns activities to target or advanced phases. This guide indicates `Target` and `Adanced` in the activity title. We recommend implementing key protections first, following the [Microsoft Zero Trust Rapid Modernization Plan](/en-us/security/zero-trust/zero-trust-ramp-overview).

-# Microsoft Security Exposure Management for AI | Microsoft Learn
+# Improve posture to get ready for AI | Microsoft Learn
 
-**Security imperative: Get ready for AI** **Job to be done: Improve posture**
+Improving posture to get ready for AI means establishing a defensible device, application, data, software, and infrastructure baseline before AI systems and agents inherit the environment. The work reduces reachable attack surface, closes common control gaps, and prioritizes remediation where it reduces the most business risk.
 
-Improving posture to get ready for AI focuses on establishing a defensible device baseline, cutting reachable attack surface, and closing gaps across the software estate. It ensures effort lands where it reduces risk, and that controls an AI agent inherits are already governed.
+This guidance provides detailed implementation continuity for work described in the [Secure your foundations](/en-us/security/saf/scenarios/ai-security/security-foundations) AI security transformation theme. Use the [Microsoft Security Adoption Framework (SAF)](../security-adoption-model) to coordinate this work across business scenarios, security disciplines, roles, technologies, and technical solutions.
 
-### Context and problem
+## Why this work matters
 
-AI gives attackers new tools to discover, analyze, and chain vulnerabilities faster, letting them probe more paths and move through environments more quickly. Yet most of the weaknesses they exploit are familiar: unmanaged devices, devices that don't meet compliance requirements, work data that leaves managed apps, unnecessary internet-facing exposure, unpatched software, vulnerable open-source dependencies, and flaws in the code organizations write.
+AI gives attackers new ways to discover, analyze, and chain vulnerabilities at greater speed. Many of the weaknesses they exploit remain familiar:
 
-What's changed is how quickly attackers can link those gaps into a path to critical systems, so one weak spot can lead to a much broader compromise. AI adoption raises the stakes, because AI agents can inherit the posture they're deployed into: the devices they run on, the services they can reach, and the software they depend on. That makes basic security hygiene urgent: organizations need a strong security foundation in place before they adopt AI, and they need to keep it strong as threats evolve.
+- unmanaged or noncompliant devices;
+- organizational data leaving managed applications;
+- unnecessary internet-facing exposure and attack paths to critical assets;
+- unpatched software and operating systems;
+- vulnerable open-source dependencies and software supply chains;
+- weaknesses in application and infrastructure code; and
+- unmanaged identities, credentials, and secrets.
 
-## Solution
+AI adoption raises the stakes because AI systems and agents can inherit the posture of the devices, identities, services, data, software, and infrastructure they can reach. Strengthening these foundations reduces risk before AI increases scale and connectivity.
 
-To help your organization establish a strong security foundation, we have guidance outlined in [Secure Now](https://aka.ms/SecureNow), within [Microsoft Security Exposure Management](/en-us/security-exposure-management/microsoft-security-exposure-management). These initiatives closes one of those familiar gaps:
+## Prioritize posture improvements
 
-- Manage organizational devices brings devices under management in Microsoft Intune.
-- Implement device compliance requirements holds them to a standard enforced through Conditional Access.
-- Protect organizational data in managed applications keeps work data in managed apps, even on devices you don't manage.
-- Internet-Facing Exposure cuts what's reachable from the internet and protects the services that must stay exposed.
-- Patching and vulnerability management keeps software and operating systems current.
-- Software Supply Chain Security secures the open-source dependencies and pipelines you build on.
-- Code scanning and remediation finds and fixes vulnerabilities in the code you write.
+Use [Secure Now](https://aka.ms/SecureNow) and [Microsoft Security Exposure Management](/en-us/security-exposure-management/microsoft-security-exposure-management) to review current recommendations, prioritize work, and track progress. Connect the implementation work to SAF so priorities, ownership, and measures are sustained after an individual initiative is complete.
 
-Together, they help you improve posture to get ready for AI transformation. Secure Now is updated as threats and Microsoft security capabilities evolve, so check it for the latest recommended actions and use [security initiatives](/en-us/security-exposure-management/initiatives) to track progress against your targets.
+| Initiative | Durable outcome | Primary SAF connection | Implementation resource |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| Manage organizational devices | Devices that access organizational resources are known, managed, monitored, and assigned to accountable owners. | [Security posture management](../security-adoption-discipline-posture), [endpoints](../deploy/endpoints) | [Manage devices with Intune](../manage-devices-with-intune-overview) |
+| Implement device compliance requirements | Access decisions include device health and policy compliance instead of relying on identity alone. | [Access and identities](../security-adoption-discipline-identity-access), [endpoints](../deploy/endpoints) | [Set up compliance policies](../manage-devices-with-intune-compliance-policies) and [require device compliance](../manage-devices-with-intune-require-compliance) |
+| Protect organizational data in managed applications | Work data remains protected in approved applications, including on devices the organization does not manage. | [Data security](../security-adoption-discipline-data), [endpoints](../deploy/endpoints) | [Protect apps](../manage-devices-with-intune-app-protection) and [implement data loss prevention](../manage-devices-with-intune-dlp-mip) |
+| Reduce internet-facing exposure | Unnecessary exposure and reachable attack paths to critical assets are removed or controlled. | [Security posture management](../security-adoption-discipline-posture), [infrastructure](../deploy/infrastructure), [networks](../deploy/networks) | [Microsoft Security Exposure Management](/en-us/security-exposure-management/microsoft-security-exposure-management) |
+| Improve patching and vulnerability management | Remediation is prioritized by asset criticality, reachability, exploitability, and business impact. | [Security posture management](../security-adoption-discipline-posture), [infrastructure security](../security-adoption-discipline-infrastructure) | [Secure Now](https://aka.ms/SecureNow) |
+| Secure the software supply chain | Dependencies, build systems, artifacts, and publishing processes use approved, observable security controls. | [Development security](../security-adoption-discipline-development), [development security implementation patterns](/en-us/security/saf/disciplines/development/implementation-patterns) | [Microsoft Security Development Lifecycle](https://www.microsoft.com/securityengineering/sdl/) and [protect the software supply chain](../sfi/protect-software-supply-chain) |
+| Scan and remediate code | Security weaknesses are found and fixed through repeatable engineering workflows before and after deployment. | [Development security](../security-adoption-discipline-development), [applications](../deploy/applications) | [Secure source code with GitHub Advanced Security](../sfi/secure-source-code-github-advanced-security) |
 
-## Guidance
+## Coordinate the work through SAF
 
-Security practitioners can improve posture in their organizations by following these initiatives informed by Secure Now. Learn more about how to [prioritize strengthening AI-readiness.](prioritizing-defense-overview)
+Treat the initiatives as connected parts of the security program:
 
-| **Initiatives** | **Resource** |
-| --- | --- |
-| Manage organizational devices | [Secure Now - Manage organizational devices](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/secure-now) |
-| Implement device compliance requirements | [Secure Now - Implement device compliance requirements](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/secure-now) |
-| Protect organizational data in managed applications | [Secure Now - Protect organizational data in managed applications](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/secure-now) |
-| Internet-Facing Exposure | [Secure Now - Internet-Facing Exposure](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/secure-now) |
-| Patching and vulnerability management | [Secure Now - Patching and vulnerability management](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/secure-now) |
-| Software Supply Chain Security | [Secure Now - Software Supply Chain Security](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/secure-now) |
-| Code scanning and remediation | [Secure Now - Code scanning and remediation](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/secure-now) |
+- Use [Strengthen posture and compliance](../security-adoption-scenario-improve-posture) to define the overall business outcome and measures.
+- Use [Adopt and secure AI](../security-adoption-scenario-secure-ai) to connect foundation work to AI adoption and AI-specific risk.
+- Use [Security posture management](../security-adoption-discipline-posture) to maintain inventory, exposure analysis, prioritization, remediation, and verification.
+- Use [Security roles and responsibilities](../security-adoption-roles) to assign accountable owners and cross-team decision rights.
+- Use [technologies](../deploy/overview) and [technical solutions](../implement-overview) to reach canonical implementation guidance.
+- Use the [AI security workshop](../workshop-zero-trust-ai-security) to assess implementation areas and create a roadmap.
 
-## Outcomes
+## Outcomes and measures
 
-- Devices meets a known standard: managed, compliant devices share one security configuration, and helps protect organizational data in managed apps, even on devices you don’t manage.
-- Effort lands where it reduces risk: internet exposure and attack paths to critical assets set the order of work, not severity score alone.
-- Address underlying sources of findings: each step removes a class of finding—an unmanaged device, an exposed endpoint, an outdated component, a leaked secret—rather than one instance at a time.
-- AI agents inherit governed foundations: managed devices, a measured external footprint, and a current, scanned software estate are in place before agents arrive, rather than bolted on after.
+Expected outcomes include:
 
-## Key success factors
+- managed and compliant devices use an approved security baseline;
+- data remains protected in managed applications and approved repositories;
+- attack paths from internet-facing systems to critical assets trend down;
+- vulnerability and patch work is prioritized according to business risk;
+- software dependencies, pipelines, code, and artifacts use repeatable security controls; and
+- AI systems and agents inherit a governed, measured foundation rather than unmanaged exposure.
 
-Consider tracking the following indicators with the tools and reporting your organization already uses, and compare results over time against your own baseline:
+Consider measures such as:
 
-- Percentage of critical assets with a named accountable owner
-- Percentage of corporate devices enrolled in Microsoft Intune and compliant with policy
-- Percentage of Microsoft 365 app users covered by app protection policies, including on devices you don’t manage
-- Number of attack paths from internet-facing assets to a critical asset, trending down
-- Patch compliance against service level agreement, reported by internet exposure and asset criticality
-- Percentage of production builds that automatically produce a software bill of materials
-- Initiative score against target score, with the 14-day drift for each domain
-
-## Summary
-
-The initiatives with recommended actions can help measurably reduce risk. Create a strong foundation, cut the exposed surface, patch what you buy, patch what you borrow, and secure what you build.
-
-**By prioritizing posture initiatives, you can reduce your organization’s exposure before AI agents inherit it.**
\ No newline at end of file
+- percentage of critical assets with a named accountable owner;
+- percentage of corporate devices enrolled in management and compliant with policy;
+- percentage of applicable users covered by application protection policies;
+- number of reachable attack paths from internet-facing assets to critical assets;
+- patch and vulnerability remediation performance by asset criticality and service-level objective;
+- percentage of production builds that use approved pipelines, code scanning, dependency controls, and software bills of materials; and
+- Secure Now or exposure-management initiative progress compared with the organization's target and baseline.
\ No newline at end of file

-As you establish the Security Architecture discipline, this article provides guidance on how to apply 10 immutable laws of security risk as practical tips as you establish and modernize the [Security Architecture discipline](security-adoption-discipline-architecture).
+This article provides 10 immutable laws of security and 10 laws of cybersecurity risk that capture durable realities about security controls, attackers, people, process, and technology.
 
-This guidance is part of the **Microsoft Security Adoption Framework (SAF)** and supports the Security Architecture discipline with practical design and prioritization heuristics.
+These laws are part of the **Microsoft Security Adoption Framework (SAF)** and are used across strategy, governance, architecture, development, engineering, operations, and SecOps to test assumptions, understand recurring constraints and failure patterns, and make informed risk tradeoffs. Historically, these laws were commonly used in security architecture guidance, and architecture continues to apply them, but they are cross-cutting foundations for SAF rather than architecture-owned concepts.
 
 ## Review the immutable laws of security
 
-Architecture exists to identify challenging requirements and translate them into actionable guidance to reduce security risk, limit damage, and keep systems available over time. At the foundation of this work are the immutable laws of security.
+Security work across SAF requires translating requirements into actionable guidance to reduce security risk, limit damage, and keep systems available over time. At the foundation of this work are the immutable laws of security.
 
-These laws describe uncomfortable truths about security that help you to plan effective control, avoid common misconceptions that undermine security architecture, and create organizational risk.
+These laws describe uncomfortable truths about security that help teams plan effective controls, avoid common misconceptions, and make better risk decisions.
 
 | **Immutable law** | **Architecture impact** |
 | --- | --- |
@@ -63,13 +65,13 @@ These laws describe uncomfortable truths about security that help you to plan ef
 
 ## Apply the ten laws of cybersecurity risk
 
-Even after understanding how security control is potentially lost and the impact on security architecture, this isn't enough information to design a system. Security architects must also understand:
+Even after understanding how security control is potentially lost, this isn't enough information to make effective decisions. Teams across SAF also need to understand:
 
 - What are we optimizing for? - Where do we concentrate effort? - What tradeoffs are acceptable?
 
-To figure out these questions, we can apply 10 common laws of cybersecurity risk. Each set of laws deals with different aspects of cybersecurity.
+To answer these questions, we can apply 10 common laws of cybersecurity risk. Each set of laws addresses different aspects of cybersecurity.
 
-| **Law** | **Architecture implication** | **Modernization guidance** |
+| **Law** | **Risk implication across SAF** | **Decision guidance** |
 | --- | --- | --- |
 | **1. Security success is ruining the attacker's ROI** | Design architectures that increase attacker cost and reduce payoff, especially for high‑value assets. | - Concentrate controls around identity, privileged access, and sensitive data.- Reduce flat trust zones; segment systems so compromise doesn’t scale. - Prioritize protections that break common attacker chains, not special cases. |
 | **2. Not keeping up is falling behind** | Static architectures fail. Architecture must assume continuous evolution. | - Security architecture is never done. It must be operationally sustainable and continuously improved.- Design for continuous update (patching, configuration, policy).- Prefer cloud‑native and managed services that evolve faster than on-premises or bespoke systems.- Ensure visibility and inventory are architectural requirements, not afterthoughts. |

 | **9. Encryption alone isn't a data protection solution** | Cryptology is only as secure as the keys that unlock it. | - Encryption is important, but is ineffective without secure implementation and operation. - Architect centralized key management and access governance. - Protect decryption paths as aggressively as encrypted storage. - Combine encryption with identity, monitoring, and policy enforcement. |
 | **10. Technology doesn't solve people and process problems** | Architecture must assume imperfect humans and processes. | - Modernize security architecture to reduce the blast radius of human error. Don't let clicking on a single phishing email cause your security posture to fail. - Design systems that are resilient to error. - Automate guardrails where possible. - Avoid architectures that depend on flawless manual operation. |
 
-## Build an architecture
+## Apply both law sets in decision-making
 
-As a security architect you can use these two tables as complementary lenses. One to validate technical soundness and the other to drive risk-based prioritization. When combined, they form a practical decision framework for architectural design and modernization.
+Use these two tables as complementary lenses. One helps validate technical soundness and the other helps drive risk-based prioritization. When combined, they form a practical decision framework for security and risk decisions across SAF, including architecture design and modernization.
 
-| **Laws** | **Aim** | **Architectural use** | **Questions answered** |
+| **Laws** | **Aim** | **SAF decision use** | **Questions answered** |
 | --- | --- | --- | --- |
 | **Immutable laws of security** | Capture technical truths that always hold. | Ensure architectures don't violate technical reality.Test assumptionsValidate trust boundaries.Avoid false confidence. | *Is the architecture fundamentally sound*?*Does the design rely on something that can easily be bypassed*?*Are we assuming technology can make up for untrusted admins, weak passwords, or physical access methods*?*Are we mistaking encryption, isolation, or tools for actual control*? |

 # Adopt secure development planning imperatives | Microsoft Learn
 
-This article defines the key imperatives for integrating security into development practices as part of the [Development Security discipline](security-adoption-discipline-development).
+This article defines the planning imperatives for integrating security into development practices as part of the [Development Security discipline](security-adoption-discipline-development).
 
-This guidance is part of the **Microsoft Security Adoption Framework (SAF)** and provides planning imperatives that support consistent implementation of the Development Security discipline.
+This guidance is part of the **Microsoft Security Adoption Framework (SAF)**. Use these imperatives to translate the discipline into planning and release expectations. Use [Shift DevOps to DevSecOps](security-adoption-discipline-development-security) for the operating-model and process changes that put them into practice.
 
-Modern organizations rely on rapid software development to deliver innovation, meet business requirements, maintain competitive advantage, and respond to changing business needs. While DevOps enables this agility, it also introduces new security risks as code, infrastructure, and deployment processes evolve more quickly.
-
-To securely adopt DevOps practices, organizations must integrate security into development strategy, workflows, and delivery processes, and adopt DevSecOps practices that secure application delivery across the lifecycle.
+Modern organizations depend on rapid software delivery to innovate and respond to change. Integrate security into development strategy, workflows, and release decisions so that delivery speed does not create unmanaged security or operational risk.
 
 ## Outcomes
 
-Adopting the planning imperatives in this article enables organizations to:
+Use these planning imperatives to:
 
-- Reduce the introduction of security weaknesses into production workloads.
-- Improve consistency of production readiness decisions.
-- Reduce friction between development, security, and operations.
-- Improve resilience of applications and delivery infrastructure.
-- Sustain innovation velocity while managing security and operational risk.
+- Reduce security weaknesses in production workloads.
+- Make production-readiness decisions more consistent.
+- Reduce unhealthy friction between development, security, and operations.
+- Improve the resilience of workloads and delivery infrastructure.
+- Sustain delivery velocity while managing security and operational risk.
 
 ## Recognize the scope of development security
 
-Development security applies to more than application code. Organizations should define security requirements and activities across all components involved in designing, building, deploying, and operating workloads.
+Plan for more than application code. Include the people, identities, tools, environments, automation, dependencies, and infrastructure used to design, build, deploy, and operate workloads.
 
-Organizations must account for security risks across:
+Account for:
 
-- Application logic and services
-- Infrastructure automation/Infrastructure‑as‑code (IaC) deployments
-- Build and release pipelines
-- Deployment configurations and operational scripting
-- Developer environments and service identities
-- Third-party dependencies and supply chain components
+- Application logic, services, and APIs.
+- Infrastructure as code and deployment configurations.
+- Source repositories, build systems, and release pipelines.
+- Developer environments and service identities.
+- Third-party and open-source components.
+- Production platforms and operational tooling.
 
-Recognizing this full scope helps organizations define security requirements that reflect how modern workloads are delivered, rather than limiting security to application code review late in the lifecycle.
+Use the [Development Security discipline](security-adoption-discipline-development) for the full scope and its relationships with other SAF disciplines.
 
 ## Account for key risks
 
-Organizations should explicitly include the following risks when defining requirements:
+Include these risk areas when defining requirements and priorities:
 
-| **Risk area** | **Example impact** |
+| Risk area | Example impact |
 | --- | --- |
-| Application design flaws | Unauthorized access, data exposure, persistent logic flaws. |
-| Pipeline compromise | Injection of malicious code into build artifacts. |
-| Developer environment compromise | Theft of credentials or elevation of privileges. |
-| DevOps tooling misuse | Unauthorized changes via automation or integrations. |
-| Supply chain vulnerabilities | Introduction of malicious or vulnerable dependencies. |
-
-These risks directly inform the planning imperatives defined in this article and must be addressed through design, process, and governance decisions.
-
-These risks affect both application workloads and the infrastructure used to build and operate them.
-
-## Integrate security into strategy/lifecycle
+| **Application design and implementation** | Unauthorized access, data exposure, or persistent flaws in business logic. |
+| **Development infrastructure and automation** | Stolen credentials, unauthorized changes, or tampered build artifacts. |
+| **Developer environment** | Compromised identities, source code, tools, or privileged access. |
+| **Software supply chain** | Malicious or vulnerable dependencies that affect the organization or downstream customers. |
+| **Operations** | Extended exposure or disruption caused by weak configuration, monitoring, patching, or recovery. |
 
-Security must be incorporated into development strategy, not applied as a post-release control.
+Use these risks to shape design, workflow, assurance, and governance decisions for both the workload and the systems used to deliver it.
 
-Organizations must define security requirements alongside functional requirements and align them with:
+## Integrate security into strategy and the lifecycle
 
-- Development strategy
-- Architectural planning
-- Delivery workflows
-- Operational support models
+Define security, privacy, safety, and compliance requirements alongside business, functional, and operational requirements. Connect them to:
 
-Security outcomes are shared responsibilities owned by engineering and operations roles, supported by security specialists.
+- Product and development strategy.
+- Architecture and design.
+- Delivery and release workflows.
+- Operational support and recovery models.
 
-Security enables innovation, it isn't a gate applied after delivery.
+Use a continuous Security Development Lifecycle (SDL) approach:
 
-Organizations must adopt a continuous Secure Development Lifecycle (SDL) approach that includes:
+- Define requirements while teams still have practical design options.
+- Align architecture and implementation with those requirements.
+- Integrate security into infrastructure automation and delivery pipelines.
+- Validate important requirements throughout delivery and before release.
+- Track findings in normal engineering workflows and prioritize remediation by risk.
+- Feed vulnerabilities, incidents, and operational lessons back into planning and design.
 
-- Defining security requirements early in design.
-- Aligning security requirements with architecture and implementation.
-- Integrating security with infrastructure automation.
-- Performing continuous security validation.
-- Tracking security findings.
-- Prioritizing remediation.
-- Applying security findings to release readiness decisions so that security issues are treated as production blockers when necessary.
+Product and engineering teams are accountable for the functionality, security, reliability, and operational outcomes of the software they deliver. Development, security, and operations roles have distinct responsibilities. Security specialists define and interpret security requirements, provide expertise and reusable patterns, enable teams with tools and education, challenge risk decisions, and advise authorized decision makers.
 
-Security must be continuously evaluated and improved as application architectures, risks, and delivery models evolve.
+## Set minimum production viability in the secure definition of done
 
-## Define minimum production viability criteria
+Use **minimum production viability** as the release quality gate within the team's **secure definition of done**. It is the minimum set of development, security, and operations requirements that a workload needs for production use. A minimum viable product is not production-ready based on functionality alone.
 
-Workloads must meet minimum viability criteria before production release. These criteria define whether a workload is safe, compliant, and operationally ready for production use across three dimensions:
+Before each production release, verify all three dimensions:
 
-- **Development (dev)**: Development stakeholders define minimum functional requirements necessary to meet business needs and customer/user value.
-- **Security (sec)**: Security stakeholders define minimum requirements necessary to meet regulatory obligations, sustain organizational security posture, and support detection and response of active threats.
-- **Operations (ops)**: Operations stakeholders define minimum performance, quality, and supportability requirements necessary for the workload to operate reliably in production environments.
-
-Production viability criteria:
-
-- Ensure workloads are safe to deploy and operate in production environments.
-- Act as release decision inputs and must be enforced consistently across development workflows.
+| Requirement | Minimum outcome for production use |
+| --- | --- |
+| **Development** | The software meets the required business and user needs. |
+| **Security** | The software meets the security, safety, privacy, and compliance requirements appropriate to its risk. |
+| **Operations** | The software meets the quality, performance, reliability, supportability, monitoring, and recovery requirements for production use. |
 
-Production viability criteria evolve based on changes to:
+Treat these dimensions as concurrent inputs to one release decision, not as sequential maturity stages. Tailor the rigor to the workload's business impact, exposure, and regulatory obligations.
 
-- Application delivery models.
-- Threat conditions.
-- Organizational risk tolerance.
-- Compliance requirements.
+Define decision authority and escalation paths explicitly. For an exception, record the unmet requirement, business rationale, compensating controls, expiration date, and remediation plan. Only a person with delegated authority may approve the exception and accept the residual risk.
 
 ## Integrate security into development workflows
 
-Security must be embedded directly into development and delivery processes. Organizations should:
-
-- Define security requirements within development workflows.
-- Integrate security activities into:
-    - Design processes
-    - Build pipelines
-    - Deployment workflows (CI/CD)
-- Implement security validation mechanisms such as:
-    - Code scanning
-    - Dependency validation
-    - Configuration checks
-
-Security findings must be treated the same as production defects and incorporated into release decisions.
-
-Security validation should occur continuously through the delivery, not only at release checkpoints.
-
-## Balance and harmonize requirements
-
-Organizations must define how development, security, and operational requirements are balanced in software delivery decisions. Production workloads must meet requirements across:
-
-- Business functionality.
-- Security resilience.
-- Speed of innovation.
-- Operational reliability and performance.
-
-Organizations must define shared delivery objectives and performance metrics that:
+Use the same planning, backlog, defect, approval, and release mechanisms for security work that teams use for other engineering work.
 
-- Align to shared performance and delivery objectives across development, security, and operations.
-- Avoid domination by a single domain.
-- Prioritize outcomes based on:
-    - Organizational risk tolerance.
-    - Regulatory obligations.
-    - Business accountability.
+Integrate security activities into:
 
-The balance must adapt as threat conditions evolve, delivery models change, and organizational priorities shift.
+- **Design**: Apply secure patterns, threat modeling, and architecture review where risk warrants them.
+- **Build**: Validate code, dependencies, secrets, infrastructure as code, and configurations.
+- **Delivery**: Protect repositories, branches, pipelines, identities, artifacts, and release actions.
+- **Operations**: Monitor, patch, detect, respond, recover, and feed lessons back into engineering.
 
-## Establish shared accountability
-
-Effective DevSecOps requires shared ownership across development, security, and operations teams with a view to:
-
-- Aligning ownership of production viability criteria.
-- Aligning delivery objectives across disciplines.
-- Reducing silos and unhealthy friction that creates security gaps, delivery delays, and operational instability.
+Manage security findings through the normal defect workflow and release decision process. Block release when an unmet requirement exceeds the risk that an authorized decision maker can accept. Validate continuously instead of relying only on a final checkpoint.
 
 ## Apply policy-driven security guardrails
 
-Policy-driven guardrails should enforce controls without introducing excessive friction. Guardrails should include:
+Use policy-driven guardrails to apply requirements consistently without creating unnecessary delivery friction. Include:
 
 - Identity and access requirements.
 - Configuration and compliance standards.
 - Deployment and release controls.
 
-Guardrails should be:
-
-- Integrated into platform foundations (for example landing zones).
-- Embedded into development/deployment workflows.
-- Enforced automatically when possible.
-
-This approach ensures security requirements are consistently applied while maintaining delivery velocity.
+Integrate guardrails into platform foundations, development workflows, and deployment automation. Automate repeatable checks when practical, tune noisy controls, and preserve human review for consequential decisions.
 
-For a balanced approach to security and speed of innovation, review adoption using [policy-driven guardrails](/en-us/azure/cloud-adoption-framework/ready/enterprise-scale/dine-guidance).
+For a balanced approach to security and delivery speed, review [policy-driven guardrails](/en-us/azure/cloud-adoption-framework/ready/enterprise-scale/dine-guidance).
 
 ## Sustain and improve
 
-Security doesn't remain effective as a static set of controls and must evolve over time.
-
-Organizations must continuously evaluate and update development security practices in response to changes in:
-
-- Threat conditions and attacker behavior.
-- Application architectures and delivery models.
-- Regulatory obligations.
-- Organizational risk tolerance.
-- Production viability criteria.
-- Development delivery processes.
-- Security governance practices.
-
-Security practices must evolve alongside the systems they protect.
-
-### Alignment techniques
-
-Teams must align to:
-
-- **Define common goals**: Development, security, and operations leaders should collaboratively define delivery objectives and performance metrics for workload delivery, to support consistent release planning.
-- **Prevent single‑domain decision dominance**: Delivery decisions should account for development, security, and operational requirements to avoid imbalances that might negatively impact workload reliability, compliance, or business functionality.
-- **Prioritize continuous improvement over static release criteria**: Development security practices should be iteratively refined over time as application delivery models, threat conditions, and organizational priorities evolve.
-- **Establish shared delivery context across stakeholder roles**: Development, security, and operations teams should maintain a shared understanding of:
-    - Business urgency and delivery timelines
-    - Relevant threat conditions and risk exposure
-    - Operational availability and supportability requirements
-- **Monitor delivery friction introduced by security requirements**: Security requirements may introduce delivery friction. Leaders should evaluate whether this friction contributes to risk reduction (for example, by enabling earlier identification of vulnerabilities) or unnecessarily delays workload delivery without materially improving production resilience.
-- **Incorporate development security into planning and resource allocation**: Security requirements for application workloads should be incorporated into development planning and resource allocation alongside functionality and operational support requirements.
-- **Define shared delivery performance objectives**: Performance and success metrics for application workloads should reflect development, security, and operational delivery outcomes.
-
-## Align workflows with security requirements
-
-Security must be operationalized through development workflows. Organizations must define and align workflows for:
-
-- Architectural design activities.
-- Build and deployment processes.
-- Issue tracking and remediation workflows.
-
-Security findings must be:
+Update development security practices as workloads, threats, regulations, delivery models, and business priorities change.
 
-- Prioritized and tracked.
-- Managed alongside production defects.
-- Incorporated into release readiness decisions.
+- Define shared objectives for functionality, security, reliability, and delivery flow.
+- Use metrics that show both risk reduction and the effect of controls on engineering work.
+- Prevent any one discipline from dominating tradeoffs by default.
+- Review delivery friction and remove steps that add little risk reduction.
+- Incorporate security requirements into product planning and resource allocation.
+- Refine minimum production viability criteria based on vulnerabilities, incidents, testing, and production telemetry.
 
-Workflow alignment ensures that security requirements are consistently enforced throughout delivery.
\ No newline at end of file
+Improve incrementally. Prioritize the highest-risk gaps and the foundations that make secure delivery easier to sustain.
\ No newline at end of file

 # Shift DevOps to DevSecOps | Microsoft Learn
 
-As you create or modernize a [Development Security discipline](security-adoption-discipline-development), this article outlines how integrating security into development practices enables the shift from developer operations (DevOps) to developer-security-operations (DevSecOps), and helps secure application delivery.
-
-This guidance is part of the **Microsoft Security Adoption Framework (SAF)** and extends the Development Security discipline with implementation-oriented DevSecOps adoption guidance.
-
-Modern organizations rely on rapid software development to deliver innovation, respond to changing business requirements, and maintain competitive advantage. DevOps enables this agility through continuous integration and delivery. However, increased speed also introduces new security risks.
+Use DevSecOps to operationalize the [Development Security discipline](security-adoption-discipline-development). DevSecOps integrates security into development and operations so that teams can manage software risk while delivering reliable capabilities at the speed the business needs.
 
-Continuous release cycles reduce the time between design decisions and production deployment, increasing the likelihood that weaknesses are introduced into production environments, including:
+This guidance is part of the **Microsoft Security Adoption Framework (SAF)**. It focuses on the operating-model and process changes needed to make security part of normal engineering work.
 
-- Application design weaknesses
-- Vulnerable dependencies
-- Configuration errors
-- Infrastructure automation flaws
-- Poor secrets management or hygiene.
+DevSecOps is not a separate security framework, a final gate, or a maturity stage that begins after DevOps is complete. It is the security dimension of modern software delivery.
 
-## DevOps risk
+## Security risk in modern development environments
 
-Modern DevOps environments expand the attack surface across development, pipeline, and production systems. DevOps tools such as source code repositories, pipelines, and automation systems are high-value targets for attackers.
+Modern development creates powerful paths from an idea to production. Source repositories, developer endpoints, build systems, automation, service identities, artifacts, dependencies, and cloud platforms can all influence what reaches a production environment.
 
-If malicious code is introduced early, it might pass through existing security checks and reach production systems.
+Attackers target these paths because compromise can provide access to:
 
-Common attack objectives include:
+- Proprietary source code and intellectual property.
+- Developer, workload, and service identities.
+- Credentials, secrets, and production data.
+- Build artifacts and deployment configurations.
+- Customer or partner environments through software supply-chain compromise.
 
-- Injecting malicious code into build artifacts.
-- Compromising developer identities or service accounts.
-- Accessing or exfiltrating production data.
+Security risk can enter through several related areas:
 
-Attackers often target custom applications and development environments to gain access to:
-
-- Sensitive organizational or customer data.
-- Proprietary business logic and intellectual property.
-- Production infrastructure through compromised development systems.
-- Downstream customers through software supply chain compromise.
-
-Potential security risks are summarized in the following diagram:
-
-[![Diagram illustrates DevOps environments and security threats.](media/develop/secure-devops-environments/diagram-enterprise-devops-overview-inline.png)](media/develop/secure-devops-environments/diagram-enterprise-devops-overview-expanded.png#lightbox)
-
-### Application and development risk
-
-Application workloads can be compromised through weaknesses introduced during development or through compromise of the infrastructure used to build and deploy them.
-
-| **Risk** | **Target** | **Potential outcome** |
+| Risk area | Examples | Potential impact |
 | --- | --- | --- |
-| **App design/implementation** | Security issues introduced during design or development may expose workloads to attack techniques such as:- Improper input validation- Insecure authentication or authorization logic- Weak or improperly implemented cryptography- Exposure of sensitive data through application logic | These weaknesses might allow attackers to:- Access or manipulate application data- Execute unauthorized operations- Maintain persistent access through implanted logic flaws. |
-| **Dev infrastructure/automation** | Attacks might target:- Source code repos- Build pipelines- Deployment automation- Infrastructure-as-code (IaC) templates- Develop endpoints or service identities | Compromise might allow attackers to:- Insert malicious code into build artifacts- Modify deployment configurations- Maintain persistent access through implanted logic flaw- Obtain credentials or secrets used in production environments. |
-| **Dev software supply chain** | Applications commonly rely on:- Third‑party libraries- Open‑source packages- Container images- Platform services | Vulnerabilities or malicious code introduced through these dependencies might affect:- Organizational production workloads- Customer or partner environments |
-
-Integrating security into development processes reduces the likelihood that these risks propagate into production release.
-
-## Shifting left
-
-Shift left is a security engineering approach that integrates security earlier in the development lifecycle.
+| **Application design and implementation** | Insecure authorization, improper input validation, weak cryptography, unsafe handling of data, or flaws in business logic | Unauthorized access, data exposure, manipulation of business processes, or persistent compromise |
+| **Development infrastructure and automation** | Compromised developer endpoints, repositories, pipelines, build agents, infrastructure-as-code templates, or service identities | Malicious changes to code or configuration, stolen credentials, tampered artifacts, or unauthorized deployment |
+| **Software supply chain** | Vulnerable or malicious packages, container images, tools, extensions, or platform services | Compromise of organizational workloads or downstream customers and partners |
+| **Operations** | Weak configuration, inadequate monitoring, delayed patching, or incomplete recovery plans | Longer exposure, greater damage, and slower restoration of business services |
 
-Instead of validating security late in the process, organizations embed it into:
+Protect both the software and the systems used to create, deliver, and operate it.
 
-- Envisioning
-- Design
-- Development
-- Operations
+## Shift security earlier, then validate continuously
 
-This reduces remediation cost and risk exposure.
+Shifting left means bringing security into development decisions early enough to change the outcome, rather than discovering problems after design and implementation are complete.
 
-To support this approach, organizations should"
+Integrate appropriate security practices into:
 
-- Use structured best practices such as the [Security Development Lifecycle (SDL)](https://www.microsoft.com/securityengineering/sdl/practices) early in the process, rather than late when issues become expensive and difficult to fix.
-- To sustain this approach, integrate governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) into development strategy.
+- Ideation and planning.
+- Architecture and design.
+- Development and testing.
+- Build and release.
+- Deployment and operations.
 
-## What is DevSecOps?
+Early integration reduces the cost and disruption of fixing security issues while giving teams more options for addressing risk. Use proven practices such as the [Microsoft Security Development Lifecycle (SDL)](https://www.microsoft.com/securityengineering/sdl/practices), and include governance, risk, privacy, safety, and compliance requirements during planning rather than treating them as a final release gate.
 
-DevSecOps delivers on the Shift Left approach by extending DevOps and embedding security into every stage of the software development lifecycle - from idea inception through design, development, and operations.
+Shifting left does not eliminate the need to validate later. Assume that people, automation, and controls can fail. Recheck important requirements before release, monitor the workload in production, and feed operational lessons back into design and engineering. This combination of early action and continuous validation provides defense in depth.
 
-- In traditional development approaches, security validation was often performed as a final quality gate before release. This created delays, increased remediation cost, and allowed vulnerabilities to persist until late in the lifecycle.
-- DevSecOps shifts security earlier and embeds it continuously into development and operational processes.
-- DevSecOps reduces friction between development, operations, and security teams, aligning them around shared goals of innovation speed, reliability, and security resilience, and enabling teams to address the most important issues early and continuously.
-- DevSecOps integrates security into:
+## Set minimum production viability in the secure definition of done
 
-    - Architectural design
-    - Application implementation
-    - Infrastructure automation
-    - Deployment and operational processes
+Use **minimum production viability** as the release quality gate within the team's **secure definition of done**. It is the minimum set of development, security, and operations requirements that a workload needs for production use. A minimum viable product is not production-ready based on functionality alone.
 
-### Benefits
+Before each production release, verify all three dimensions:
 
-DevSecOps enables development, security, and operations teams to:
-
-- Identify and remediate issues earlier in the lifecycle.
-- Reduce exposure in production.
-- Maintain delivery speed while managing risk.
-
-Security becomes part of how software is built and delivered, rather than a control applied after delivery.
-
-[![Graphic showing how development, security, and operations fit together](media/development-security-operations.png)](media/development-security-operations.png#lightbox)
-
-## Secure innovation lifecycle
-
-Innovation typically progresses through two lifecycle stages:
-
-| **Stage** | **Details** |
+| Requirement | Minimum outcome for production use |
 | --- | --- |
-| **Idea incubation** | A capability is designed, implemented, and validated for initial production use. It begins with a new idea |
-| **Initial release** | A **first production release** meets the minimum product criteria for safe product use.- **Development**: Functionality meets the minimum business requirements.- **Security**: Capabilities meet the regulatory compliance, security, and safety requirements for production use.- **Operations:** Functionality meets the minimum quality, performance, and supportability requirements to be a production system. |
-
-After initial release, development becomes iterative as workloads evolve with:
-
-- Changing risk tolerance
-- Application requirements and maturity
-- Regulatory obligations
-- Threat conditions
+| **Development** | The software meets the required business and user needs. |
+| **Security** | The software meets the security, safety, privacy, and compliance requirements appropriate to its risk. |
+| **Operations** | The software meets the quality, performance, reliability, supportability, monitoring, and recovery requirements for production use. |
 
-[![Diagram showing how DevSecOps keeps the development cycle agile and continuously improving](media/develop-security-agile.png)](media/develop-security-agile.png#lightbox)
+Treat these dimensions as concurrent inputs to one release decision, not as a sequence from Development to DevOps to DevSecOps. Keep security present from ideation through production operations.
 
-## Integrate security into development
+Tailor the rigor to the workload's business impact, exposure, and regulatory obligations. Improve or sustain the required outcomes with each release.
 
-Traditional development approaches validate security late in the lifecycle, as a final gate before release after design and implementation are complete. In modern development environments, delaying validation increases:
+[![DevSecOps lifecycle showing that minimum production viability combines development, security, and operations requirements at the first production release and improves continuously afterward.](media/develop-security-agile.png)](media/develop-security-agile.png#lightbox)
 
-- Vulnerability complexity
-- Remediation cost
-- Operational delays and disruption
-- Increased risk exposure to active exploitation
+## Integrate security into engineering workflows
 
-DevSecOps integrates security continuously throughout development and operations, to address issues earlier, reduce risk, and improve consistency.
+Security is most effective when it uses the same mechanisms as other engineering work. Avoid a separate process that forces product and engineering teams to discover, translate, and maintain duplicate requirements.
 
-### Key practices
+Map the path from idea to production and ongoing operations. Identify:
 
-Security must be embedded into existing development processes to be effective, scalable, and sustainable. It should be integrated directly into how apps are designed, built, deployed, and operated, not implemented in a separate or parallel workflow. We recommend:
+- The people and teams who make product, architecture, risk, release, and operational decisions.
+- The repositories, branches, tools, identities, environments, and automation involved.
+- The events that trigger builds, tests, approvals, deployments, and rollbacks.
+- The security activities required at each stage.
+- The path for resolving design flaws, vulnerabilities, dependency issues, and incidents.
 
-- Mapping end-to-end workflows from idea through development, deployment, and ongoing operations.
-- Defining clear roles, tools, and responsibilities for security at each stage of the lifecycle.
-- Establishing consistent remediation paths for vulnerabilities, defects, and design issues.
+Then integrate security into normal workflows:
 
-Tailor security practices based on workload risk. Business-critical applications require greater rigor, while lower-risk scenarios can follow streamlined approaches.
+- Track security requirements and defects in the same backlog and work-management systems used for other engineering work.
+- Use the same prioritization language for security and nonsecurity defects so teams can make informed tradeoffs.
+- Include security expertise in architecture and design decisions.
+- Protect high-impact branches and release actions with appropriate review and approval.
+- Document the code-to-production path so teams can see where changes are validated and who can authorize them.
+- Use blameless postmortems to capture security lessons and improve the system rather than assigning blame.
 
-At a minimum, ensure that you:
+## Automate repeatable security work
 
-- Identify the stages, people, and technologies involved in your development lifecycle.
-- Define how security activities integrate into each stage, rather than treating them as separate checkpoints.
-- Establish processes for handling both major changes and routine fixes throughout the lifecycle.
+Automation helps teams apply controls consistently and reduces the effort required to follow secure practices.
 
-## Automate security into development and deployment
+Use automation to:
 
-Automation is essential to enforce security consistently and at scale across development and operations.
+- Apply policy and configuration checks.
+- Scan code, dependencies, secrets, infrastructure as code, and deployment configurations.
+- Generate and preserve provenance information and software bills of materials where appropriate.
+- Enforce branch, build, artifact, and release protections.
+- Use short-lived federated identities instead of long-lived pipeline secrets where possible.
+- Create repeatable, secure environments and deployment patterns.
+- Feed security findings into the team's normal remediation workflow.
 
-- Integrate security controls and tooling directly into CI/CD pipelines.
-- Automate key activities such as threat modeling, code scanning, validation, and policy enforcement.
-- Use Infrastructure as Code (IaC) to enable repeatable, secure deployments.
+Use automation to help engineers act, not flood them with low-quality findings. Tune tools, assign remediation responsibilities and service levels, and provide access to security expertise when teams need help interpreting results.
 
-Platform foundations such as Azure landing zones can support this approach by
+Platform foundations such as [Azure landing zones](/en-us/azure/cloud-adoption-framework/ready/landing-zone/design-area/platform-automation-devops) can provide reusable patterns for governance, security, and deployment automation. Use platform engineering and paved paths to make the secure approach the easiest practical approach.
 
-Platform foundations such as [Azure landing zones](/en-us/azure/cloud-adoption-framework/ready/landing-zone/design-area/platform-automation-devops) can support this approach by providing standardized patterns for security, governance, and DevOps integration.
-
-## Expected outcomes
+## Apply rigor based on business risk
 
-Organizations that shift from DevOps to DevSecOps can:
+Not every workload requires identical controls. Use a risk-based baseline that accounts for:
 
-- Reduce the likelihood that vulnerabilities are introduced into production workloads
-- Limit the ability of attackers to exploit development infrastructure or automation
-- Improve resilience of applications to evolving attack techniques
-- Support regulatory and organizational compliance requirements
-- Sustain innovation velocity without increasing operational or security risk
+- Business criticality and potential financial impact.
+- Customer, partner, safety, or regulatory consequences.
+- Data sensitivity and privilege.
+- Exposure to external users and untrusted input.
+- The ability to affect other systems or downstream customers.
+- The expected lifetime and support model of the software.
 
-## Tips on navigating the journey
+Establish a standard baseline for production software, stronger assurance for high-impact workloads, and a governed exception process for temporary prototypes or urgent business needs. For an exception, record the unmet requirement, business rationale, compensating controls, expiration date, and remediation plan. Only a person with delegated authority may approve the exception and accept the residual risk.
 
-Adopting DevSecOps requires organizational and cultural changes.
+## Assign accountability, responsibilities, and decision authority
 
-### Education and culture changes
+DevSecOps changes how development, security, and operations teams work together. Product and engineering teams are accountable for the functionality, security, reliability, and operational outcomes of the software they deliver. Security specialists have distinct responsibilities: define and interpret security requirements, advise and enable teams, challenge risk decisions, and provide expertise and reusable patterns.
 
-These are critical early steps. The team you have must develop new skills and adopt new perspectives to understand the DevSecOps model.
+Assign decision authority separately from delivery responsibilities. Only a person with delegated authority may approve an exception or accept residual risk. Escalate decisions that exceed the team's authority.
 
-Education and culture change takes time, focus, executive sponsorship, and regular follow up to help individuals fully understand and see the value of the change.
+Leaders can support this model by:
 
-Changing cultures and skills drastically can sometimes tap into the professional identity of individuals, creating potential for strong resistance. It's critical to understand and express the why, what, and how of the change for each individual and their situation.
+- Setting shared goals for functionality, security, reliability, and delivery.
+- Making business urgency and likely security impact visible to the whole team.
+- Ensuring no single function wins every tradeoff by default.
+- Funding security as part of the product and engineering plan rather than as an external afterthought.
+- Expecting continuous improvement instead of immediate perfection.
+- Modeling respect for the expertise and constraints of other disciplines.
 
-### Change takes time
+Teams need time to develop skills and shared practices. Make the change easier to adopt by explaining why it matters, providing practical training and automation, and improving incrementally based on experience.
 
-You can only move as fast as your team can adapt to the implications of doing things in new ways. Teams must do their existing jobs while they transform.
+## Manage friction deliberately
 
-It's critical to carefully prioritize what is most important and to manage expectations of how fast this change can happen.
+Every control adds some cost or delay. The goal is not to eliminate friction but to put the right friction in the right place.
 
-Focusing on a crawl, walk, run strategy, where the most important and foundational elements come first, serves your organization well.
+- **Healthy friction** prompts useful review, threat modeling, testing, or approval at a point where the decision can reduce meaningful risk.
+- **Unhealthy friction** delays delivery without proportional risk reduction, produces excessive false positives, or requires teams to repeat work across disconnected processes.
 
-### Change introduces (temporary) friction
+Measure the effect of controls on both risk and engineering flow. Remove steps that provide little value, improve noisy tools, automate repeatable checks, and preserve deliberate human review for consequential decisions.
 
-All new technologies, methodologies, and other changes introduce friction and confusion. It's critical to focus on healthy friction that drives critical thinking to reduce risk while avoiding unhealthy friction that slows down processes with limited benefit or risk reduction.
+Modernize incrementally. Prioritize the highest-risk gaps and the foundational practices that make later improvements easier. Keep delivery moving while changing how software is built and secured.
 
-### Limited resources
-
-A challenge that organizations usually face early on is to find talent and skills in both security and application development.
-
-As organizations begin to collaborate more effectively, they might find hidden talent, such as developers with a security mindset or security professionals with a development background.
-
-### Ongoing shifts
-
-Apps are changing fast. In addition to new features, the technical definition and composition of an application is fundamentally changing with the introduction of technologies such as cloud, serverless, and AI.
-
-This shift is changing development practices, application security, and even empowers nondevelopers to create applications.
-
-### Consider an SRE model
-
-Some DevSecOps implementations combine operations and security responsibilities into a **site reliability engineer (SRE)** role.
-
-While such a model can work, it's often an extreme change from existing enterprise culture and practices.
+## Expected outcomes
 
-If you're considering an SRE model, we recommend that you start by embedding security into DevOps using practical quick wins and incremental progress outlined in this guidance to ensure you're getting good return on investment (ROI) and meeting immediate needs.
+Organizations that integrate security into DevOps can:
 
-This incrementally adds security responsibilities to your operations and development personnel, which moves teams closer to an SRE end-state.
\ No newline at end of file
+- Reduce the likelihood that design and implementation flaws reach production.
+- Reduce compromise of developer environments, repositories, pipelines, and automation.
+- Improve software supply-chain integrity.
+- Detect and remediate security issues earlier and more consistently.
+- Improve resilience and recovery when failures or attacks occur.
+- Sustain delivery velocity without allowing security risk to grow unchecked.
