-# Use the Microsoft security adoption model to modernize SecOps | Microsoft Learn
+# Establish a Security Operations discipline | Microsoft Learn
 
-This article helps security and technology teams establish and modernize a Security Operations (SecOps) discipline that detects, investigates, and responds to active threats that bypass preventive controls.
+This article helps security and technology teams establish and modernize a Security Operations (SecOps) discipline that detects, investigates, contains, and supports recovery from active threats.
 
-This guidance is part of the **Microsoft Security Adoption Framework (SAF)**, a broader body of guidance for planning, prioritizing, and implementing end-to-end security modernization. SAF connects business scenarios, security disciplines, and technical implementation so that strategy, architecture, operations, and controls work together rather than as isolated recommendations.
+This guidance is part of the **Microsoft Security Adoption Framework (SAF)**. SAF connects business scenarios, security disciplines, and technical implementation so that strategy, architecture, engineering, operations, and controls work together.
 
-Within SAF, SecOps is an operational security discipline. It defines the mission, outcomes, roles, processes, and operating model needed to manage active attacks across the technology estate. Use [SecOps technology](security-operations-technology) and related implementation guidance when you need control-specific and product-level implementation details.
+Within SAF, **SecOps** is the discipline for managing active threats and compromise. A **security operations center (SOC)** is one organizational construct for executing SecOps functions. Organizations can use other structures while delivering the same SecOps outcomes.
 
-## What's SecOps?
-
-SecOps maintain and restore the security assurances of the system as live adversaries attack it. The NIST Cybersecurity Framework describes the SecOps functions of Detect, Respond, and Recover well.
-
-- **Detect** - SecOps must detect the presence of adversaries in the system, who are incentivized to stay hidden in most cases, allowing them to achieve their objectives unimpeded. This can take the form of reacting to an alert of suspicious activity or proactively hunting for anomalous events in the enterprise activity logs.
-- **Respond** - Upon detection of potential adversary action or campaign, SecOps must rapidly investigate to identify whether it's an actual attack (true positive) or a false alarm (false positive) and then enumerate the scope and goal of the adversary operation.
-- **Recover** - The ultimate goal of SecOps is to preserve or restore the security assurances (confidentiality, integrity, availability) of business services during and after an attack.
-
-### Risk mitigation
-
-The most significant security risk most organizations face is from human attack operators.
-
-With notable exceptions, risk from automated/repeated attacks have been mitigated significantly for most organizations by signature and machine learning based approaches built into anti-malware.
-
-While human attack operators are challenging to face because of their adaptability, they're operating at the same "human speed" as defenders, which help level the playing field.
-
-SecOps has a critical role to play in limiting the time and access an attacker can get to valuable systems and data. Each minute that an attacker has in the environment allows them to continue to conduct attack operations and access sensitive or valuable systems.
-
-## Why this discipline?
-
-Not all attacks can be prevented. Even with strong security architecture and posture management that blocks most attacks, threat actors sometimes gain initial access to environments.
-
-SecOps focuses on managing those active attacks and security incidents, limiting the damage attackers can cause after compromise. Effective SecOps reduces risk by:
-
-- Detecting malicious activity quickly.
-- Shortening attacker dwell time.
-- Containing lateral movement and impact.
-- Supporting recovery and organizational resilience.
-
-Within the security adoption model, SecOps represents the post‑compromise, reactive side of security, complementing security posture management, which focuses on proactive risk reduction and attack prevention.
-
-[![Diagram of Security Operations and Security Posture Management showing their complementary roles in risk reduction.](media/security-adoption-discipline-operations.png)](media/security-adoption-discipline-operations.png#lightbox)
-
-Without an effective SecOps discipline, attackers who gain access can operate undetected, escalate privileges, move laterally, and inflict maximum business damage.
+Use [SecOps implementation patterns](/en-us/security/saf/disciplines/security-operations/implementation-patterns), [technology guidance for SecOps](security-operations-technology), and related implementation guidance for control-specific and product-level details. For high-impact compromise pathways, align SecOps with the [privileged access scenario](security-adoption-scenario-privileged-access) and [SecOps incident operations](security-adoption-discipline-security-operations-incidents).
 
 ## Mission and outcomes
 
-The mission of the SecOps discipline is to limit the business impact of cyberattacks by rapidly detecting, investigating, and responding to threats across the modern technology estate.
-
-Regardless of team size or operating model, mature SecOps delivers these outcomes:
+The mission of SecOps is to limit the business impact of cyberattacks by rapidly detecting, investigating, containing, and learning from threats across the technology estate.
 
-- **Rapid threat response** – Timely detection and containment of threats across identities, endpoints, infrastructure, applications, and data
-- **Shared threat intelligence** – Centralized signals and insights that inform analysts, automation, and downstream security controls
-- **Proactive threat discovery** – Threat hunting and attack simulation to uncover emerging techniques and attacker behavior
+Active attackers adapt as defenders detect and disrupt them. Combine automation and machine-speed analysis with human expertise, judgment, accountability, and oversight to act quickly without losing decision quality.
 
-SecOps teams may range from a single individual to large globally distributed 24/7 operations, and functions may be partially or fully outsourced. Regardless of structure and size, the outcomes remain the same.
+SecOps complements Security Posture Management. Security Posture Management reduces exposure and prevents attacks; SecOps detects and manages active threats and compromise. Both continuously exchange insights to reduce organizational risk.
 
-### Adopt Zero Trust in SecOps
+Regardless of team size or operating model, deliver these outcomes:
 
-Security Operation (SecOps) is foundational to a Zero Trust strategy. Zero Trust assumes compromise and focuses on minimizing impact when controls fail. SecOps turns that assumption into action by continuously detecting, investigating, and responding to threats across the environment.
+- **Rapid threat response**: Detect, investigate, and contain threats across identities, endpoints, infrastructure, applications, data, networks, operational technology (OT), and AI.
+- **Coordinated recovery**: Restore the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of affected business services through coordinated technical and operational action.
+- **Shared threat intelligence**: Convert signals, investigations, and external intelligence into actionable insights for analysts, automation, security controls, and partner teams.
+- **Proactive threat discovery**: Use threat hunting and attack simulation to find attacker activity, test assumptions, and identify detection or control gaps.
+- **Continuous improvement**: Feed incident and exercise learning into SecOps, Security Posture Management, architecture, engineering and operations, and security strategy.
 
-In a Zero Trust model, prevention alone is insufficient. Organizations must expect attackers to bypass controls and rely on SecOps to identify malicious activity early, contain attacks quickly, and generate insights that improve security posture over time.
+## Apply Zero Trust to SecOps
 
-Within our security adoption model, SecOps guidance focuses on the operational capabilities required to support Zero Trust across the organization, including monitoring, detection, investigation, response, automation, and continuous learning.
+Zero Trust assumes compromise and limits the effect of control failure. Apply that principle to SecOps:
 
-- **Centralize detection and visibility**: Integrate logs and telemetry from across the environment—including identities, endpoints, applications, and infrastructure—into a centralized detection and investigation capability. This ensures SecOps has consistent, cross‑domain visibility to detect compromise early and understand attacker behavior.
-- **Automate response and containment**: Use orchestration and automation to execute repeatable response actions, such as isolating compromised devices or disabling risky accounts. Automation reduces response time, lowers analyst cognitive load, and ensures consistent execution under pressure.
-- **Proactively hunt for threats**: Treat threat hunting as a core SecOps capability. Use hypothesis‑driven hunting and advanced analytics to find attacker activity that evades automated detections, reducing dwell time and uncovering gaps in controls.
-- **Manage alerts and incidents effectively**: Tune detections to reduce noise and ensure analysts focus on meaningful alerts. Standardize investigation and response workflows using playbooks so incidents are handled consistently and efficiently.
-- **Continuously reduce exposure based on risk**: Use attack‑path analysis and exposure insights to identify conditions that could enable compromise. Prioritize remediation based on business impact and likelihood, so effort is focused where it matters most.
-- **Continuously evolve SecOps processes**: Regularly review detections, playbooks, and response outcomes based on real incidents and threat intelligence. Feed these learnings back into SecOps strategy to ensure capabilities adapt as attackers, technologies, and business priorities change.
+- **Establish visibility**: Integrate relevant telemetry across the environment so SecOps can detect compromise, investigate attacker behavior, and understand business impact.
+- **Verify through detection and investigation**: Use analytics, threat intelligence, hunting, and investigation to validate activity instead of trusting a single signal.
+- **Contain rapidly and limit blast radius**: Use tested processes, automation, and orchestration to disrupt attacks while preserving evidence and avoiding unnecessary business impact.
+- **Learn and improve**: Use incidents, exercises, threat intelligence, and operational metrics to improve detections, playbooks, preventive controls, architecture, and priorities.
 
-By aligning SecOps to Zero Trust principles, organizations move from reactive incident handling to a resilient operating model where every incident strengthens detection, response, and prevention across the enterprise.
+## Apply the discipline
 
-## How to apply this discipline
+Use a continuous operating loop that aligns SecOps work to business risk:
 
-To apply the SecOps discipline effectively, focus on establishing a coordinated approach to detecting, responding to, and recovering from threats across the organization:
-
-1. **Define a threat detection and response strategy aligned to business risk** Establish a clear approach for identifying, prioritizing, and responding to threats based on their potential business impact.
-2. **Ensure consistent detection and response across the environment** Apply a unified approach to monitoring, investigation, and response across identities, devices, applications, and infrastructure.
-3. **Standardize processes for detection, response, and recovery** Provide clear guidance to ensure incidents are handled consistently, reducing response time and limiting impact.
-4. **Align SecOps with business priorities and critical scenarios** Prioritize detection and response efforts to focus on protecting critical assets and minimizing the impact of security incidents.
-5. **Continuously improve through insights and feedback** Use learnings from incidents, threat intelligence, and operational metrics to strengthen detection capabilities and improve response over time.
+1. **Align to business risk** Prioritize business services, attack paths, and threat scenarios by potential organizational impact.
+2. **Establish visibility** Define telemetry, detection, investigation, and data-retention requirements across the technology estate.
+3. **Detect and investigate** Identify suspicious activity, validate incidents, determine scope and impact, and preserve evidence.
+4. **Contain and recover** Coordinate technical and business actions that disrupt attackers and restore security assurances.
+5. **Learn and improve** Convert incident and exercise findings into improvements across detection, posture, architecture, engineering and operations, and strategy.
 
 ## Manage change
 
-SecOps modernization is a continuous improvement journey, not a one-time tooling deployment. The goal is to steadily improve the organization’s ability to reduce attacker impact when compromises occur.
-
-[![Screenshot of security operations mission summary with key actions and Zero Trust alignment highlighted.](media/security-adoption-discipline-operations-mission.png)](media/security-adoption-discipline-operations-mission.png#lightbox)
-
-A modern SecOps approach aligned with Zero Trust principles emphasizes:
+Modernize SecOps as a continuous improvement program, not a one-time tooling deployment. Prioritize:
 
-- **Mission alignment** - Prioritizing what matters most to the business when alerts and threats exceed your capacity to respond with humans and automation, including AI.
-- **Continuous learning** - Adapting detections, skills, and processes as threat actors, platforms, and business priorities change.
-- **Collaboration and sharing** - Treating SecOps as a team effort across security, IT operations, engineering, legal, communications, and leadership.
+- **Mission alignment**: Focus limited human and automated capacity on threats and assets with the greatest potential business impact.
+- **Operational learning**: Adapt detections, skills, processes, and technology as attackers, platforms, and business priorities change.
+- **Cross-functional collaboration**: Integrate SecOps with teams that design, build, operate, govern, and rely on the environment.
+- **Sustainable execution**: Measure operational effectiveness, reduce unnecessary analyst workload, and preserve critical monitoring and response during major incidents.
 
-Threat actors tend to reuse techniques that are cheap, effective, and reliable until they fail, so it's critical to capture and share threat intelligence as insights on past attacks. SecOps threat intelligence should directly inform security control design, prioritization, and posture improvement, alongside business and compliance requirements.
+[![Diagram showing the SecOps mission, operating loop, and Zero Trust alignment.](media/security-adoption-discipline-operations-mission.png)](media/security-adoption-discipline-operations-mission.png#lightbox)
 
 ## Discipline roles and collaborators
 
-The SecOps discipline is typically led by a dedicated SecOps team. In smaller organizations, SecOps responsibilities might be part-time or shared across roles but still require clear ownership.
+SecOps job functions describe the work and outcomes required. Organizations can assign these functions across people, teams, service providers, AI agents, tools, and automation while preserving human accountability, decision authority, and oversight.
 
-Primary roles in this discipline typically include:
+Define accountability for SecOps outcomes, responsibility for execution, decision authority for incident and business-impact decisions, and escalation paths for risk acceptance. Assign risk-acceptance decisions only to people with delegated authority.
 
-- SecOps / SOC manager
-- Tier 1 triage analysts
-- Tier 2 investigation analysts
-- Threat hunters (Tier 3)
-- Detection engineers
-- SecOps platform and data engineers
-- Digital forensics and incident response specialists
-- Threat intelligence analysts
-- Incident coordination and management roles
-- Attack simulation specialists (red team, purple team, penetration testing)
+See [SecOps roles](security-adoption-discipline-security-operations-roles) for the durable job functions and partner relationships used to execute this discipline.
 
-Key collaborators include:
-
-- **Technical engineering and operations teams** – Enable logging and support investigation, containment, and recovery of systems they design and run.
-- **Architecture roles** – Continuously improve the design of systems and controls based on incident learnings from SecOps threat intelligence.
-- **Application and product teams** – Update software and services in response to incident insights.
-- **Security Strategy, Integration, and Governance discipline** – Set priorities, metrics, and accountability for SecOps investments. Provide support and coordination during major incidents.
+## Alignment with other disciplines
 
-Effective SecOps depends on tight feedback loops between incident response and system design.
+Integrate SecOps with the broader security operating model:
 
-## Alignment with other disciplines
+- **Security Posture Management**: Use incident and threat insights to prioritize exposure reduction, preventive controls, and remediation.
+- **Access and Identities**: Use identity telemetry to detect and investigate attacks; improve identity controls based on incident learning.
+- **Data Security**: Coordinate investigations of data theft, extortion, insider risk, and privacy-related events.
+- **Security Architecture**: Use attack and incident findings to improve system design, trust boundaries, resilience, and detection requirements.
+- **Development Security and technical engineering and operations**: Add telemetry, correct weaknesses, improve recovery, and sustain controls in the systems these teams build and operate.
+- **Strategy, Integration, and Governance**: Set priorities, success measures, accountability, decision authority, and investment direction based on business risk and operational evidence.
 
-SecOps operates as part of a broader security operating model and is tightly integrated with other disciplines:
+Effective SecOps creates a feedback loop from active threats to prevention and long-term modernization:
 
-- **Security Posture Management discipline**: Focuses on preventing incidents; SecOps manages the incidents that still occur.
-- **Access and Identities discipline**: Identity telemetry is a primary detection and investigation signal.
-- **Data Security discipline**: SecOps investigates data theft, extortion, insider risk, and privacy incidents.
-- **Security Architecture discipline**: Ensures detection and response mechanisms align with intended system design.
-- **Strategy, Integration, and Governance discipline**: Defines SecOps priorities, metrics, and success criteria.
+**Detect and investigate → contain and recover → learn → improve posture, architecture, engineering and operations, and strategy**
 
 ## Alignment with technology pillars
 
-The SecOps discipline operates across all technology pillars and must detect and contain attacks wherever they occur.
+Apply SecOps across the technology estate:
+
+- **Identities**: Detect account compromise, privilege abuse, token theft, and lateral movement.
+- **Endpoints**: Find and contain compromised devices and collect evidence about attacker activity.
+- **Infrastructure**: Detect and respond to threats in cloud, on-premises, edge, and operational environments.
+- **Applications**: Monitor email, collaboration, business, custom, and software-as-a-service applications for attack activity.
+- **Data**: Investigate theft, manipulation, destruction, encryption, and misuse of sensitive data.
+- **Networks**: Use network telemetry and controls for investigation context and containment, including when encryption limits content visibility.
+- **AI**: Detect attacks on AI systems and use governed AI capabilities to accelerate analysis and execution under human oversight.
+
+## Related SAF guidance
 
-- **Identities**: This is a top priority for SecOps because identities are primary attack entry points. Almost all multi-stage attacks rely on identity attacks (pass-the-hash/ticket/etc.) to laterally traverse and gain access to more organizational assets, often using privileged accounts associated with IT administrators or administrative service accounts.
-- **Endpoints**: Endpoints are common footholds, a base of operations, and local attack tool storage for attackers. It's critical to quickly locate compromised endpoints to contain damage and gain insights into attackers objectives and capabilities.
-- **Infrastructure**: Effective detection and response are important because threat actors frequently target high-value cloud and on-premises infrastructure assets that enable broad compromise when breached.
-- **Apps**: Rapidly detection and response to attacks on email, collaboration, line of business, and other apps is critical because attackers often use them to enter and laterally traverse an organization to access business assets.
-- **Data**: Attackers often target data for intellectual property theft, encryption to gain leverage for extortion or ransomware, planning future attacks, and other purposes. Additionally, SecOps may be involved in or collaborate on data related investigations related to privacy, insider risk, and others.
-- **Network**: Just like legitimate communications, threat actor communications and attack operations travel over network connections. SecOps focuses on network sensor and data is still valuable for context and containment, even as encryption reduces visibility.
-- **AI**: As AI emerges as an attack surface, new tools and skills are needed for effective detection and investigation. AI attack volume is increasing as threat actors adopt AI technology. SecOps can also take advantage of AI to automate analysis and other processes.

-# Microsoft security best practices overview | Microsoft Learn
+# Microsoft security best practices | Microsoft Learn
 
-Microsoft security best practices are designed to help organizations protect their digital estates by reducing risk, improving resilience, and enabling secure productivity.
+**Security best practices apply at many levels.** They help organizations make informed decisions about managing security risk and improving resilience. Best practices can address people, processes, and technology across strategy, governance, architecture, implementation, and operations.
 
-- At the core of these best practices is the [Zero Trust security model](zero-trust-overview). Zero Trust assumes that threats exist both inside and outside the network, and emphasizes verifying every access request, enforcing least privilege access, and segmenting resources as we assume breach.
+**Microsoft security guidance includes many forms of best practices.** These range from strategic principles and organizational practices to security standards and frameworks, secure configuration baselines and benchmarks, architecture, assessments, technology guidance, and implementation practices. These forms of guidance provide different perspectives and levels of detail and are designed to work together rather than as a single checklist or prescribed approach.
 
-Zero Trust principles are reinforced through a combination of engineering best practices, frameworks, benchmarks, and assessment tools.
+**Standards and frameworks provide established security practices.** They organize security objectives, practices, controls, or requirements into structures that organizations can use to guide security programs, assess progress, and communicate alignment. Microsoft guidance helps organizations connect these frameworks to practical security work and technology implementation.
 
-## Best practices and recommendations
+**Best practices must be adapted to organizational context.** Business priorities, risk, regulatory and policy requirements, threat environment, technology estate, existing capabilities, resources, and organizational structure can affect which practices are most important and how they should be implemented.
 
-- **[Microsoft's Secure Future Initiative (SFI)](sfi/secure-future-initiative-overview)**
+Use the following resources based on what you are trying to accomplish.
 
-    A series of best practices and security learning based on Microsoft's multi-year efforts to increasingly secure the way in which we design, build, test, and operate our products. SFI provides a series of best practice patterns that you can learn from and implement. SFI tackles security by pillars. Objectives for each pillar align to one or more [NIST Cybersecurity Framework functions](sfi/secure-future-initiative-overview#sfi-pillars-zero-trust-and-nist).
-- **[Microsoft Entra security recommendations](/en-us/entra/fundamentals/configure-security)**
+## Establish a security foundation with Zero Trust
 
-    Check identity and app security configuration and posture. Recommendations aligns to SFI themes. These best practices are included in the [Zero Trust Assessment tool](assessment/overview).
-- **[Microsoft Intune device security recommendations](/en-us/intune/intune-service/protect/zero-trust-configure-security)**
+Use [Zero Trust](zero-trust-overview) as a security foundation for designing, implementing, and operating security controls across your organization.
 
-    Ensure tenant-level governance and device compliance. Protect data on devices and in transit, and enforce secure access to organizational data. These best practices are included in the [Zero Trust Assessment tool](assessment/overview).
-- **[Azure networking security best practices](/en-us/azure/networking/security/zero-trust-network-security)**
+Zero Trust applies three principles across business, security, and technology decisions: verify explicitly, use least privilege access, and assume breach.
 
-    Assess and harden network posture with Azure DDoS protection, Azure Firewall, Azure Web Application Firewall on Application Gateway or Azure Front Door. These best practices are included in the [Zero Trust Assessment tool](assessment/overview).
-- **[Data security best practices](/en-us/purview/zero-trust-microsoft-purview)**
+## Organize and improve your security program with SAF
 
-    Check Microsoft Purview configuration settings for data security posture. These best practices are included in the [Zero Trust Assessment tool](assessment/overview).
-- The **[Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark (MCSB)](/en-us/security/benchmark/azure/overview)**
+Use the [Microsoft Security Adoption Framework (SAF)](security-adoption-model) to connect business priorities and risk to coordinated security work and technology implementation.
 
-    Provides a series of best practices and recommendations for improving the security of workloads, data, and services on Azure.
-- Other Microsoft Defender products such as [Defender for Cloud](/en-us/azure/defender-for-cloud/concept-cloud-security-posture-management) and [Security Exposure Management](/en-us/security-exposure-management/microsoft-security-exposure-management), and [Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager](/en-us/purview/compliance-manager) also monitor and assess your enterprise security posture, providing actionable security and compliance insights and recommendations.
-- External best practices and framework also provide Zero Trust security principles and guidance. [Learn more](security-zero-trust-frameworks).
\ No newline at end of file
+SAF helps business, technology, and security roles collaborate across business scenarios, security disciplines, technologies, and technical solutions.
+
+## Use established security baselines and benchmarks
+
+**Security baselines provide tested starting points.** They help organizations apply established security recommendations consistently rather than developing every security configuration from the beginning.
+
+Microsoft provides security baselines and benchmarks for different technologies and environments, including:
+
+- **Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark (MCSB):** Provides security recommendations for improving the security of cloud workloads, data, and services. See [Overview of the Microsoft cloud security benchmark](/en-us/security/benchmark/azure/overview).
+- **Windows and Windows Server security baselines:** Provide Microsoft-recommended configuration settings for securing Windows devices and servers. See [Windows security baselines](/en-us/windows/security/operating-system-security/device-management/windows-security-configuration-framework/windows-security-baselines) and [configure security baselines for Windows Server 2025](/en-us/windows-server/security/osconfig/osconfig-how-to-configure-security-baselines).
+- **Microsoft 365 Apps for enterprise security baseline:** Provides recommended configuration settings for Microsoft 365 Apps and guidance for balancing security with productivity requirements. See [Security baseline for Microsoft 365 Apps for enterprise](/en-us/microsoft-365-apps/security/security-baseline).
+- **Microsoft Edge security baseline:** Provides recommended security configuration settings for Microsoft Edge. See [Microsoft Edge security baseline settings reference for Microsoft Intune](/en-us/intune/device-security/security-baselines/ref-v2-edge-settings).
+- **Microsoft Intune security baselines:** Provide deployable groups of recommended security settings for Windows devices and supported security technologies managed with Intune. See [Use security baselines to help secure Windows devices you manage with Microsoft Intune](/en-us/intune/device-security/security-baselines/overview).
+
+**A security baseline is a starting point, not a universal configuration.** Evaluate and adapt baselines based on organizational risk, regulatory and policy requirements, technology dependencies, operational needs, and productivity requirements.
+
+## Assess your Zero Trust implementation
+
+Use the [Zero Trust assessment](assessment/overview) to evaluate your current implementation, identify security gaps, and prioritize improvements across Zero Trust technology controls.
+
+Assessment results can provide a practical starting point for prioritizing improvements and measuring progress over time.
+
+## Secure specific technologies
+
+Use [technology security guidance](deploy/overview) when you need to secure a particular part of your technology environment.
+
+The guidance applies Zero Trust principles across identities, endpoints, applications, data, infrastructure, networks, and AI and connects to more detailed implementation guidance.
+
+## Apply security standards and frameworks
+
+Use [Security standards and frameworks](security-standards-and-frameworks) when your organization uses an established security standard or framework to structure security objectives, practices, controls, or requirements.
+
+Standards and frameworks capture and organize security practices from different authorities, communities, and areas of expertise. Organizations can use them to structure security programs, establish common expectations, assess progress, and communicate alignment.
+
+Microsoft mappings connect framework objectives to SAF guidance, security capabilities, technology implementation, and relevant Microsoft product guidance. Organizations can use these mappings to help align security work with framework objectives and requirements without treating framework alignment or compliance as the complete measure of security success.
+
+## Learn from Microsoft's security engineering practices
+
+Use the [Microsoft Secure Future Initiative (SFI)](sfi/secure-future-initiative-overview) to learn from security engineering practices, patterns, and lessons from Microsoft's efforts to strengthen the security of its products and services.
+
+SFI complements SAF and other Microsoft security guidance with engineering practices and lessons that organizations can consider as they improve their own security programs.

-# Microsoft security platform technologies | Microsoft Learn
+# Microsoft security products and platforms | Microsoft Learn
 
-This article describes Microsoft security services and how they work together as a unified system to deliver protection across [technology pillars](deploy/overview) that include identities, devices, applications, data, AI, and infrastructure.
+Microsoft security products and platforms provide capabilities to protect identities, endpoints, applications, data, infrastructure, networks, and AI and to support security operations across these environments. These products work together by sharing signals and context and integrating protection, policy, detection, investigation, and response capabilities.
 
-Modern enterprise security shifted from perimeter-based protection to an identity-driven, cloud-integrated model. Organizations must secure users, devices, applications, and data across hybrid and multicloud environments while continuously adapting to evolving threats.
+The [Security Adoption Framework (SAF)](security-adoption-model) provides a durable model for organizing desired outcomes, security work, technologies, and technical implementation. Microsoft products and platforms provide capabilities that help organizations implement and operate that security.
 
-Microsoft provides an integrated set of cloud-based services that work together to share signals, apply consistent policies, enforce controls, and coordinate detection and response across the environment.
+A Microsoft security product can support multiple SAF areas, and implementing a security outcome frequently requires capabilities from multiple products and platforms.
 
-## Security outcomes
+## Explore Microsoft security products and platforms
 
-Integrated Microsoft security delivers the following outcomes:
+Use the following product families to find Microsoft implementation and product guidance relevant to your security requirements. The SAF relationship identifies where each product family most directly connects to SAF. These are primary relationships, not exclusive mappings. Many products support multiple SAF technologies, security disciplines, business scenarios, and technical solutions.
 
-- **Unified signal visibility**: Telemetry is continuously collected and centralized across identities, devices, applications, data, and infrastructure, and converted into centralized, actionable signals.
-- **Identity-driven decision making**: Access and enforcement decisions are based on identity, device state, risk signals, and session context.
-- **Consistent enforcement**: Zero Trust controls are applied across endpoints, cloud services, and applications at access time and during use.
-- **Integrated detection and response**: Signals and alerts are correlated across domains to detect and respond to threats as unified operations.
-- **Continuous validation and improvement**: Detection and risk signals feed back into policy decisions to strengthen protection over time.
+| Primary SAF relationship | Microsoft products and platforms | Capabilities |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| **Technology: Identity** | Microsoft Entra, Microsoft Defender for Identity | Manage identities and access, govern privileges, evaluate identity and access risk, and detect attacks against identity infrastructure. |
+| **Technology: Endpoints** | Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint | Manage and assess device configuration and compliance, protect endpoints, detect threats, and support investigation and response. |
+| **Technologies: Applications and Data** | Microsoft Defender for Office 365 | Protect email and collaboration services from phishing, malicious content, business email compromise, and other threats. |
+| **Technology: Applications** | Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps | Discover and protect cloud applications, assess application activity and risk, and apply controls to cloud application sessions. |
+| **Technology: Data** | Microsoft Purview | Discover, classify, protect, and govern data and reduce risks such as inappropriate access, data loss, and insider threats. |
+| **Technology: Infrastructure** | Microsoft Defender for Cloud, Azure security capabilities | Improve cloud security posture and protect cloud and hybrid infrastructure and workloads. |
+| **Technology: Network** | Azure network security services | Segment, connect, monitor, and protect network traffic and network-access paths across cloud and hybrid environments. |
+| **Discipline: Security Posture** | Microsoft Security Exposure Management | Identify and prioritize exposure across identities, devices, applications, and cloud resources and help teams focus remediation on material risks. |
+| **Discipline: SecOps/SOC** | Microsoft Defender XDR, Microsoft Sentinel | Support security monitoring, detection, triage, investigation, hunting, automation, incident response, and coordinated response across Microsoft and third-party environments. |
+| **Discipline: Development Security** | GitHub Advanced Security, Microsoft Defender for Cloud | Integrate security into software development and DevOps workflows to identify and reduce risk in code, dependencies, pipelines, and cloud applications. |
+| **Cross-cutting security work** | Microsoft Security Copilot | Use AI to assist security analysis, investigation, threat intelligence, and response while people maintain appropriate judgment, oversight, and accountability. |
 
-## Core security services
+For detailed configuration, deployment, and operational guidance, use the documentation for the relevant Microsoft product or platform. Product documentation is the authoritative source for current product capabilities and implementation procedures.
 
-Core security services span multiple technology pillars, each contributing signals, context, and enforcement across the platform.
+## How Microsoft products support SAF
 
-| **PillarPrimary service** | **Protection** | **Primary portal** |
-| --- | --- | --- |
-| **Identity and access**Microsoft EntraMicrosoft Defender for Identity. | Microsoft Entra controls access for users, workloads, and applications. It evaluates identity, device, and session signals to make access decisions.Defender for Identity monitors hybrid identity infrastructure to detect attacks. | [Microsoft Entra admin center](https://entra.microsoft.com/)[Microsoft Defender portal](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/) |
-| **Devices/endpoints**Microsoft Defender for EndpointMicrosoft Intune | Defender for Endpoint collects endpoint telemetry and detects threats.Microsoft Intune assesses device compliance and enforces policy. | [Microsoft Defender portal](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/)[Microsoft Intune admin center](https://intune.microsoft.com/) |
-| **Email and collaboration**Defender for Office 365 | Protects Exchange and collaboration services (Microsoft Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive) from malware, malicious links/attachments, and business email compromise. | [Microsoft Defender portal](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/) |
-| **Data**Microsoft Purview | Enforces data protection and data loss prevention (DLP) policies across endpoints and cloud services. | [Microsoft Purview portal](https://sip.purview.microsoft.com/) |
-| **Infrastructure/cloud workloads**Microsoft Defender for Cloud | Improves security posture and provides threat detection across cloud and hybrid workloads. | [Microsoft Azure portal](https://ms.portal.azure.com/)[Microsoft Defender portal](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/) |
-| **Networks**Azure networking services | Segment and protect networks. | [Microsoft Azure portal](https://ms.portal.azure.com/) |
-| **SaaS/cloud apps**Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps | Provides visibility into cloud app usage and monitors user activity to detect risky behavior. | [Microsoft Defender portal](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/) |
-| **Posture/risk**Microsoft Security Exposure Management | Identifies, prioritizes, and reduces exposure across identities, devices, cloud resources, and applications. | [Microsoft Defender portal](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/) |
-| **Threat detection/response**Microsoft Defender XDR | Correlates signals across Defender services and produces unified incidents for investigation and response. | Microsoft Defender portal |
-| **Security operations**Microsoft Sentinel | Aggregates telemetry from Microsoft and third-party sources for centralized analysis, investigation, and response. | [Microsoft Azure portal](https://ms.portal.azure.com/)[Microsoft Defender portal](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/) |
-| **Developer/app security**Defender for DevOps (in Defender for Cloud)GitHub Advanced Security | Secures code, dependencies, and build pipelines, and enforces security governance across DevOps workflows. | [Microsoft Defender portal](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/)GitHub interface |
-
-## Network protection services
-

-
-| **Service** | **Protection** | **Integration** |
-| --- | --- | --- |

Uses Microsoft threat intelligence to block known malicious traffic. | Defender for Cloud evaluates configuration posture.Diagnostic logs are ingested into Azure Monitor/Log Analytics and analyzed by Microsoft Sentinel for detection and correlation. |
-| **Azure DDoS Protection** | Mitigates volumetric, protocol, and application-layer attacks. -| **Azure Network Watcher** | Provides network diagnostics, monitoring, and flow-level visibility across Azure resources. | NSG flow logs and diagnostics are ingested into Log Analytics and can be analyzed in Microsoft Sentinel.Defender for Cloud evaluates underlying resource configuration state such as NSG settings, rather than Network Watcher directly. |

-## Security workflow
-
-Security services operate as a continuous pipeline. Signals are continuously collected, evaluated, enforced, and used to drive detection and response.
-
-| **Pipeline** | **Action** | **Key activity** |
-| --- | --- | --- |
-| **Stage 1: Signal collection** | Security services generate telemetry across identities, devices, applications, and infrastructure. | - Defender for Endpoint collects device telemetry.- Microsoft Intune evaluates device compliance.- Defender for Identity monitors on-premises identity activity.- Defender for Cloud Apps monitors SaaS activity.- Defender for Cloud monitors infrastructure/workload configuration and activity. |
-| **Stage 2: Policy decisions** | Signals are evaluated to determine access conditions and control actions. | Microsoft Entra Conditional Access evaluates identity risk, device trust, location, and session context. |
-| **Stage 3: Control enforcement** | Security controls are applied across identity, device, session, data, and network layers. | Enforcement points include:- Conditional Access (MFA/restrictions)- Intune (device compliance)-Defender for Cloud Apps (session control)- Microsoft Purview (DLP)- Azure networking (connectivity restrictions). |
-| **Stage 4: Detection and response** | Signals and alerts are correlated to detect, investigate, and remediate threats. | Microsoft Defender XDR correlates signals from all Defender products into unified incidents.Microsoft Sentinel centralizes logs, incidents, hunting, and security orchestration, automation, and response (SOAR) across the entire environment—including third-party sources. |
-| **Feedback loop** | Detection outcomes feed back into policy decisions to continuously improve protection. | Risk and threat signals inform real-time policy updates, enabling adaptive and automated protection. |
+SAF and Microsoft product families serve different purposes. SAF organizes security around why security improvement is needed, what outcomes organizations are trying to achieve, what security work must be performed, what technologies must be protected, and how security capabilities are implemented and operated.
 
-## Security service integration
+Microsoft security products and platforms provide technical capabilities that help implement this work. The relationship is many-to-many: a product can support multiple SAF technologies, disciplines, business scenarios, and technical solutions, while a security outcome typically requires capabilities from multiple products and platforms.
 
-Microsoft security services integrate through multiple flows operating as a cohesive pipeline, forming a continuous system of protection.
+For example, protecting access to business resources can require identity controls from Microsoft Entra, device state from Microsoft Intune and Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, data protection from Microsoft Purview, detections from Microsoft Defender, and monitoring and response through Microsoft Sentinel.
 
-- **Signals (telemetry)** capture activity across identities, devices, applications, and other resources.
-- **Context (identity, device posture, and data classification)** enriches signals to improve accuracy and decision-making.
-- **Policy** defines what access is allowed or blocked based on evaluated conditions.
-- **Actions** enforce decisions through automated controls and response.
+Use SAF to determine the security outcomes, security work, and technology requirements you need to address. Use Microsoft product guidance to plan, configure, deploy, and operate the capabilities that help implement them.
 
-As signals move through the platform, they're enriched, evaluated against policy, and acted on, creating a continuous cycle of protection and response.
+## An integrated security platform
 
-### How services integrate
+Microsoft security products can share security signals and context across identities, devices, applications, data, infrastructure, and cloud services. These integrations help organizations coordinate prevention, protection, detection, investigation, and response across environments.
 
-The table summarizes how security services consume signals and context from each out, and what they output and action.
+Common integration patterns include:
 
-| **Service** | **Consumes** | **Outputs** |
-| --- | --- | --- |
-| **Microsoft Entra ID** | **Signals**: Authentication activity (sign-ins, risk events). Device compliance status from Microsoft Intune.**Context**: Device context for access decisions from Defender for Endpoint. Session context for access decisions from Defender for Cloud Apps. | **Actions**: Conditional Access decisions (allow, block, restrict, require controls). |
-| **Microsoft Intune** | **Signals**: Managed devices inventory, health, compliance state. **Context**: Identity association from Microsoft Entra ID. | **Outputs**: Device compliance posture to Microsoft Entra ID. Device audit logs to Microsoft Sentinel. |
-| **Microsoft Purview** | **Signals**: Enterprise data across Microsoft 365, SaaS apps, and on-premises systems.**Context**: Data classification (sensitivity labels, content inspection, user activity). | **Outputs**: Insider risk and data loss protection (DLP) alerts to Defender XDR. Compliance and audit logs to Microsoft Sentinel.**Actions**: DLP enforcement across endpoints (Defender for Endpoint), and sessions (Defender for Cloud Apps). |
-| **Defender for Endpoint** | **Signals**: Endpoint telemetry (process, file, network activity).**Context**: Microsoft Entra ID (identity context). Microsoft Intune (device posture). Microsoft Purview (DLP policies). | **Outputs**: Endpoint alerts and telemetry to Defender XDR and Microsoft Sentinel.**Actions**: Endpoint enforcement (device isolation, blocking, remediation). |
-| **Defender for Identity** | **Signals**: Active Directory identity signals. | **Output**: Identity threat alerts to Defender XDR and Microsoft Sentinel. |
-| **Defender for Cloud Apps** | **Signals**: SaaS app activity (cloud usage). Network and shadow IT telemetry from Defender for Endpoint.**Context**: Session and authentication context from Microsoft Entra ID. DLP policies from Microsoft Purview. | **Outputs**: Cloud app alerts to Defender XDR and Microsoft Sentinel.**Actions**: Session enforcement (block, monitor, restrict access). |
-| **Defender for Cloud** | **Signals**: Resource operation information from Azure. Server/workload telemetry from Defender for Endpoint.**Context**: Resource configuration and posture. | **Outputs**: Security alerts and posture insights to Defender XDR and Microsoft Sentinel. |
-| **Microsoft Security Exposure Management** | **Signals**: Device risk scores from Defender for Endpoint. Cloud resource inventory, posture, exposure, and attack surface findings from Defender for Cloud. Identity inventory and risk signals from Microsoft Entra. SaaS app inventory, risk, and usage context from Defender for Cloud Apps.**Context**: Unified exposure and risk correlation. | **Outputs**: Exposure insights and risk correlations to Microsoft XDR and Microsoft Sentinel. |
-| **Defender XDR** | **Signals**: Alerts from Defender for Endpoint (devices), Defender for Identity (identity signals), Defender for Office 365 (email and collaboration), Defender for Cloud Apps (SaaS/app activity). Extra signals from Microsoft Purview (DLP, insider risk, data classification), Microsoft Entra ID Protection (identity risk signals), and Defender for Cloud (workload/cloud posture). | **Outputs**: Correlated alerts, incidents to Microsoft Sentinel.**Actions**: Automated cross-domain response. |

-# Align security adoption with industry Zero Trust frameworks | Microsoft Learn
+# Map Zero Trust standards and frameworks to SAF | Microsoft Learn
 
-This article provides an overview of well known Zero Trust frameworks, and shows how [Microsoft's Zero Trust adoption model](security-adoption-model) helps you to move from framework understanding to adoption at scale.
+Zero Trust is a security approach expressed through multiple industry and government standards, reference models, strategies, and maturity models. Each source answers a different question. The Microsoft Security Adoption Framework (SAF) mappings help organizations connect that external structure to security work, roles, technologies, architecture, and implementation guidance.
 
-Zero Trust isn't a single framework. It's a security model that aligns with multiple industry and government standards. These standards aren't competing solutions. Each addresses a different aspect of Zero Trust, such as defining core concepts, assessing progress, or coordinating adoption across an organization.
-
-While industry frameworks help define what Zero Trust should achieve, organizations still need a way to translate that guidance into a specific strategy and architecture for solution planning, design, and deployment.
-
-Microsoft's Zero Trust adoption model does just that. It provides a reference strategy and architecture that aligns to and builds on industry frameworks to accelerate Zero Trust adoption and implementation.
+Use this page as a router. The mappings don't replace the authoritative sources, imply one-to-one structural equivalence with SAF, or by themselves demonstrate achievement, maturity, or compliance. Start with the canonical [Security standards and frameworks](security-standards-and-frameworks) hub for the broader relationship between standards, SAF, and implementation.
 
 Tip
 
-Microsoft offers a rich set of security adoption workshops - the *Security Adoption Framework (SAF) workshops*. Our structured adoption model guidance aligns with the expert-led guidance from Microsoft Unified delivered in those workshops. Learn more about [SAF workshops](workshop-business-overview).
-
-## NIST Zero Trust
-
-[National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Special Publication (SP) 800‑207 Zero Trust Architecture](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/207/final) establishes an industry-recognized definition of Zero Trust architecture. It explains what Zero Trust is and how trust decisions are made, independent of any specific vendor, product, or deployment roadmap.
-
-NIST SP 800-207 is most useful when organizations need a common, authoritative definition of Zero Trust concepts that can be shared across security, IT, and architecture teams.
-
-### NIST features
-
-NIST explicitly positions Zero Trust as an architecture where access to resources is never implicitly trusted.
-
-Zero Trust principles in NIST include:
-
-- Assuming compromise (breach) to drive a holistic and practical security approach.
-- Verifying trust explicitly before granting access to assets.
-- Limiting the blast radius by granting the least privilege necessary.
-
-Key architectural concepts focus on:
-
-- Continuous dynamic evaluation of access requests using contextual signals.
-- Centralized policy decision logic that evaluates signals against organizational policy.
-- Policy enforcement functionality close to protected resources applies the decision.
-
-The Zero Trust conceptual architecture defined by NIST focuses on how access decisions are evaluated and enforced using policy engines, enforcement points, and contextual signals.
-
-Note that:
-
-- NIST SP 800-270 doesn't define technology pillars or security domains such as identity, endpoints, or data protection.
-- Identity, device posture, applications, and data are modeled as subjects, resources, and sources of context that inform trust decisions, rather than as separate architectural domains.
-
-Microsoft’s [security adoption model](security-adoption-model) builds on this architecture by applying its principles and components within an operational framework.
-
-While NIST defines how trust decisions are made and enforced, our adoption model organizes these capabilities across security disciplines and technology pillars to guide business planning, ownership, solution design, implementation, and progress tracking.
-
-### Implementation
-
-Implementation guidance is provided in [NIST SP 1800-35 Implementing a Zero Trust Architecture](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/1800/35/final).
-
-For this implementation guidance:
-
-- NIST collaborated with 24 vendors, including Microsoft, on developing a guide with practical steps for organizations eager to implement cybersecurity reference designs for Zero Trust.
-- Microsoft participated as one of the vendors providing technology to implement Zero Trust capabilities across:
-    - Identity and access management.
-    - Endpoint management and configuration.
-    - Threat protection and monitoring.
-    - Secure access to distributed resources.
+Microsoft offers expert-led Security Adoption Framework (SAF) workshops through Microsoft Unified. SAF guidance aligns with these workshops. Learn more about [SAF workshops](workshop-business-overview).
 
-This diagram is the result of the NIST SP 1800-35 collaboration. It can be downloaded from [Microsoft Cybersecurity Reference Architecture (MCRA)](https://aka.ms/MCRA). Learn more about [MCRA](microsoft-reference-architecture)
+## Choose the source that fits the decision
 
-[![Diagram showing Microsoft products mapped to NIST Zero Trust Architecture.](media/adoption-map-national-institute.png)](media/adoption-map-national-institute.png#lightbox)
-
-## CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model
-
-The [Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) Zero Trust Maturity Model](https://www.cisa.gov/zero-trust-maturity-model) is organized around adoption and assessment. This maturity model helps organizations organize and assess their current posture, prioritize improvements, and track progress.
-
-### CISA features
-
-Unlike NIST, CISA doesn't define a reference architecture and instead evaluates capabilities independently of specific design patterns.
-
-- The model uses pillar-based domains, including Identity, Devices, Networks/Environment, Applications/Workloads, and Data.
-- It also defines three cross-cutting capabilities - Visibility and Analytics, Automation and Orchestration, and Governance.
-- And it captures four maturity stages: Traditional, Initial, Advanced, and Optimal.
-- Governance is also not treated as a standalone pillar, but as a cross-cutting capability that ensures business alignment, clear ownership, and measurable outcomes across all domains.
-
-### Implementation
-
-The model aligns with and informs the Microsoft security adoption model, while Microsoft further extends it by introducing disciplines such as Architecture to bridge conceptual frameworks like NIST SP 800‑207 with practical implementation.
-
-| **CISA** | **Adoption discipline/pillar** | **Details** |
+| Source | Best used for | Continue to |
 | --- | --- | --- |
-| **Identity**Identity covers authentication, authorization, identity risk, lifecycle. Apps and workloads cover app access controls, workload identity, and secure app interaction. | **Discipline**: Identity and Access**Technology**: Identity | Access control in Microsoft spans both identity and application layers while CISA separates them. |
-| **Governance**Enterprise-wide policies, controls, and enforcement. | **Discipline**: Strategy, Integration, GovernanceSecurity Architecture**Technology**: All. | CISA’s policy and control capabilities map directly to SecOps outcomes. Microsoft adds extra focus on other aspects of governance (business alignment, risk management, roles, and more), and dedicated focus on architectural discipline and reference architectures. |
-| **Devices**Device inventory, posture, compliance; network segmentation, secure connectivity, environmental controls. Including nontraditional, constrained, and specialized devices. | **Discipline**: Identity and Access, Infrastructure security, OT/IoT security**Technology**: Endpoints | Infrastructure trust is established through device health and controlled connectivity, aligning with the Zero Trust goal to minimize blast radius and lateral movement.Microsoft considers OT/IoT devices as a distinct discipline due to unique ownership, and risk management reasons. |
-| **Apps and workloads**Apps & Workloads covers application access controls, workload identity, and secure application interaction. | **Discipline**: Development Security**Technology**: Apps | CISA’s workload focus aligns with DevSecOps goals by embedding security into application and service lifecycles, rather than treating it as a post‑deployment activity. |
-| **Networks**Network segmentation, secure connectivity, environmental controls. | **Discipline**: Identity and Access**Technology**: Networks | Microsoft combines all access (identity, apps, and networks) into a single discipline to help drive clear strategy, architecture, and policy consistency across technologies. |
-| **Data**Data classification, inventory, access control, encryption, and protection independent of network location. | **Discipline**: Data Security**Technology**: Data | Both models place data as a primary protection target, and reinforce the Zero Trust shift from perimeter security to data‑centric controls. |
-| **Visibility & Analytics, Automation & Orchestration**Telemetry collection, continuous monitoring, detection, response automation, and policy enforcement at scale. | **Discipline**: SecOps**Technology**: All | CISA’s cross‑cutting capabilities map directly to SecOps outcomes that include detecting threats, automating response, and continuously reassessing trust across all domains. |
-| **Maturity stages across all pillars** | Security posture | Posture management is the core purpose of the CISA model: assess current state, identify gaps, prioritize improvements, and track Zero Trust progress over time. |
-
-For information, see [Implementing the CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model with Microsoft cloud services](cisa-zero-trust-maturity-model-intro).
+| **NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture** | A vendor-neutral definition of Zero Trust architecture, policy decision and enforcement concepts, deployment models, and use cases. | [NIST SP 800-207](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/207/final) and [NIST SP 1800-35 implementation guidance](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/1800/35/final) |
+| **CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model** | Assessing progress across five pillars, three cross-cutting capabilities, and four maturity stages. | [CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model mapping and implementation guidance](cisa-zero-trust-maturity-model-intro) |
+| **The Open Group Security and Zero Trust body of knowledge** | Connecting Zero Trust principles, capabilities, roles, collaboration models, and Architecture Building Blocks across business, security, and technology teams. | [The Open Group Zero Trust model mapping](/en-us/security/saf/framework-mappings/open-group-zero-trust) |
+| **DoD Zero Trust Strategy** | Navigating U.S. Department of Defense Zero Trust pillars, capability areas, activities, and implementation outcomes. | [DoD Zero Trust Strategy mapping and implementation guidance](dod-zero-trust-strategy-intro) |
 
-## The Open Group Zero Trust Reference Model
+## NIST Zero Trust Architecture
 
-The Open Group [Zero Trust Reference Model](https://www.opengroup.org/forum/security/Zerotrust) approaches Zero Trust from an enterprise capability and integration perspective. Rather than defining specific implementation steps, it describes the capabilities and governance structures that organizations need to define, integrate, and operate Zero Trust at scale.
+[NIST SP 800-207](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/207/final) defines an abstract Zero Trust architecture in which access to resources isn't implicitly trusted. It describes continuous, context-informed evaluation, policy decision logic, and enforcement close to protected resources.
 
-### Open Group features
+[NIST SP 1800-35](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/1800/35/final) provides implementation examples developed by the NIST National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence with collaborators, including Microsoft. Use it when moving from the SP 800-207 concepts to reference designs and technology integration.
 
-Features include:
-
-- **Capabilities + Architecture Building Blocks (ABBs)** define security capabilities that drive durable security outcomes and the people, process, and technology to enable them.
-- **Collaboration and Integration Models** show how to integrate security with strategy, risk management, operations, and other aspects of the organization.
-
-The capabilities are composed of people, process, and technology elements working together:
-
-- **People**: defined as roles in [The Open Group Roles and Glossary standard](https://publications.opengroup.org/s252)
-- **Process**: defined as architecture building blocks (ABBs) in the same Zero Trust Reference Model standard
-- **Technology**: defined as ABBs in the same Zero Trust Reference Model standard
-
-This diagram shows these capabilities:
-
-[![Diagram showing The Open Group Security Capabilities from the Zero Trust Reference model.](media/adoption-zero-trust-open.png)](media/adoption-zero-trust-open.png#lightbox)
-
-This diagram shows how these capabilities align to the functions of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (NIST CSF):
-
-[![Diagram that shows The Open Group Security Capabilities mapped to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework functions.](media/adoption-zero-trust-open-capabilities.png)](media/adoption-zero-trust-open-capabilities.png#lightbox)
-
-### Implementation
+## CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model
 
-The model maps to our recommended adoption model.
+The [CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model](https://www.cisa.gov/zero-trust-maturity-model) organizes maturity around Identity, Devices, Networks, Applications and Workloads, and Data, with the cross-cutting capabilities Visibility and Analytics, Automation and Orchestration, and Governance.
 
-| **Open Group** | **Adoption discipline** | **Alignment** |
-| --- | --- | --- |
-| **Zero Trust Strategy & Governance**Defines how organizations establish Zero Trust as a business‑aligned strategy, including governance, risk management, policy ownership, and alignment of people, process, and technology. | Strategy, Integration, and Governance | Both Open Group and Microsoft explicitly position Zero Trust as an enterprise strategy, not a technical control set. This directly supports executive alignment, ownership, and integration across the organization. |
-| **Capability-based Zero Trust architecture**Provides architectural building blocks and capability groupings to design Zero Trust architectures, without prescribing specific technologies or products. | Security architecture | This fills the space between NIST’s abstract architecture and implementation guidance, enabling architects to translate Zero Trust principles into enterprise‑scale designs. |
-| **Identity, Authentication, Authorization, and Policy Enforcement capabilities**Defines capabilities required to verify identity, evaluate trust dynamically, and enforce access decisions consistently across environments. | Identity and access | Aligns directly to access security as an adoption discipline: who can access what, under which conditions, and how that decision is enforced. |
-| **Data‑centric protection capabilities**Emphasizes protection of information regardless of location, including data classification, protection, and policy‑driven access. | Data security | Mirrors Zero Trust’s shift from perimeter security to data‑centric security, aligning naturally with data protection as an adoption domain. |
-| **Visibility, monitoring, analytics, and response capabilities**Includes capabilities for collecting telemetry, monitoring trust signals, and adapting policy based on observed risk. | SecOps | Enables continuous evaluation and enforcement—core to Zero Trust operations and security monitoring at scale. |
-| **Application and service interaction security capabilities**Addresses how applications and services participate in Zero Trust, including secure interactions, service identity, and runtime enforcement. | Dev security | Supports integrating Zero Trust into modern application lifecycles and service‑to‑service communication. |
-| **Platform and environment security capabilities**Covers secure operation of platforms, networks, and environments that host workloads, without treating the network as a trust boundary. | Infrastructure security | Aligns infrastructure security with Zero Trust principles by treating infrastructure as enforceable but not inherently trusted. |
-| **Extended environment and non‑traditional asset support**Explicitly recognizes IT/OT/IoT convergence and the need for Zero Trust capabilities across constrained and heterogeneous environments. | Infrastructure (OT/IoT security) | Matches adoption reality where OT/IoT require distinct ownership but must still align to enterprise Zero Trust strategy. |
-| **Capability‑based maturity and continuous improvement**Provides a capability model intended to assess current state, guide improvement, and adapt over time as threats and technology evolve. | Security posture | Positions Zero Trust as an ongoing program, not a one‑time deployment—aligning directly with posture management goals. |
+Use the existing [CISA mapping and implementation guidance](cisa-zero-trust-maturity-model-intro) to connect these areas to relevant SAF security disciplines and technologies and then to Microsoft implementation guidance. CISA remains the authoritative source for maturity expectations.
 
-### Map Microsoft technologies to the model
+## The Open Group Zero Trust model
 
-The Zero Trust Reference model also includes an overall summary of Zero Trust components. This diagram shows how Microsoft technologies map to those components:
+The Open Group material provides an enterprise capability and integration perspective. It connects durable Zero Trust capabilities to security roles and to process and technology Architecture Building Blocks.
 
-[![Diagram showing Microsoft technologies mapped to The Open Group Zero Trust Reference Model components.](media/adoption-zero-trust-open-mapping.png)](media/adoption-zero-trust-open-mapping.png#lightbox)

Snapshot documents are draft standards that publish interim direction for feedback before any formal standard publication. Use the [dedicated Open Group mapping](/en-us/security/saf/framework-mappings/open-group-zero-trust) for current publication-status notes, capability and role graphics, SAF mappings, and detailed ABB-to-Microsoft technology examples.
 
 ## DoD Zero Trust Strategy

-# Adopting Microsoft Secure Future Initiative (SFI) best practices | Microsoft Learn
+# Apply Microsoft Secure Future Initiative (SFI) lessons | Microsoft Learn
 
-Microsoft's Secure Future Initiative (SFI) launched as a multiyear effort to further secure the way that Microsoft designs, builds, tests, and operates its infrastructure, products, and services.
+Microsoft's Secure Future Initiative provides lessons that organizations can use to strengthen their own security programs. Many of the security practices implemented through SFI are established security practices already covered by Microsoft Zero Trust, architecture, operational, and product guidance.
 
-This article shows how your organization might consider and adopt some of these SFI best practices.
+SFI adds value by showing which practices Microsoft prioritized, why they became priorities, what Microsoft changed, and what organizations can learn from Microsoft's experience. Use the existing Microsoft security guidance linked from this section to plan and implement these practices in your environment.
 
-Note
+## How to use this guidance
 
-- We're continuously working on content that details each best practice pattern within pillars. Links to these best practices are included where available and we're planning to publish more over time.
-- Before you start, [get an overview of SFI](secure-future-initiative-overview).
+Use SFI to inform prioritization and program sequencing, not as a separate implementation framework.
 
-## Protect identities and secrets
+- Start with the [SFI overview](secure-future-initiative-overview) for context and boundaries.
+- Use [SAF](/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-adoption-model) to organize your modernization journey.
+- Use [Zero Trust guidance](../zero-trust-overview) to align principles and architecture.
+- Use product and architecture documentation for implementation details.
 
-Initiatives under this pillar aim to reduce the risk of unauthorized access by implementing and enforcing standards to control user/app authentication and authorization, and to harden the identity and secrets infrastructure. The Microsoft SFI initiative work focuses on:
+## Pillar 1: Protect identities and secrets
 
-- Passwordless, phishing-resistant multifactor authentication (MFA) (FIDO2 passkeys, certificate-based auth) for all users.
-- Deprecation of passwords, SMS OTP, etc.
-- Replacement of static credentials with managed identities and Microsoft Entra Workload ID.
-- Storage of secrets in Azure Key Vault, key protection with Managed Hardware Security Module (HSM) with role-based access control (RBAC), network isolation, and access logs.
-- Automated key rotation and HSM-backed token signing.
-- Adoption of standard SDKs with supported identity libraries (MSAL, Microsoft.Identity.Web), and avoiding custom Json Web Token (JWT) validation.
-- Periodic scanning of code pipelines, and repos for leaked secrets.
+**Security outcome Microsoft prioritized:** Reduce unauthorized access risk from weak authentication, overprivilege, exposed secrets, and long-lived credentials.

 # Protect engineering systems in the Microsoft Secure Future Initiative (SFI) | Microsoft Learn
 
-The [Secure Future Initiative (SFI) initiative](secure-future-initiative-overview) launched in November 2023 as a multiyear effort to increasingly secure the way in which Microsoft designs, builds, tests, and operates its products and services.
+This pillar focuses on improving trust across software development, build, release, and supply chain systems.
 
-SFI architecture design focuses on a set of security principles that are adopted and integrated into Microsoft culture and governance. These security principles are applied to a set of focused engineering pillars by means of processes, standards, and continuous improvements.
+## Security outcome Microsoft prioritized
 
-This article summarizes the "Protect engineering systems" SFI pillar.
+Microsoft prioritized reducing systemic engineering risk by hardening source control, build pipelines, dependency governance, and software delivery integrity controls.
 
-## Before you start
+## What Microsoft prioritized
 
-- [Learn about](secure-future-initiative-overview#sfi-pillars-zero-trust-and-nist) the SFI pillars.
-- [Review and track the latest progress on pillar objectives](secure-future-initiative-whats-new#progress-on-pillar-objectives) in the SFI What's New article.
-- Learn about [Zero Trust principles](../zero-trust-overview), and [NIST CSF functions and categories](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/CSWP/NIST.CSWP.29.pdf).
-- [Get a list of NIST categories and acronyms](secure-future-initiative-overview#nist-functions) to help as you review the table in this article.
+- Better inventory and governance of engineering assets
+- Stronger controls for source code access
+- Secure-by-default pipeline standards
+- Tighter supply chain risk controls for dependencies and artifacts
+- Better security signal quality in engineering workflows
 
-## Pillar and objectives
+## Lessons from SFI implementation
 
-The "Protect engineering systems" pillar aims for strengthening security across development and engineering by operationationalizing the asset inventory, implementing Zero Trust principles, securing pipelines, and strengthening isolation and resiliency.
+- High-impact engineering risk reductions require coordinated identity, policy, and pipeline controls.
+- Standardized engineering patterns reduce control drift and improve response speed.
+- Secure supply chain outcomes depend on both technical controls and governance rigor.
 
-Microsoft objectives and Zero Trust/NIST mapping for this pillar are summarized in the following table.
